questions.title: A useful skill
questions.text: Describe a useful skill you learned outside school. You should say: what the skill is; who or what helped you learn it; how you have used it; and explain why it matters to you. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: An enjoyable journey
questions.text: Describe a journey you enjoyed. You should say: where you went; how you travelled; who you travelled with; and explain what made the journey enjoyable. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: Something you repaired
questions.text: Describe something you repaired or had repaired. You should say: what the object was; what was wrong with it; how it was repaired; and explain how you felt about the result. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: Learning throughout life
questions.text: Why do adults continue learning new skills? Should employers or individuals pay for this learning? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

Their dense feathers trap a layer of air, and a thick layer of fat lies beneath the skin. In the worst storms, thousands of birds huddle together, taking turns to move from the cold edge of the group to the warm centre.

questions.title: Lecture: The zip fastener
questions.text:

In 1913 the engineer Gideon Sundback produced a much better design, using interlocking teeth. The name zipper was first used for rubber boots that had the fastener, and only much later did zips become common on clothing.

They also eat dead leaves and produce casts that are rich in nutrients. Charles Darwin was so fascinated by them that he spent decades studying their behaviour.

An egg can weigh about a ____ (3) of the female's weight Lecturer: The kiwi, a flightless bird found only in New Zealand, is unusual in many ways. Its nostrils are at the tip of its long beak, which it uses to smell insects and worms underground. The female lays an extremely large egg, which can weigh about a fifth of her body weight.

questions.title: Lecture: Noise in offices
questions.text:

Main complaint: noise from phone ____ (2)

questions.title: Lecture: The Venus flytrap
questions.text:
Listen and complete the notes. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer. This is a short practice drill with synthesised playback. It grows naturally only in North and South ____ (1)
Insects provide the plant with ____ (2)
The trigger hairs must be touched ____ (3) Lecturer: The Venus flytrap grows naturally only in a small area of North and South Carolina in the United States. Its soil is poor in nutrients, so the plant catches insects to obtain nitrogen. The trap closes only when tiny trigger hairs are touched twice within about twenty seconds, which stops it closing on raindrops.

questions.title: Lecture: Morse code
questions.text:
Listen and complete the notes. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer. This is a short practice drill with synthesised playback. It was developed for the electric ____ (1)
The letter E is a single ____ (2)
The first long-distance message was sent to ____ (3) Lecturer: Morse code was developed in the 1830s and 1840s for use with the electric telegraph. Letters are represented by combinations of short and long signals, known as dots and dashes. The most common letters were given the shortest codes; the letter E, for example, is a single dot. In 1844 the first long-distance message was sent from Washington to Baltimore.

questions.title: Lecture: The first photographs
questions.text:
Listen and complete the notes. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer. This is a short practice drill with synthesised playback. The oldest surviving photograph shows the view from a ____ (1)
Its exposure took several ____ (2)
Daguerre announced his process in ____ (3) Lecturer: The oldest surviving photograph taken from nature was made in France in the 1820s by Nicephore Niepce. It shows the view from a window, and the exposure took at least several hours. In 1839 Louis Daguerre announced a process that produced sharp images in minutes rather than hours, and photography quickly became popular.

questions.text: Do you usually go to bed early or late? When was the last time you stayed up very late? Do you find it easy to get up after a late night? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Concentration
questions.text: Is it easy for you to concentrate when you study or work? What things distract you most? What helps you to focus? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Memory
questions.text: Do you have a good memory? What kind of things do you find easy to remember? What do you do to help you remember important things? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Teamwork
questions.text: Do you prefer to work alone or in a team? Did you do much group work at school? What makes a good team member? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Primary School
questions.text: What do you remember about your primary school? Who was your favourite teacher there? How is primary school different now from when you were a child? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Exams
questions.text: How do you usually prepare for exams? Do you feel nervous before an exam? Do you think exams are a fair way to test students? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Libraries
questions.text: How often do you visit a library? What did you use the library for when you were younger? Do you think libraries are still useful today? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Computers
questions.text: What do you use a computer for? When did you first learn to use a computer? Could you live without a computer? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: The Internet
questions.text: How much time do you spend online each day? What websites do you visit most often? How did you use the internet when you were younger? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Diaries and Journals
questions.text: Have you ever kept a diary or journal? Why do some people like to write down what happens each day? Do you use a planner to organise your time? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Letters and Postcards
questions.text: When did you last write a letter by hand? Do you ever send postcards when you travel? Do you think people will stop sending letters completely? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Magazines
questions.text: Do you read magazines? What kind of magazines are popular in your country? Do you prefer reading articles in print or online? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Poetry
questions.text: Did you learn any poems at school? Do you ever read poetry now? Is there a famous poet from your country? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Jokes and Laughter
questions.text: Do you like telling jokes? What kind of things make you laugh? Is it important to have a sense of humour? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Street Art
questions.text: Is there any street art or public art in your city? Do you think street art makes a city more attractive? Would you like to see more art in public places? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Handmade Things
questions.text: Have you ever made something by hand? Do you prefer handmade or factory-made products? Are traditional crafts popular in your country? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: Recycling
questions.text: Do you recycle at home? What kinds of things do people recycle where you live? Is recycling taught in schools in your country? Give natural answers with relevant detail. This is a short Part 1 practice drill, not a complete 4–5 minute interview.

questions.title: A Kind Act by a Stranger
questions.text: Describe a time when a stranger did something kind for you. You should say: where you were; who the stranger was; what they did; and explain how you felt about it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Street You Know Well
questions.text: Describe a street that you know well. You should say: where it is; what you can find there; how often you go there; and explain why you know it so well. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Piece of Good News
questions.text: Describe a piece of good news you received. You should say: what the news was; when you received it; who told you; and explain why it was good news for you. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Useful Online Course or Video
questions.text: Describe an online course or video that taught you something useful. You should say: what it was about; how you found it; what you learned from it; and explain why it was useful to you. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Were Very Busy
questions.text: Describe a time when you were very busy. You should say: when it was; what you had to do; how you managed your time; and explain how you felt during that time. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Person Who Is Good at Their Job
questions.text: Describe a person you know who is very good at their job. You should say: who the person is; what their job is; what they do in their work; and explain why you think they are good at it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Place Where You Like to Relax
questions.text: Describe a place where you like to relax. You should say: where it is; how often you go there; what you do there; and explain why it helps you relax. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Long Walk You Took
questions.text: Describe a long walk you once took. You should say: where you walked; who you were with; what you saw on the way; and explain how you felt at the end of the walk. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Borrowed Something
questions.text: Describe a time when you borrowed something from someone. You should say: what you borrowed; who you borrowed it from; why you needed it; and explain how you felt about borrowing it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: An Important Decision Made by Your Family
questions.text: Describe an important decision that your family made together. You should say: what the decision was; when it was made; how your family reached the decision; and explain how it affected you. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Skill You Would Like to Learn
questions.text: Describe a skill you would like to learn in the future. You should say: what the skill is; how you would learn it; how long it might take; and explain why you want to learn it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Saw a Beautiful View
questions.text: Describe a time when you saw a beautiful view. You should say: where you were; what you could see; who you were with; and explain why the view was so memorable. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Club or Group You Belong To
questions.text: Describe a club or group that you belong to or used to belong to. You should say: what kind of group it is; how you joined it; what the members do together; and explain why you like being part of it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Small Business You Know
questions.text: Describe a small business that you know. You should say: what the business is; where it is; who runs it; and explain why you think it is successful or unsuccessful. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Had to Be Patient
questions.text: Describe a time when you had to be patient. You should say: when it was; what you were waiting for; what you did while you waited; and explain how you managed to stay patient. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Film You Would Watch Again
questions.text: Describe a film you would like to watch again. You should say: what the film is; when you first watched it; what it is about; and explain why you would like to watch it again. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Tradition in Your Country
questions.text: Describe a traditional custom or practice in your country. You should say: what the tradition is; when it takes place; what people do; and explain why it is important to people. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Taught Yourself Something
questions.text: Describe something you taught yourself to do. You should say: what you learned; why you decided to learn it; how you taught yourself; and explain how you felt when you were able to do it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: An Outdoor Activity You Enjoyed
questions.text: Describe an outdoor activity that you enjoyed doing. You should say: what the activity was; where you did it; who you did it with; and explain why you enjoyed it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Received Good Service
questions.text: Describe a time when you received very good service in a shop or restaurant. You should say: where you were; what happened; who served you; and explain why you think the service was so good. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Goal You Hope to Achieve
questions.text: Describe a goal you hope to achieve in the next few years. You should say: what the goal is; when you set it; what you are doing to achieve it; and explain why this goal matters to you. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Were Surprised
questions.text: Describe a time when something surprised you. You should say: when it happened; where you were; what the surprise was; and explain how you reacted. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Room You Remember From Childhood
questions.text: Describe a room you remember from your childhood. You should say: where the room was; what it looked like; what you did there; and explain why you remember it so well. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: An Interesting Job
questions.text: Describe a job that you think would be interesting to do. You should say: what the job is; what people in this job do; what skills it needs; and explain why you think it would be interesting. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Shared Something
questions.text: Describe a time when you shared something with other people. You should say: what you shared; who you shared it with; why you decided to share it; and explain how you felt about sharing it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Public Event You Attended
questions.text: Describe a public event that you attended, such as a concert, match or show. You should say: what the event was; where and when it took place; who you went with; and explain what made it memorable. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Solved a Problem
questions.text: Describe a time when you solved a difficult problem. You should say: what the problem was; when it happened; how you solved it; and explain how you felt when the problem was solved. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Healthy Habit You Have
questions.text: Describe a healthy habit that you have. You should say: what the habit is; when you started it; how often you do it; and explain how it has helped you. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Famous Place in Your Country
questions.text: Describe a famous place in your country that you have visited. You should say: where it is; why it is famous; what you did there; and explain what you thought of it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Apologised
questions.text: Describe a time when you apologised to someone. You should say: who you apologised to; what had happened; how you apologised; and explain how the other person reacted. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Child You Know
questions.text: Describe a child you know well. You should say: who the child is; how you know them; what they are like; and explain how you feel about spending time with them. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: Something You Bought Recently
questions.text: Describe something you bought recently that you are pleased with. You should say: what it is; where you bought it; why you chose it; and explain why you are pleased with it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Worked With Others
questions.text: Describe a time when you worked with other people to complete a task. You should say: what the task was; who you worked with; what your role was; and explain whether you enjoyed working in this way. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Place With Lots of Water
questions.text: Describe a place you have visited where there was a lot of water, such as a waterfall or coast. You should say: where it was; when you went there; what you did there; and explain how you felt about the place. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Tried New Food
questions.text: Describe a time when you tried food you had never eaten before. You should say: what the food was; where you tried it; who you were with; and explain whether you liked it and why. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Useful Object in Your Home
questions.text: Describe an object in your home that you find very useful. You should say: what the object is; how long you have had it; how you use it; and explain why it is so useful. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Gave Someone Advice
questions.text: Describe a time when you gave someone advice. You should say: who you advised; what the situation was; what advice you gave; and explain whether the advice was helpful. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Historical Period You Find Interesting
questions.text: Describe a period in history that you find interesting. You should say: what the period is; how you learned about it; what happened at that time; and explain why it interests you. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Stayed in an Unusual Place
questions.text: Describe a time when you stayed somewhere unusual. You should say: where you stayed; why you stayed there; what the place was like; and explain how you felt about staying there. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Person Who Speaks Another Language Well
questions.text: Describe a person you know who speaks a foreign language well. You should say: who the person is; which language they speak; how they learned it; and explain what you think of their ability. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Missed an Appointment
questions.text: Describe a time when you missed an important appointment. You should say: what the appointment was; why you missed it; what happened as a result; and explain how you felt about it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Sport You Enjoy Watching
questions.text: Describe a sport that you enjoy watching. You should say: what the sport is; where you watch it; who you watch it with; and explain why you enjoy watching it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Moved to a New Place
questions.text: Describe a time when you moved to a new home or a new area. You should say: where you moved to; why you moved; what the new place was like; and explain how you felt about the move. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Piece of Clothing Someone Gave You
questions.text: Describe a piece of clothing that someone gave you. You should say: what it is; who gave it to you; when you wear it; and explain how you feel about it. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: An Exciting Book You Read
questions.text: Describe an exciting book that you have read. You should say: what the book was; when you read it; what it was about; and explain why you found it exciting. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time You Were Very Tired
questions.text: Describe a time when you felt very tired. You should say: when it was; why you were so tired; what you did about it; and explain how you felt afterwards. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Place You Would Like to Visit Again
questions.text: Describe a place you have visited that you would like to visit again. You should say: where it is; when you went there; what you did there; and explain why you would like to return. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Time Technology Did Not Work
questions.text: Describe a time when a piece of technology did not work when you needed it. You should say: what the technology was; what you were trying to do; what you did when it failed; and explain how you felt about the situation. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Good Friend From School
questions.text: Describe a friend you made at school. You should say: who the friend is; how you met; what you did together; and explain why you became good friends. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: A Change That Would Improve Your Town
questions.text: Describe a change that would improve the town or city where you live. You should say: what the change is; how it could be made; who would benefit from it; and explain why you think it would be an improvement. You have one minute to prepare and may make notes. Speak for one to two minutes.

questions.title: Kindness in Modern Society
questions.text: Do you think people today are less kind to strangers than in the past? Why are people sometimes unwilling to help others in public? How can parents teach children to be kind? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Streets and Public Spaces
questions.text: What makes a street pleasant to walk along? Should city centres be closed to cars? Who should pay for the upkeep of public spaces? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Good and Bad News
questions.text: Why does the news focus so much on negative events? Should news organisations report more good news? How do people usually share important news in your country now? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Online Learning
questions.text: What are the advantages of learning online compared with learning in a classroom? Which subjects are difficult to learn online? Will online learning replace traditional schools in the future? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Busy Lives
questions.text: Why do people seem to be busier today than in the past? Is being busy a sign of success? How can people balance work and free time better? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Success at Work
questions.text: What qualities help people succeed in their jobs? Is it more important to enjoy your job or to earn a high salary? Should companies reward experience or results? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Stress and Relaxation
questions.text: Why do so many people feel stressed nowadays? Do people in cities find it harder to relax than people in the countryside? Should employers help their staff to manage stress? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Walking and Health
questions.text: Why do fewer people walk to work or school than in the past? How could towns encourage people to walk more? Is walking a good form of exercise for everyone? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Sharing and Borrowing
questions.text: Why are sharing schemes, such as bike or tool sharing, becoming popular? Are people more willing to share things with friends or with strangers? Could sharing reduce the amount people buy? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Family Decision-Making
questions.text: Who usually makes important decisions in families in your country? Should children be involved in family decisions? How has decision-making in families changed over the last few decades? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Learning New Skills as an Adult
questions.text: Why do some adults stop learning new things? Is it harder to learn a new skill as an adult than as a child? Should governments pay for adults to retrain? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Natural Beauty and Tourism
questions.text: Why do people travel to see natural scenery? Can tourism damage places of natural beauty? How can popular natural sites be protected? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Clubs and Communities
questions.text: Why do people join clubs and societies? Are young people less interested in joining groups than older people? How do communities benefit from local clubs? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Small Businesses and Large Companies
questions.text: What difficulties do small businesses face today? Why do some people prefer to buy from small local shops? Should governments support small businesses? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Patience and Modern Life
questions.text: Has technology made people less patient? In what situations is patience most important? Can patience be learned? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Cinema and Streaming
questions.text: Why do people still go to the cinema when they can stream films at home? Do films influence the way people behave? Should governments fund their country’s film industry? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Cultural Traditions
questions.text: Why are some traditions disappearing? Should young people be expected to keep traditions alive? How can traditions be adapted to modern life? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Self-Teaching
questions.text: What are the benefits of teaching yourself a skill? What are the limits of learning without a teacher? Has the internet made teachers less important? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Outdoor Activities and Children
questions.text: Do children spend less time outdoors than in the past? What are the benefits of outdoor play for children? Should schools organise more outdoor activities? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Customer Service
questions.text: What makes good customer service? Has customer service improved or got worse in recent years? Will robots and computers replace people in customer service? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Personal Goals
questions.text: Why is it important for people to set goals? Do young people today have different goals from their parents’ generation? What should people do if they fail to reach a goal? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Surprises and Routine
questions.text: Do people generally prefer routine or surprises? Why do some people dislike change? Is it good for children to have a strict routine? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Homes and Childhood
questions.text: How do the homes children grow up in affect them? Should children have their own bedroom? How have family homes changed in your country? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Choosing a Career
questions.text: What influences people’s choice of career? Should young people follow their parents’ advice about careers? Is it better to choose a career early or to try different jobs first? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Generosity
questions.text: Why are some people more generous than others? Is it better to give money or time to charity? Should rich people be expected to give more to society? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Public Events
questions.text: Why do people enjoy attending live events? Should large public events be free for everyone? What problems can big events cause for local residents? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Problem-Solving
questions.text: Is problem-solving a skill that schools should teach directly? Do people solve problems better alone or in groups? How has technology changed the way people solve everyday problems? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Healthy Habits
questions.text: Why do people find it difficult to change unhealthy habits? Who is most responsible for people’s health: individuals, families or governments? Should unhealthy food be taxed? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Famous Places and Overtourism
questions.text: Why do some tourist sites become extremely crowded? Should the number of visitors to famous places be limited? How do local people feel about large numbers of tourists? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Apologies and Forgiveness
questions.text: Why do some people find it difficult to apologise? Is it important for public figures to apologise for their mistakes? Are apologies viewed differently in different cultures? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Children and Responsibility
questions.text: At what age should children start to have responsibilities at home? Are children today given too much freedom? How can parents teach children to manage money? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Consumer Choices
questions.text: Why do people buy things they do not need? Does advertising make people less satisfied with what they have? Should people try to buy fewer new products? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Cooperation at Work
questions.text: Why do some teams work better than others? Is competition between colleagues good or bad for a company? What makes a good team leader? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Water and the Environment
questions.text: Why is access to clean water still a problem in many places? How can individuals save water at home? Should water be more expensive to encourage people to use less? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Food and Culture
questions.text: Why do people enjoy trying food from other countries? Is traditional food becoming less popular with young people? Should schools teach children how to cook? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Objects and Design
questions.text: What makes an everyday object well designed? Why do people replace things that still work? Should manufacturers be required to make products that last longer? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Advice and Experience
questions.text: Who do young people turn to for advice nowadays? Is advice from older people always useful? Why do people sometimes ignore good advice? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Learning From History
questions.text: Why is it important to study history? Should history lessons focus on local or world history? Can people really learn from mistakes made in the past? Discuss reasons, comparisons and examples. This is a two-minute discussion drill; a full examiner-led Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes.

questions.title: Unusual Places to Stay
questions.text: Why are unusual places to stay becoming popular with travellers? Is travelling more about the experience or the destination? questions.text: Many languages are borrowing more and more words from English. Why is this happening? Is it a threat to those languages? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Wealthy People and Charity
questions.text: Some very wealthy people give large sums of money to charity. Why do they do this? Should the rich be required to give more of their wealth to others? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Adults Leaving Sports Clubs
questions.text: Fewer adults are joining local sports clubs than in the past. Why is this happening? What can be done to encourage more adults to take part? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Emojis Instead of Words
questions.text: People increasingly use emojis and other symbols instead of words when they write messages. Why is this? Is it having a negative effect on language? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Holidays at Home
questions.text: Instead of travelling, many people now spend their holidays at home or close to where they live. Why are people doing this? Is it a positive or negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Forgotten Playground Games
questions.text: Many traditional games that children used to play together are no longer played. Why is this happening? Does it matter? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Diets From the Internet
questions.text: Many people follow diets that they have found on the internet. Why do people do this? What are the risks? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Women in Senior Positions
questions.text: The number of women in senior positions in business and government is increasing. Why is this happening? What further changes are needed? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Electronic Toys
questions.text: Many children's toys are now electronic rather than simple objects such as dolls and wooden blocks. Why has this change happened? Is it a positive or negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Art Made With AI
questions.text: Some artists now use artificial intelligence to help them create their work. Why do they use it? Can work produced in this way be called art? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Remote Workers in Small Towns
questions.text: People who can work remotely are moving from large cities to small towns. Why are they moving? How does this affect the towns they move to? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Teenagers With Part-Time Jobs
questions.text: Many teenagers have a part-time job while they are still at school. Why do teenagers work? Is this a positive or negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Celebrities Entering Politics
questions.text: A number of celebrities from sport and entertainment have become politicians. Why do voters support them? Is this a positive or negative development? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Loyal Sports Fans
questions.text: Many people support the same sports team passionately throughout their lives. Why are people so loyal to their teams? Is this kind of loyalty a good thing? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Paying for Online Content
questions.text: More people are paying subscriptions for online news, music and films. Why are people willing to pay? Will free online content disappear in the future? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.title: Buying Lottery Tickets
questions.text: Millions of people buy lottery tickets every week, even though their chances of winning are very small. Why do people buy them? Should governments run national lotteries? Give reasons for your answer and include relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words. Suggested time: 40 minutes.

questions.text: Do you prefer to plan your weekends in advance or decide what to do on the day? Why? Original, unofficial practice task.

questions.text:
Describe a time when the weather caused you to change a plan.

You should say:
- what you had planned

- what you did instead
and explain how you felt about the change.

You have 1 minute to prepare. Speak for 1-2 minutes. Original, unofficial practice task.

questions.text: Is it better for organisations to prepare several alternative plans or concentrate on making one plan work well? Original, unofficial practice task.

questions.title: Public Funding for Nuclear Fusion Energy
questions.text:
Governments should allocate billions of dollars of public research funding to developing commercial nuclear fusion energy.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. As the world grapples with escalating energy demands and the catastrophic consequences of climate change, the search for abundant, zero-emission baseload power is paramount. I strongly agree that national governments should commit billions of dollars in public research funding to accelerate the development of commercial nuclear fusion power.

The primary justification for funding fusion research is its unparalleled potential as the ultimate clean energy source for human civilization. Unlike fossil fuels, nuclear fusion produces zero greenhouse gas emissions or toxic atmospheric pollutants. Unlike conventional nuclear fission, fusion does not produce high-level long-lived radioactive waste, relies on abundant isotopes such as deuterium extracted from seawater, and carries negligible risk of catastrophic runaway meltdowns. If successfully developed, commercial fusion could provide reliable baseload electricity to complement intermittent renewable systems and support power-intensive industries. Given the urgent need to decarbonize global energy systems, exploring fusion technology represents a valuable avenue for long-term energy security.

Critics often argue that nuclear fusion has absorbed massive public expenditures for decades without delivering commercial electricity, famously remaining far from commercialization. They contend that public funds should be spent deploying proven renewable technologies like solar panels and wind turbines today. While deploying current renewables is vital, solar and wind suffer from weather intermittency and storage limitations. Recent experimental milestones have demonstrated scientific net energy gain under laboratory conditions, suggesting that further progress is attainable with sustained commitment, even though formidable engineering hurdles remain.

In conclusion, while nuclear fusion is not an immediate substitute for existing clean technologies, allocating public funding to fusion research is a prudent long-term investment in diversifying future zero-carbon energy options. Allocating substantial public funding to fusion development is a visionary investment in a prosperous, carbon-free future.

questions.title: Mandatory Water Efficiency in Buildings
questions.text:
Building codes should mandate rainwater harvesting systems and low-flow plumbing fixtures in all newly constructed residential properties.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. Freshwater scarcity is becoming one of the most critical environmental challenges of the twenty-first century, exacerbated by population growth and climatic shifts. I strongly agree that municipal building regulations should legally mandate rainwater collection systems and low-flow sanitary fixtures in all new residential developments.

The primary argument for mandatory water efficiency in construction is the conservation of municipal water supplies and the reduction of urban stormwater runoff. Domestic households consume immense quantities of treated potable water for non-drinking purposes, such as toilet flushing, laundry, and garden irrigation. Installing rainwater harvesting tanks allows homes to capture precipitation for these domestic tasks, directly reducing pressure on reservoirs and subterranean aquifers during prolonged droughts. Simultaneously, low-flow aerated faucets and dual-flush toilets cut household water consumption substantially without compromising user comfort. Capturing rainwater on-site also reduces peak runoff volumes, mitigating urban flash flooding and easing strain on municipal storm sewer networks.

Property developers frequently object that mandatory water fixtures increase upfront construction expenses and raise home purchase prices. While installing storage tanks and specialized plumbing does entail modest initial capital outlays, these costs are rapidly recouped through lower monthly municipal water utility bills. Over the operational life of a home, water efficiency features deliver substantial financial savings for homeowners while safeguarding the regional environment.

To conclude, mandatory residential water conservation standards represent a practical and necessary policy. Incorporating rainwater harvesting and efficient plumbing into building codes protects vital water reserves and creates sustainable, flood-resilient communities.

questions.title: Attending University Locally versus Moving Away
questions.text:
It is more advantageous for young adults to attend university in their hometown while living with parents than to move to an institution in another city.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. Completing a tertiary degree is a major developmental milestone, and prospective students often face the choice between staying in their hometown or relocating to an institution elsewhere. Although staying home offers clear financial benefits, I believe that moving to a university in a different city provides far superior personal, academic, and professional advantages.

The foremost benefit of moving away from home is the rapid development of independence, self-reliance, and practical life competencies. When students live independently in dormitories or shared flats, they must manage their own personal finances, cook meals, organize household schedules, and resolve conflicts with housemates without parental intervention. This autonomy builds emotional maturity, resilience, and adaptability, which are essential attributes for navigating adult life and professional careers. Furthermore, studying in a major metropolitan educational hub exposes young adults to diverse cultures, broadening their worldview and establishing expansive professional networks that extend far beyond their childhood community.

Admittedly, attending a local university while living with family significantly reduces accommodation and living expenditures, shielding students from crippling debt. For economically disadvantaged families, this cost-saving can make the difference between pursuing higher education or entering the low-wage labor market. However, students who relocate can offset expenses through university scholarships, part-time campus employment, and student loan programs, investments that are rewarded by the accelerated personal growth that independent living cultivates.

In conclusion, while local study offers short-term economic comfort, moving to another city to pursue a degree fosters lifelong independence and self-confidence. The personal growth gained from independent living far outweighs the financial convenience of staying home.

questions.title: Autonomous Cargo Drone Delivery in Rural Regions
questions.text:
Governments should permit and subsidize autonomous aerial drones to deliver medical supplies and consumer goods to remote rural communities.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. Access to essential goods and emergency medical supplies in remote, mountainous, and rural communities is frequently obstructed by rugged terrain and deteriorating road infrastructure. I strongly support the proposal for governments to authorize and subsidize autonomous cargo drones to service isolated rural populations.

The most compelling justification for autonomous drone transport is life-saving speed and operational reliability in healthcare logistics. In remote rural valleys, transporting blood supplies, antivenoms, vaccines, and emergency pharmaceuticals by ground vehicle can take hours or even days over treacherous unpaved roads, particularly during seasonal floods or landslides. Autonomous cargo drones bypass terrestrial obstacles entirely, traveling in direct aerial flight paths to deliver critical medical cargo in minutes. Pilot programs in rugged regions globally have already demonstrated that drone delivery drastically cuts infant mortality and improves emergency trauma outcomes. Furthermore, for regular consumer packages, electric drones eliminate diesel delivery truck emissions, providing an eco-friendly freight solution.

Critics, however, raise valid concerns regarding mid-air collisions, acoustic noise pollution, and visual intrusion in tranquil rural landscapes. They fear that swarms of commercial drones will endanger low-flying light aircraft and disturb wildlife. These risks can be managed effectively through strict aviation corridor regulations, mandatory automated collision-avoidance transponders, and altitude limits. Drones should be designated specific flight paths and noise thresholds to protect rural tranquility.

In conclusion, autonomous aerial delivery bridges the geographic divide between urban centers and isolated communities. Authorizing and subsidizing cargo drones saves rural lives, promotes regional equity, and modernizes logistics for remote populations.

questions.title: Maritime Freight Route Electrification
questions.text:
International maritime authorities should mandate that all coastal cargo vessels switch to battery-electric or hydrogen propulsion by 2035.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. Commercial shipping transports the vast majority of global trade, but the maritime industry remains one of the world's most heavily polluting sectors. I strongly agree that international maritime regulators should mandate that coastal cargo vessels transition entirely to battery-electric or green hydrogen propulsion systems within the coming decade.

The primary argument for mandatory zero-emission shipping is the urgent need to eliminate toxic port air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Traditional maritime vessels burn unrefined heavy fuel oil, which releases massive quantities of sulfur oxides, nitrogen oxides, and carcinogenic particulate matter directly into coastal shipping lanes and densely populated port cities. These maritime emissions cause thousands of premature respiratory deaths annually and contribute significantly to ocean acidification and global warming. Mandating zero-emission battery and hydrogen powertrains on coastal shipping routes—where vessels travel predictable distances between domestic ports—is technically feasible with current technology and will immediately transform port air quality and marine ecology.

Shipowners and maritime logistics operators protest that retrofitting existing fleets and building hydrogen bunkering infrastructure will require colossal capital investments, warning that freight shipping rates will surge. While initial transition costs are significant, coastal electric vessels exhibit drastically lower operating and maintenance expenses than diesel engines, saving money over vessel lifespans. Furthermore, international regulatory deadlines are precisely what is needed to mobilize private investment and drive technological economies of scale in marine battery manufacturing.

In conclusion, burning toxic fossil fuels along our coastlines is an obsolete, hazardous practice. Enforcing a strict zero-emission deadline for coastal cargo ships protects coastal public health and spearheads maritime decarbonization.

questions.title: Subsidising Electric Agricultural Machinery
questions.text:
Governments should subsidize agricultural farmers to replace diesel-powered tractors and harvesters with battery-electric machinery.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. The agricultural sector is heavily reliant on internal combustion diesel engines to operate heavy machinery, including tractors, combine harvesters, and irrigation pumps. I strongly support the implementation of government subsidies to assist farmers in transitioning from fossil-fuel machinery to battery-electric agricultural equipment.

The foremost justification for subsidizing electric farm machinery is the substantial reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and toxic particulate air pollution. Heavy diesel engines emit massive volumes of carbon dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and black carbon soot directly over food crops and rural communities. Electric agricultural tractors produce zero point-of-use emissions, improving local air quality for farmworkers and shielding crops from soot deposition. When charged using on-farm solar panels or rural wind turbines, electric machinery enables farms to become self-sufficient, carbon-neutral operations. Furthermore, electric motors possess significantly fewer moving parts than diesel engines, drastically reducing recurring maintenance expenses and oil replacement costs for farmers over the lifespan of the equipment.

Agricultural trade associations contend that electric machinery is currently prohibitively expensive and that battery technology lacks the energy density required for continuous, heavy plowing during tight harvest windows. They fear that frequent recharging downtime would disrupt seasonal planting. While high battery weight and charging infrastructure remain challenges, modern electric farm tractors feature swappable battery packs and fast-charging systems that eliminate operational downtime. Public subsidies are precisely what is needed to lower initial capital costs and stimulate domestic charging infrastructure in rural agricultural basins.

In conclusion, decarbonizing agriculture is vital for meeting global climate targets. Subsidizing electric agricultural machinery lowers farm operating costs, protects rural health, and accelerates the transition to sustainable farming.

questions.title: Instantaneous Communication and Societal Patience
questions.text:
The widespread availability of instantaneous digital messaging and high-speed internet has fundamentally reduced human patience and emotional resilience.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. In today's hyper-connected society, communication, entertainment, and commercial services are accessible in fractions of a second via smartphones. I firmly agree with the proposition that continuous reliance on instantaneous digital services has eroded human patience and weakened emotional resilience across contemporary society.

The central argument supporting this view is the neurobiological conditioning toward immediate gratification fostered by digital platforms. When individuals grow accustomed to receiving instant message replies, one-click deliveries, and on-demand streaming entertainment, their tolerance for delay, ambiguity, and natural friction declines dramatically. People become visibly agitated when website loading speeds drop by seconds or when replies are delayed by minutes. This diminished patience directly impairs deep cognitive focus and sustained intellectual effort; individuals increasingly abandon demanding tasks, such as reading complex literature or mastering musical instruments, because these pursuits require prolonged, unrewarded persistence. Over time, the inability to endure delays undermines attentional stamina.

Furthermore, instantaneous gratification damages emotional resilience in personal relationships and professional careers. Real life cannot be streamlined with a digital tap; building lasting marriages, raising children, and advancing in a career require enduring conflict, disappointment, and slow, incremental progress. When people conditioned for immediate results encounter unavoidable setbacks or interpersonal friction, they experience intense frustration, anxiety, and premature despair, lacking the emotional stamina to persevere through difficulty.

While optimists argue that rapid communication enhances organizational efficiency, speed must not be confused with emotional health. In conclusion, ubiquitous instant gratification has undeniably diminished societal patience, making the deliberate cultivation of endurance and contemplative slowness an urgent personal necessity.

questions.title: Employee Choice in Flexible Working Hours
questions.text:
Companies should allow full-time employees to determine their own working hours rather than enforcing fixed core business schedules.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. The conventional nine-to-five office schedule was conceived during the industrial manufacturing era to coordinate assembly-line production. In today's digital knowledge economy, I strongly agree that companies should permit full-time employees to determine their own working hours rather than enforcing rigid fixed schedules.

The primary justification for autonomous scheduling is the significant enhancement of employee productivity and cognitive performance. Human biological chronotypes vary substantially; some individuals reach peak intellectual focus in the early morning hours, while others perform best late at night. Forcing all workers into identical operating schedules forces many to work during biological downtime, producing chronic mental fatigue and mediocre output. Granting workers temporal autonomy enables them to align demanding tasks with their natural peak energy periods, yielding higher quality work in shorter timeframes. Furthermore, flexible hours allow employees to balance parental duties, medical appointments, and commuting around peak traffic congestion, substantially reducing stress and elevating job satisfaction and company retention.

Skeptics, however, contend that unregulated working hours hinder inter-departmental collaboration, delay emergency client responses, and make project management chaotic. They fear that teams cannot coordinate when members are online at disparate times. However, modern asynchronous collaboration tools, shared digital project boards, and brief designated weekly synchronization windows allow teams to collaborate seamlessly without requiring synchronous presence during every working hour. Mature organizations evaluate tangible outcomes and project milestones rather than hours spent at a desk.

In conclusion, rigid corporate schedules are an outdated relic of the industrial past. Granting employees the freedom to choose their working hours unleashes individual productivity, fosters trust, and creates an adaptable corporate culture.

questions.title: Natural Artistic Genius versus Deliberate Practice
questions.text:
Exceptional achievement in creative arts such as painting and music is primarily the result of disciplined deliberate practice rather than innate talent.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. The origins of extraordinary artistic mastery have long fascinated educators, psychologists, and the general public. While natural aptitude often provides an initial spark, I firmly agree that world-class achievement in painting, music, and sculpture is overwhelmingly the product of thousands of hours of disciplined, deliberate practice.

The foremost evidence supporting the primacy of deliberate practice is the neurological and technical complexity inherent in artistic mastery. Virtuoso musicians and master painters are not born with pre-programmed motor dexterity or color perception; these capabilities develop through years of rigorous, repetitive training. Deliberate practice involves setting specific technical objectives, receiving continuous expert feedback, and methodically correcting errors. Even prodigies such as Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart underwent intensive, daily musical instruction from early childhood under his father's strict supervision before composing masterworks in adulthood. Cognitive neuroscience demonstrates that sustained practice physically reorganizes neural pathways and increases myelin insulation along nerve fibers, enabling the lightning-fast finger coordination and expressive nuance that spectators mistake for effortless innate genius.

Proponents of innate talent argue that thousands of individuals practice instruments for decades without ever achieving greatness, suggesting that an inborn genetic gift is indispensable. However, mere mindless repetition is not equivalent to deliberate practice. Most amateurs practice passively without seeking rigorous critique or expanding their comfort zones. What separates masters from average practitioners is not mysterious genetics, but an exceptional capacity for sustained, focused, and self-critical labor over many years.

In conclusion, while innate interest may initiate the artistic journey, extraordinary achievement is forged through relentless, disciplined practice. Believing in innate genius diminishes the immense dedication required to attain true artistic mastery.

questions.title: Weighting Teaching Quality in Universities
questions.text:
Universities should evaluate and promote academic faculty members primarily on the quality of their classroom teaching rather than on their published research.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. In contemporary higher education, academic career advancement and tenure decisions are overwhelmingly governed by the quantity and prestige of published research papers. I strongly agree that universities should reform this model and evaluate faculty primarily on the quality of their classroom teaching and pedagogical mentorship.

The primary justification for prioritizing teaching quality is fulfilling the fundamental institutional obligation to undergraduate and graduate students. Students invest substantial tuition fees and years of their lives in university education, expecting inspiring, rigorous, and personalized instruction that prepares them for professional careers and civic life. Under the current publish-or-perish regime, professors frequently treat teaching as an unwelcome distraction from laboratory research and grant writing, delegating lectures to inexperienced graduate assistants or delivering uninspired, outdated monologues. Reorienting tenure evaluations toward teaching excellence incentivizes professors to adopt interactive pedagogies, design engaging curricula, and provide meaningful individual mentorship, dramatically enhancing student intellectual development and academic retention.

University administrators often argue that research publications generate institutional prestige, attract high-value commercial patents, and secure external government research grants that finance university operations. While cutting-edge scientific research is undeniably vital, universities can easily maintain specialized research tracks alongside dedicated teaching professorships. Teaching quality should not be relegated to second-class status. After all, excellent teaching directly inspires the next generation of researchers who will conduct future discoveries.

In conclusion, a university's greatest legacy lies in the intellect, character, and capability of its graduates. Evaluating faculty primarily on teaching excellence restores educational integrity and ensures that students receive the transformative education they deserve.

questions.title: Print Journalism versus Digital News Portals
questions.text:
Traditional print newspapers provide a more reliable and balanced understanding of current events than digital news websites and social media portals.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. The rise of the digital internet has precipitated a dramatic decline in the readership of traditional printed newspapers, with most citizens consuming news via digital portals and social feeds. Despite the convenience of digital media, I firmly agree that print newspapers offer a substantially more reliable, balanced, and thoughtful understanding of current affairs.

The foremost advantage of print journalism is the editorial discipline and thorough fact-checking enforced by publication deadlines. Printed newspapers operate on a deliberate twenty-four-hour editorial cycle. Journalists and professional copy editors possess the time to verify sources, cross-examine evidence, and provide historical context before ink hits paper. In stark contrast, digital news platforms operate under relentless twenty-four-seven competition for immediate clicks, incentivizing the publication of unverified rumors, sensationalist headlines, and emotionally polarizing commentary designed to attract digital advertising revenue. Print media filters out chaotic breaking noise, delivering coherent, verified analysis that respects readers' intelligence.

Furthermore, the physical format of a newspaper prevents the algorithmic echo chambers that plague digital consumers. When readers open a broadsheet newspaper, they encounter diverse articles on foreign diplomacy, domestic economics, science, and the arts that they would never have deliberately searched for online. Digital platforms, by contrast, use opaque algorithms to serve content that reinforces users' preexisting prejudices, narrowing their worldview. Print newspapers provide an editorially curated, shared civic reality essential for democratic consensus.

In conclusion, while digital media offers immediate speed, print journalism provides depth, accountability, and comprehensive perspective. Engaging with printed newspapers cultivates a more mature and well-rounded understanding of global events.

questions.title: Hiring Generalists versus Technical Specialists
questions.text:
Large organizations should prioritize hiring generalists with broad problem-solving capabilities rather than narrow technical specialists.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. Modern corporations and public agencies operate in an era characterized by volatile market shifts, rapid technological disruption, and cross-disciplinary challenges. In this dynamic environment, I strongly agree that organizations should prioritize hiring versatile generalists who possess broad problem-solving skills rather than narrow technical specialists.

The primary merit of hiring generalists is their intellectual agility, cognitive adaptability, and ability to connect disparate ideas. Technical specialists often view corporate challenges through the rigid lens of their specific discipline, developing intellectual blind spots that prevent creative breakthroughs. In contrast, generalists possess diverse knowledge across multiple domains, enabling them to synthesize information from marketing, engineering, and psychology to solve multifaceted organizational problems. Furthermore, in an economy where specific software languages and technical tools become obsolete every few years, generalists excel at learning new skills rapidly, making them far more resilient and valuable during corporate pivots and restructuring.

Proponents of specialization argue that complex modern fields, such as advanced artificial intelligence, corporate tax law, and biomedical engineering, require deep, specialized technical expertise that generalists cannot provide. While deep technical knowledge is undeniably necessary for executing specific complex tasks, organizations can easily contract external technical experts or employ specialized teams supervised by generalist leaders. Without broad thinkers who understand overall strategic context, ethical implications, and human dynamics, specialized technical solutions often fail to integrate into real-world business operations.

In conclusion, while specialists perform vital technical execution, generalists provide the strategic vision, adaptability, and cross-functional leadership essential for long-term organizational success. Prioritizing generalist talent builds adaptable, future-proof organizations.

questions.title: Relocating Government Agencies to Regional Towns
questions.text:
National governments should relocate major administrative ministries and civil service departments out of capital cities into regional towns.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. In most nations, political power, administrative civil service jobs, and public expenditure are overwhelmingly concentrated in a single crowded capital metropolis. I strongly agree that national governments should decentralize governance by relocating major ministries and administrative agencies into regional provincial towns.

The primary justification for decentralizing government ministries is stimulating regional economic growth and reducing geographic inequality. Capital cities often suffer from extreme housing hyperinflation, paralyzing traffic gridlock, and overloaded public infrastructure, while regional towns experience economic stagnation, youth depopulation, and decaying services. Dispersing large government departments—such as agriculture, transportation, and environmental agencies—into provincial centers infuses regional economies with thousands of stable, high-paying public sector jobs. These civil servants spend money on local housing, hospitality, and retail, creating a powerful economic multiplier effect that revitalizes regional communities and stems the brain drain of educated youth to the capital.

Critics contend that dispersing government ministries undermines administrative coordination, increases travel expenses for inter-agency meetings, and faces resistance from civil servants who refuse to relocate away from capital cultural amenities. While physical relocation requires logistical adjustments, contemporary high-speed teleconferencing, collaborative cloud platforms, and modern rail networks make daily face-to-face meetings in the capital completely unnecessary. Furthermore, policy makers who live and work among regional citizens develop a far more grounded understanding of national challenges than bureaucrats insulated inside an elite capital bubble.

In conclusion, decentralizing government departments revitalizes neglected regional economies while easing capital congestion. Relocating public administration promotes geographic fairness and connects government directly to the people it serves.

questions.title: Mandatory Microchip Identification for Pets
questions.text:
Governments should legally mandate subcutaneous microchip identification for all domestic dogs and cats and impose fines on unregistered pet owners.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. Domestic companion animals bring immense joy to millions of households, but stray, abandoned, and lost pets pose significant animal welfare and public safety challenges in urban communities. I firmly agree that governments should mandate permanent subcutaneous microchip registration for all domestic dogs and cats and enforce strict fines on non-compliant pet owners.

The foremost benefit of mandatory microchipping is the rapid reunification of lost animals with their families and the reduction of euthanasia rates in animal shelters. Traditional collar tags frequently fall off, break, or become illegible when animals become lost or escape during storms. An inert, rice-sized subcutaneous microchip contains a unique identification code scannable by any veterinary clinic or municipal animal control officer. Immediately identifying the registered owner allows lost pets to be returned within hours, sparing families emotional distress and preventing overcrowding in public shelters. This system saves municipalities millions of dollars in animal sheltering expenditures and prevents the heartbreaking euthanasia of healthy, loved companion animals.

Equally important, mandatory microchip registration establishes legal accountability for pet abandonment and animal cruelty. Unscrupulous owners often abandon pets on roadsides when medical expenses rise or when they relocate, leaving animals to starve or reproduce uncontrollably. A universal microchip registry legally links every pet to a responsible owner, enabling authorities to prosecute abandonment and neglect. While opponents may argue that microchipping imposes costs on low-income pet owners, governments can easily sponsor free microchipping clinics in municipal parks, eliminating financial barriers.

In summary, mandatory pet microchipping protects animal welfare, promotes responsible pet guardianship, and eases burdens on municipal animal shelters. It represents an essential, humane standard for civilized societies.

questions.title: Cross-Border Scientific Collaboration and Peace
questions.text:
International scientific collaboration on global challenges such as climate change and disease does more to promote global peace than formal diplomatic treaties.

Do you agree or disagree? Support your point of view with reasons and examples. Write 200-300 words. Maintaining international peace and security has historically been the domain of professional diplomats negotiating formal bilateral treaties and security pacts. However, I strongly agree with the statement that cross-border scientific collaboration plays a far more powerful and enduring role in fostering international peace and mutual understanding.

The primary reason scientific cooperation fosters deep peace is that science provides a shared, universal language rooted in empirical truth, rationality, and common human survival. When multinational teams of astronomers, climatologists, and virologists work together on collaborative endeavors—such as the International Space Station, global climate modeling, or vaccine development—they build profound relationships based on mutual respect and shared objectives that transcend geopolitical rivalries. During the height of the Cold War, joint biomedical research between American and Soviet scientists successfully eradicated smallpox, demonstrating that common scientific missions build bridges of trust even when political diplomacy is completely deadlocked. Science humanizes adversaries and establishes durable communication channels that resist political tensions.

In contrast, formal diplomatic treaties and political accords are often fragile, transactional, and vulnerable to unilateral abandonment whenever domestic political regimes change or nationalistic tensions flare. Treaties often manage symptoms of hostility through compromises, whereas scientific partnerships foster genuine cross-cultural friendship and collaborative problem-solving among intellectuals who influence public policy. Solving borderless planetary threats like pandemics and ecological collapse reminds nations of their shared vulnerability, rendering militaristic conflict increasingly irrational.

In conclusion, while diplomatic treaties are necessary legal frameworks, scientific collaboration builds the genuine human trust that underpins lasting peace. Empowering the global scientific community is one of humanity's greatest investments in international stability.

questions.title: Mandatory Soundproofing in Multi-Story Apartments
questions.text:
