It began as a marketing idea in Japan in the 1960s, when a company sold a step counter whose name meant ten-thousand-step meter. More recent studies suggest that health benefits increase with more steps but begin to level off at lower totals for many people, especially older adults.

questions.title: Edmond Albius and vanilla
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Type the missing words in each blank. Vanilla comes from an orchid native to Mexico, where it is pollinated by local [[b1]]. When the plant was grown elsewhere, it flowered but produced almost no pods. In 1841, Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved boy on the island of Réunion, developed a quick way to pollinate each flower by [[b2]]. His method is still used today, and the intensive [[b3]] it requires helps explain why vanilla is so expensive. Vanilla comes from an orchid native to Mexico, where it is pollinated by local bees. When the plant was grown elsewhere, it flowered but produced almost no pods. In 1841, Edmond Albius, a twelve-year-old enslaved boy on the island of Réunion, developed a quick way to pollinate each flower by hand. His method is still used today, and the intensive labour it requires helps explain why vanilla is so expensive.

questions.title: Countdown timers at crossings
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Many cities have installed countdown timers at pedestrian crossings, showing how many seconds remain before the lights change. The idea is simple: if people know exactly how much time they have, they can decide whether it is safe to start crossing, and fewer will be caught in the middle of the road when traffic starts moving. Several studies have found that pedestrians generally like the timers and feel safer with them. However, the timers can also be seen by drivers. Some research suggests that drivers approaching a junction use the countdown to judge whether they can get through before the light turns red, and some of them speed up. For this reason, a few cities have experimented with timers that are visible only to pedestrians, or have combined them with longer crossing times. The overall effect on safety appears to depend on the design of the junction.

questions.title: Rules on parking spaces
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. For much of the twentieth century, many cities required every new building to include a minimum number of parking spaces. A block of flats might need at least one space per apartment, and a restaurant a certain number per table. These rules were intended to prevent a shortage of on-street parking, but critics argue that they have had costly side effects. Parking takes up valuable land and can add significantly to the cost of building homes, costs that are passed on to residents whether or not they own a car. By guaranteeing cheap or free parking everywhere, the rules may also encourage people to drive rather than walk or use public transport. In recent years, a growing number of cities have removed their minimum parking requirements. Supporters point out that this does not ban parking: developers can still build as many spaces as they think their customers want.

questions.title: Singapore's hawker centres
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In the 1960s and 1970s, the government of Singapore began moving thousands of street food sellers, known as hawkers, off the streets and into purpose-built food centres. The main reasons were hygiene and public health: food was being prepared without clean water or proper waste disposal. The new hawker centres provided running water, drainage and regular inspections, while allowing sellers to continue offering cheap, freshly cooked dishes. Over time, the centres became an important part of daily life, places where people of different backgrounds and incomes eat side by side. In 2020, Singapore's hawker culture was added to UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. Yet its future faces challenges. Many hawkers are elderly, the work involves long hours for modest profits, and fewer young people are willing to take it on, so schemes have been introduced to train and support new hawkers.

questions.title: Bus bunching
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Anyone who has waited a long time for a bus, only to see two or three arrive together, has experienced bus bunching. It happens even when buses leave the depot at perfectly regular intervals. Suppose one bus is delayed slightly, perhaps by traffic. By the time it reaches the next stop, more passengers have gathered, so boarding takes longer and the bus falls further behind. Meanwhile, the bus following it finds fewer passengers waiting, moves faster, and gradually catches up. Eventually the two travel together, leaving a long gap behind them. The problem is self-reinforcing, so small delays grow over the length of a route. Transport operators use several methods to reduce it. Drivers can be asked to wait at certain stops to restore even spacing, passengers can be allowed to board through all doors, and dedicated bus lanes reduce the delays that start the process.

questions.title: Paving you can feel
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The textured paving found at many pedestrian crossings and railway platforms was invented in Japan in the 1960s by Seiichi Miyake, who wanted to help a friend who was losing his sight. The first tiles were laid in the city of Okayama in 1967. The system uses two main patterns. Raised dots warn people with visual impairments that they are approaching a hazard, such as the edge of a platform or a road. Raised lines, running in the direction of travel, guide people along a safe route. The idea spread across Japan and then around the world, and in many countries it is now required by law in certain locations. Designers have had to balance different needs, however. The raised surfaces can be uncomfortable or difficult for some wheelchair users and people with walking difficulties, and inconsistent use of the patterns between cities can cause confusion.

questions.title: Monderman's streets
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Most road safety measures add something: more signs, more barriers, more traffic lights. The Dutch traffic engineer Hans Monderman argued that in some places the opposite could work better. In several town centres in the Netherlands, he removed traffic lights, road markings, kerbs and signs, creating a shared space where cars, cyclists and pedestrians mix. His reasoning was that when drivers are unsure who has priority, they slow down and pay more attention to the people around them, making eye contact instead of watching signals. Supporters report that traffic in some of these places flows smoothly at low speeds and that the areas feel more pleasant. However, the approach has critics. Organisations representing blind and partially sighted people point out that kerbs and controlled crossings are essential for them, and that relying on eye contact excludes those who cannot make it.

questions.title: Slowing traffic in towns
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The speed of a car has a dramatic effect on what happens to a pedestrian in a collision. At low speeds, most people who are hit survive; as speed increases, the risk of death rises steeply. For this reason, many towns use traffic calming measures in residential streets. Instead of relying only on speed limits and enforcement, these measures physically encourage drivers to slow down. They include road humps, raised crossings, narrowed sections of road and bends deliberately added to straight streets. Their great advantage is that they work all the time, without police present. They do have drawbacks. Road humps can slow down ambulances and fire engines, create noise as vehicles brake and accelerate, and push traffic onto neighbouring streets. Designers have responded with alternatives such as speed cushions, which have gaps wide enough for the wheels of large emergency vehicles to pass through without slowing.

questions.title: Standing on both sides
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. On escalators in many cities, there is an unwritten rule: stand on one side and walk on the other. It seems efficient, but on very long escalators it may not be. In 2015 and 2016, London Underground ran a trial at Holborn station, where the escalators are unusually long. Staff asked passengers to stand on both sides and not walk. Because few people are willing to walk up a very tall escalator, the walking side had often been half empty, while queues built up at the bottom for the standing side. When everyone stood, the escalators carried significantly more people at busy times, and queues shrank. However, many passengers disliked being told not to walk, and some ignored the request. After the trial ended, most people returned to their old habits. The experiment showed that what feels fastest for an individual is not always best for the crowd.

questions.title: Memos instead of slides
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. At some companies, the most important meetings begin in silence. The online retailer Amazon became known for replacing slide presentations in senior meetings with written memos of up to about six pages. Instead of watching someone present, participants spend the first part of the meeting reading the memo quietly, and only then begin the discussion. The company's leaders argued that full sentences and paragraphs force the writer to think more clearly, because a narrative has to explain how ideas connect, whereas bullet points on slides can hide gaps in reasoning. Reading together also ensures that everyone starts the discussion with the same information, rather than pretending to have read a document in advance. The approach has critics. Writing a good memo takes a long time, and not every decision justifies that effort. Nevertheless, the idea has been copied by other organisations looking for better decisions.

questions.title: Ranking employees
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In the 1980s and 1990s, the American company General Electric became famous for a system of forced ranking. Managers had to place employees into categories: roughly the top twenty percent, who were rewarded, the middle seventy percent, and the bottom ten percent, who were often asked to leave. Supporters argued that the system prevented managers from giving everyone the same average rating and ensured that poor performance was addressed. Many other large companies adopted similar methods. Over time, however, criticism grew. Because employees were compared with their colleagues, the system could discourage cooperation, since helping a teammate might lower your own ranking. It could also be unfair in a strong team, where someone had to be labelled a poor performer even if everyone was doing well. Many companies, including some early adopters, have since abandoned forced ranking in favour of more frequent conversations about performance.

questions.title: Does brainstorming work?
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The term brainstorming was popularised in the 1950s by the advertising executive Alex Osborn, who claimed that groups following his rules, such as withholding criticism and aiming for quantity, could produce far more ideas than individuals. Later research has not supported this claim. In many experiments, people who worked alone and then pooled their ideas produced more, and often better, ideas than the same number of people brainstorming together. Psychologists have identified several reasons. In a group, only one person can speak at a time, so others may forget their ideas while waiting. Some people hold back because they worry about being judged, and some put in less effort when others can carry the load. Techniques such as brainwriting, in which people write ideas down individually before sharing them, try to keep the benefits of group discussion while avoiding these problems.

questions.title: Stopping the production line
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. On a Toyota production line, any worker who notices a problem can pull a cord, called an andon cord, that alerts a team leader and, if the problem cannot be solved quickly, stops the entire line. To outsiders this seems surprising. Stopping production is expensive, and many factories had traditionally tried to keep lines moving at all costs, fixing faulty products at the end. Toyota's approach was based on the idea that problems should be solved immediately, at their source, before faults are repeated on many vehicles. It also sent a clear message that every worker was trusted and responsible for quality. The system became one of the best-known features of Toyota's production methods. Other industries have borrowed the idea. Some hospitals, for example, encourage any member of staff, regardless of seniority, to stop a procedure if they believe a patient's safety is at risk.

questions.title: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Over a noisy radio connection, letters such as B, D and P can sound almost identical, and a single misunderstood letter can cause serious problems, for example in an aircraft's call sign. For this reason, pilots and air traffic controllers use a spelling alphabet in which each letter is represented by a word: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie and so on. The current version was adopted internationally in the 1950s after extensive testing. The words were chosen so that they would be clearly distinguishable from one another and easy to pronounce for speakers of different languages, not only English. Some spellings were adjusted for this reason: Alfa is written with an f, and Juliett with two t's, so that speakers of other languages would pronounce them correctly. The alphabet is now used well beyond aviation, by the military, police, emergency services and customer service staff.

questions.title: The meaning of SOS
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The distress signal SOS was adopted at an international radio conference in 1906 and came into use in 1908. Many people believe the letters stand for save our souls or save our ship, but these phrases were invented afterwards. SOS was chosen because in Morse code it forms a simple, distinctive pattern: three dots, three dashes, three dots, sent as one continuous signal. It is easy to transmit and difficult to mistake for anything else, even by an operator with poor reception. Before SOS became universal, different countries used different signals, which could cause confusion. When the Titanic sank in 1912, its radio operators sent both the older signal and SOS. By the end of the twentieth century, Morse code had been replaced at sea by satellite-based distress systems, which can automatically send a ship's position, but SOS remains widely recognised as a call for help.

questions.title: James Biggs's white stick
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The white cane is recognised in many countries as a symbol of blindness, but its history is relatively recent. In 1921, James Biggs, an English photographer who had lost his sight, painted his walking stick white so that drivers would notice him more easily as traffic increased. In the 1930s, organisations in France and North America campaigned for white canes to be widely adopted, and many places passed laws requiring drivers to give way to pedestrians carrying one. The cane's role changed significantly after the Second World War, when a rehabilitation specialist working with blinded veterans developed a technique using a longer cane. Instead of simply supporting the user or signalling to others, it was swept from side to side in front of the body to detect obstacles, steps and kerbs. This long cane technique is still taught today, alongside guide dogs and newer electronic aids.

questions.title: Headphones and hearing
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Listening to music through headphones is one of the most common ways people expose themselves to loud sound. Inside the inner ear, tiny hair cells convert sound vibrations into signals for the brain. Very loud or prolonged noise can damage these cells, and in humans they do not grow back, so the resulting hearing loss is permanent. Often it develops gradually, and people may not notice until it is advanced. The risk depends on both volume and time: a moderately loud sound can be harmful if heard for many hours, while a very loud sound can cause damage quickly. The World Health Organization has warned that more than a billion young people are at risk because of unsafe listening habits. Some experts suggest a simple guideline: listen at no more than sixty percent of maximum volume for no more than sixty minutes at a time.

questions.title: Mediterranean eating
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The Mediterranean diet, rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, fish and olive oil, has long been associated with good health. One of the most influential studies was a large trial in Spain involving around seven and a half thousand people at high risk of heart disease. Participants were randomly assigned either to a Mediterranean diet with extra olive oil or nuts, or to advice to follow a low-fat diet. When the results were published in 2013, the Mediterranean groups had significantly fewer heart attacks, strokes and deaths from heart disease. Later, however, researchers discovered problems with how some participants had been assigned to groups. The original paper was withdrawn in 2018 and republished with a reanalysis. The main conclusions were similar, but the authors described them more cautiously. The episode shows both the value of large trials and the importance of checking how they are carried out.

questions.title: Cutting sodium slowly
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Eating too much salt raises blood pressure, which increases the risk of heart attacks and strokes. Much of the salt people eat is not added at the table but is already in processed foods such as bread, cereals and ready meals. In the early 2000s, the United Kingdom began a programme of salt reduction that worked with food manufacturers to lower the salt content of their products gradually. The key was to make changes slowly, a little at a time, so that customers did not notice a difference in taste and did not switch to other brands. Over the following decade, average salt consumption fell noticeably, and researchers linked this to falls in average blood pressure. Because the targets were voluntary, however, progress depended on the cooperation of the industry, and some experts believe it slowed when government pressure weakened in later years.

questions.title: Fluoridation
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In the early twentieth century, a dentist in Colorado noticed that many local people had brown stains on their teeth, but surprisingly few cavities. Researchers eventually linked both effects to naturally high levels of fluoride in the water supply. Fluoride makes tooth enamel more resistant to decay, but too much can cause staining. In 1945, the city of Grand Rapids in the United States became the first to add a carefully controlled amount of fluoride to its drinking water, and rates of tooth decay among children fell. Many countries followed. The practice remains debated. Critics argue that people should be able to choose whether to consume fluoride, and that the benefit is now smaller because most toothpaste contains it. Several European countries do not fluoridate their water. However, major public health organisations continue to support fluoridation at recommended levels as a safe and cheap way to reduce tooth decay.

questions.title: Risk compensation
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. When cars become safer, do drivers behave more carefully or less? A well-known study in Munich in the 1980s followed a fleet of taxis, some fitted with anti-lock brakes, which help drivers keep control when braking hard, and some without. The researchers expected the taxis with the new brakes to have fewer accidents. They did not. Observers found that drivers of the better-equipped taxis tended to follow other cars more closely and brake more sharply. This is an example of what psychologists call risk compensation: when people feel safer, they may take more risks, cancelling out some of the benefit. The idea has been used to question safety measures from seat belts to cycle helmets. However, most researchers do not conclude that safety features are useless. Rather, they argue that the real effect of a safety measure depends on how people change their behaviour in response.

questions.title: The Plimsoll line
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In the nineteenth century, many British cargo ships sailed dangerously overloaded, and hundreds were lost at sea each year. Some owners had little incentive to prevent this, because their ships and cargoes were insured, while the sailors who drowned were easily replaced. The politician Samuel Plimsoll campaigned against these so-called coffin ships, facing strong opposition from shipowners. In 1876, a law was passed requiring ships to carry a mark on their hull showing the maximum depth to which they could be loaded. This became known as the Plimsoll line. Today load lines are required by international agreement. They include several marks, because a ship floats at a different depth depending on the water: it sits lower in fresh water than in denser seawater, and extra safety margins are needed in winter seas. The simple painted line has saved countless lives.

questions.title: Where the date changes
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The International Date Line runs roughly along the one hundred and eightieth meridian, through the Pacific Ocean, and marks where one calendar day ends and the next begins. A traveller crossing it towards the west moves forward a day, while crossing towards the east moves back a day. The need for such a line was noticed centuries ago. When the survivors of Ferdinand Magellan's expedition returned to Spain in 1522 after sailing around the world westwards, they discovered that their carefully kept log was one day behind the calendar at home. The date line is not straight. It zigzags so that island groups and countries are not divided between two dates. Countries can even choose which side to be on. In 2011, Samoa moved to the other side of the line, skipping the thirtieth of December entirely, so that its working week would match those of its main trading partners, Australia and New Zealand.

questions.title: Finding longitude at sea
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. For centuries, sailors could measure their latitude from the Sun and stars, but longitude, their position east or west, was far harder to determine. Mistakes caused shipwrecks and lost cargoes. One solution was to carry an accurate clock showing the time at the home port: comparing it with local noon at sea revealed how far east or west the ship had travelled. The problem was that ordinary clocks lost accuracy on a moving ship. In 1714, the British government offered a large prize for a practical solution. John Harrison, a largely self-taught clockmaker, spent decades building a series of sea clocks. His fourth design, the size of a large pocket watch, performed remarkably well on a voyage to Jamaica in 1761. Yet the officials responsible, many of whom favoured an astronomical method, were reluctant to pay him in full. Only after years of dispute, and the involvement of the king, did he receive most of the money.

questions.title: The seven-day cycle
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Unlike the day, the month and the year, the seven-day week is not based directly on any single natural cycle. Its origins are debated, but historians point to several influences. Ancient Babylonians gave special importance to the number seven, and seven celestial bodies could be seen moving across the sky: the Sun, the Moon and five planets. A quarter of a lunar month is also roughly seven days. The Jewish tradition of a weekly day of rest spread the seven-day week further, and it was eventually adopted throughout the Roman world. Many languages still link the days to those celestial bodies: in English, Sunday and Monday refer to the Sun and the Moon, and Saturday to Saturn. The week has proved remarkably resistant to change. Revolutionary France tried a ten-day week, and the Soviet Union experimented with five- and six-day weeks, but both attempts were abandoned.

questions.title: A number for nothing
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. It is easy to take zero for granted, but for much of history it did not exist as a number. Some ancient civilisations, such as the Babylonians, used a symbol as a placeholder to show an empty position in a number, rather like the gap that distinguishes two hundred and five from twenty-five. However, they did not treat it as a number in its own right. In India, mathematicians went further. In the seventh century, the mathematician Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero, such as the result of adding zero to a number or subtracting a number from itself. Indian numerals, including zero, spread to the Islamic world, where scholars developed them further, and eventually reached Europe. There they were adopted only slowly, but the place-value system they made possible is the foundation of modern mathematics and computing.

questions.title: Fibonacci's book of calculation
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In 1202, the Italian mathematician Leonardo of Pisa, now known as Fibonacci, published a book called Liber Abaci. Having grown up partly in North Africa, where his father worked as a trade official, he had learned the numerals used by Arab merchants, which had originated in India. His book showed European readers how these numerals made practical calculations, such as converting currencies and calculating interest, far easier than with Roman numerals. The book also contains a puzzle about breeding rabbits that produces the sequence of numbers now named after him, although the sequence had been described centuries earlier by Indian mathematicians. The new numerals were not accepted everywhere at once. In 1299, the city of Florence banned them in official accounts, partly because they were easier to alter fraudulently, for example by turning a zero into a six or nine.

questions.title: Sixty minutes in an hour
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Why are there sixty minutes in an hour and sixty seconds in a minute, when most of our counting is based on tens? The answer goes back to ancient Mesopotamia, where the Babylonians used a number system based on sixty. Sixty is a convenient number because it can be divided evenly in many ways: by two, three, four, five, six, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty and thirty. This made fractions much easier to handle, especially in astronomy, and it also explains the three hundred and sixty degrees in a circle. The division of the day into twenty-four hours is usually traced to ancient Egypt, where daytime and night were each divided into twelve parts. Attempts to change these units have failed. During the French Revolution, clocks showing ten hours a day, each of one hundred minutes, were introduced, but the system was abandoned after only a couple of years.

questions.title: Prime numbers and online security
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Every time you buy something online, your payment details are protected by encryption, and some of the most widely used methods rely on prime numbers. Multiplying two large prime numbers together is easy for a computer, even if each has hundreds of digits. But reversing the process, taking the result and working out which two primes produced it, is extraordinarily difficult. With current computers, it could take an impractically long time. A system published in 1977, known as RSA after the initials of its inventors, uses this difference. It allows a website to publish a public key that anyone can use to lock a message, while only the owner of a matching private key can unlock it. Researchers are concerned that future quantum computers could solve the factoring problem much faster, which is why new encryption methods designed to resist them are already being developed and introduced.

questions.title: Three doors and a car
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Imagine a game show with three closed doors. Behind one is a car; behind the other two are goats. You choose a door. The host, who knows what is behind each door, then opens one of the doors you did not choose, always revealing a goat, and asks whether you want to switch to the remaining closed door. Most people feel it makes no difference: two doors are left, so the chance must be fifty-fifty. In fact, switching doubles your chance of winning, from one in three to two in three. Your first choice had only a one-in-three chance of being right, and the host's action does not change that; if you were wrong, the car must be behind the other door. When a magazine columnist explained this in 1990, she received thousands of letters insisting she was mistaken, including some from people with doctorates. Computer simulations have since confirmed the answer many times.

questions.title: Shared birthdays
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. How many people need to be in a room before there is a better than even chance that two of them share a birthday? Many people guess around one hundred and eighty, half the number of days in a year. The real answer is just twenty-three. With seventy people, a shared birthday is almost certain. The result seems surprising because we tend to think about the chance that someone shares our own birthday, which is low. But the question is about any two people in the room. Among twenty-three people, there are two hundred and fifty-three possible pairs, and each pair is a chance for a match. The same mathematics matters in computer security. Systems that produce short digital fingerprints for files can be attacked by searching for two different files with the same fingerprint, which is much easier than matching one particular file, a technique known as a birthday attack.

questions.title: The first-digit pattern
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. If you look at the first digits of numbers in many real-world collections of data, such as populations of towns, lengths of rivers or company accounts, you might expect each digit from one to nine to appear equally often. Surprisingly, it does not. The digit one appears first about thirty percent of the time, while nine appears first less than five percent of the time. This pattern is known as Benford's law. It was first noticed in the nineteenth century by an astronomer who observed that the early pages of books of logarithm tables, used for numbers beginning with one, were more worn than later pages. The law has a practical use. When people invent numbers, they tend to spread the first digits too evenly, so auditors sometimes check whether financial figures follow the expected pattern. A mismatch does not prove fraud, but it can suggest where to look more closely.

questions.title: The missing bullet holes
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. During the Second World War, analysts studied bombers returning from missions and recorded where they had been hit. Bullet holes were concentrated on the wings and the body of the aircraft, while the engines showed relatively few. An obvious conclusion was to add armour where the holes were most common. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out a flaw in this reasoning. The analysts were only looking at planes that had survived. Aircraft hit in the engines were less likely to return at all, so the lack of holes there did not mean the engines were rarely hit; it meant that hits there were deadly. The armour, he argued, should go where the returning planes had no damage. This mistake is called survivorship bias, and it appears in many areas. For example, studying only successful companies can make risky strategies look safer than they really are, because the failures are no longer visible.

questions.title: Ice cream and drowning
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In many places, ice cream sales and the number of drownings rise and fall together throughout the year. Does eating ice cream cause people to drown? Of course not. Both increase in hot weather, when more people buy ice cream and more people go swimming. This is a classic example of the difference between correlation and causation. Two things can move together because a third factor, sometimes called a confounding variable, affects both of them. Sometimes the link is pure coincidence; sometimes the direction of cause is reversed. For this reason, scientists prefer randomised experiments, in which people are assigned to different groups by chance, so that other factors are spread evenly between them. When experiments are impossible or unethical, researchers must use observational data with great care, trying to account for possible confounding factors before drawing conclusions about cause.

questions.title: Regression to the mean
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. When a result is unusually good or unusually bad, the next result is likely to be closer to average, simply because extreme results usually involve some luck. This is called regression to the mean, and it can easily lead to false conclusions. The psychologist Daniel Kahneman described flight instructors who believed that praising a trainee after an excellent landing made the next landing worse, while criticising a poor landing made the next one better. In fact, the changes would have happened anyway: after an exceptional performance, an average one is more likely to follow. The same effect can make policies look more successful than they are. Speed cameras, for example, are often installed at locations after an unusually high number of accidents. If accidents then fall, part of the fall may be due to regression to the mean rather than the cameras, so careful studies compare these sites with similar ones.

questions.title: The horse that could count
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In the early twentieth century, a horse in Germany called Clever Hans appeared to solve arithmetic problems, tapping his hoof to give the answer. Investigators eventually discovered that the horse was responding to tiny, unconscious changes in the posture and facial expressions of the people around him, who knew the answer. The case illustrates why modern medical trials are often double-blind. In such a trial, neither the participants nor the researchers who assess them know who is receiving the real treatment and who is receiving a placebo or a comparison treatment. If participants know, their expectations can affect how they feel and what they report. If researchers know, they may unintentionally treat patients differently or interpret results more favourably. By keeping everyone unaware until the results are analysed, double-blind trials help ensure that any difference between the groups is caused by the treatment itself.

questions.title: Repeating psychology studies
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In 2015, a large group of researchers published the results of an ambitious project. They had tried to repeat one hundred studies published in leading psychology journals, following the original methods as closely as possible. Only around a third to two fifths of the repeated studies produced clearly similar results. The project drew attention to what became known as the replication crisis. Researchers identified several contributing factors. Many original studies used small samples, which make chance findings more likely. Journals tended to publish surprising positive results rather than studies that found nothing, and researchers sometimes tried many different ways of analysing their data until one produced an interesting result. The problem is not limited to psychology. In response, many scientists now register their plans before collecting data, use larger samples and share their data, so that others can check their work more easily.

questions.title: Alfred Nobel's fortune
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist who invented dynamite, made a fortune from explosives. According to a well-known story, in 1888 a French newspaper mistakenly published his obituary when it was actually his brother who had died, and described him as a merchant of death who had grown rich by finding ways to kill people faster. Historians are not certain how much this episode influenced him, but in his will, signed in 1895, Nobel left most of his fortune to establish prizes for those who had conferred the greatest benefit on humankind in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. The first prizes were awarded in 1901. A prize in economics was added much later, in 1968, funded by Sweden's central bank in Nobel's memory, which is why it is officially not one of the original Nobel Prizes.

questions.title: Linnaeus's binomial names
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Before the eighteenth century, naturalists often identified plants and animals using long descriptive phrases in Latin, sometimes a dozen words long. The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus popularised a much simpler approach in the 1750s. He gave each species a two-part name: the first word identifies the group it belongs to, called the genus, and the second identifies the particular species. Humans, for example, are Homo sapiens. Latin was used because it was the shared language of scholars across Europe, and because, as a language no longer changing in everyday speech, its meanings were stable. The system solves a practical problem. The same animal may have many different common names in different languages and regions, while one common name may refer to several different species. A scientific name, by contrast, refers to one species only, allowing researchers anywhere in the world to be sure they are discussing the same organism.

questions.title: Gaps in the periodic table
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. In 1869, the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published a table arranging the known chemical elements in order of their atomic weight, grouping together elements with similar properties. Others had noticed patterns before, but Mendeleev took a bold step. Where the pattern suggested an element should exist but none was known, he left a gap, and he predicted the properties the missing elements would have, including their approximate weight and density. He also changed the order of some elements when their properties did not fit, suggesting that their measured weights might be wrong. Within about two decades, several of the predicted elements were discovered, including gallium and germanium, with properties remarkably close to his forecasts. These successful predictions did more than anything else to convince scientists that his table reflected a real underlying order in nature.

questions.title: A new definition of the kilogram
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. For more than a century, the kilogram was defined by a single physical object: a small cylinder of platinum and iridium kept in a secure vault near Paris since 1889. Every other measurement of mass in the world was ultimately traced back to it. This created a problem. When the cylinder was compared with its official copies over the decades, their masses were found to have drifted apart by tiny amounts, a few hundredths of a milligram. Since the cylinder was the kilogram by definition, nobody could say for certain whether it had lost mass or the copies had gained it. In 2019, scientists redefined the kilogram using a fundamental constant of nature, called the Planck constant, which can be measured with extremely precise instruments. The cylinder still exists, but it is no longer the standard, and every basic unit of measurement is now defined by constants rather than by objects.

questions.title: Counting between flash and thunder
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. During a thunderstorm, we see the flash of lightning before we hear the thunder, even though both are produced at the same moment. The reason is the enormous difference in speed between light and sound. Light travels so fast that it reaches us almost instantly, while sound travels through the air at roughly three hundred and forty metres per second. This allows a simple estimate of distance: count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, and divide by three to get the approximate distance in kilometres. Thunder itself is caused by the lightning heating the air around it to extremely high temperatures in a fraction of a second, making it expand violently. Thunder can usually be heard up to about fifteen kilometres away, and safety experts point out that if you can hear it, you are close enough to be struck, so you should move indoors.

questions.title: Astronomical distances
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Although a light-year sounds like a measure of time, it is actually a measure of distance: the distance light travels in one year, which is roughly nine and a half trillion kilometres. Astronomers use it because distances in space are so vast that kilometres become impractical. The nearest star to the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is just over four light-years away, meaning its light takes more than four years to reach us. This has an interesting consequence. When we look at distant objects, we see them not as they are now but as they were when the light left them. The Andromeda Galaxy, the most distant object easily visible to the naked eye, appears as it was around two and a half million years ago. Powerful telescopes can observe galaxies whose light set out billions of years ago, allowing astronomers to study the early history of the universe.

questions.title: Chlorophyll's colour
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Plants are green because of chlorophyll, the pigment they use to capture energy from sunlight for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light strongly, but it absorbs much less green light, which is reflected or passes through the leaf. That reflected green light is what our eyes detect. At first this seems puzzling. Sunlight contains a great deal of green light, so why would plants waste it? Scientists have proposed several explanations. One recent idea is that absorbing light in two separate colour bands helps plants keep a steady supply of energy when light conditions change rapidly, for example when clouds pass over or leaves move in the wind, protecting them from sudden surges that could cause damage. Leaves also contain other pigments, such as yellow and orange ones, which are usually hidden by the chlorophyll and become visible when it breaks down.

questions.title: Pink flamingos
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Flamingos are not born pink. Chicks hatch with grey or white feathers, and adults only become pink because of what they eat. Their diet of algae and tiny shrimp-like animals contains pigments called carotenoids, the same family of pigments that makes carrots orange. The birds' bodies break these pigments down and deposit them in their feathers, skin and legs. A flamingo that stops eating enough of these foods will gradually become paler. For this reason, zoos add carotenoids to the diet of captive flamingos to keep their colour. The colour also appears to matter in social life. Brighter birds tend to be healthier and more successful at attracting a partner, and researchers have observed that flamingos spread coloured oils from a gland near their tail onto their feathers, particularly during the breeding season, making themselves look pinker, rather like applying make-up.

questions.title: A snake's forked tongue
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. When a snake flicks its tongue, it is not tasting the air in the usual sense, and it is certainly not preparing to sting. It is collecting chemical particles from the air and the ground. The tongue carries these particles back into the mouth, where they are passed to a special sensory organ in the roof of the mouth, sometimes called the Jacobson's organ, which analyses them. The forked shape of the tongue is particularly useful. Because the two tips sample the air at slightly different points, the snake can compare the strength of a scent on its left and right sides, and turn towards the stronger one. This allows it to follow the trail of prey, or of a potential mate, with considerable accuracy. Many lizards use a similar system, and species that rely heavily on following scent trails tend to have more deeply forked tongues.

questions.title: Following the trail
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. When a foraging ant finds food, it returns to the nest laying down a chemical trail called a pheromone. Other ants follow the trail to the food and, as they return, add more pheromone, strengthening it. This simple system allows colonies to find efficient routes without any ant understanding the overall picture. In a classic experiment, ants were given two bridges of different lengths leading to the same food. At first they used both, but the ants on the shorter bridge completed their round trips faster, so pheromone built up more quickly on that route, and soon most ants were using it. Because pheromones gradually evaporate, trails to exhausted food sources fade away. Computer scientists have been inspired by this behaviour. Programs based on virtual ants laying virtual trails have been used to find efficient routes in problems such as planning deliveries and directing data through networks.

questions.title: A brainless problem solver
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The slime mould Physarum polycephalum is a single-celled organism with no brain or nervous system, yet it can solve problems that seem to require intelligence. It spreads out as a yellow network of tubes, searching for food. When it finds food, the tubes leading to it thicken, while tubes that lead nowhere shrink and disappear. In 2000, Japanese researchers showed that a slime mould placed in a maze with food at two exits would eventually form a single tube along the shortest route. Ten years later, researchers placed pieces of food on a surface in the pattern of the cities around Tokyo. The network the slime mould formed was remarkably similar to the region's actual railway network in its efficiency and resilience. The researchers suggested that studying such simple organisms could help engineers design transport and communication networks that adapt without central planning.

questions.title: Turritopsis
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. A small jellyfish known as Turritopsis dohrnii, only a few millimetres across, has earned the nickname the immortal jellyfish. Most jellyfish begin life as a polyp attached to the sea floor, grow into a free-swimming adult, reproduce and die. When this species is injured, stressed or ageing, however, it can do something extraordinary. Instead of dying, the adult sinks, transforms back into a polyp, and begins its life cycle again. Its cells change from one type into another, a process scientists are studying closely. In theory, the cycle could repeat many times. In practice, most individuals in the wild are eaten by predators or killed by disease long before this matters, so the jellyfish is not truly immortal. Researchers hope that understanding how its cells reverse their development could contribute to research on ageing and tissue repair.

questions.title: Eighteen holes
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. Why does a standard round of golf have eighteen holes? Early golf courses in Scotland had no fixed number: some had five, some seven, some twelve or more, depending on the land available. The Old Course at St Andrews, one of the most influential, originally had twenty-two holes, played out along the coast and back again. In 1764, the golfers there decided that the first four holes were too short and combined them into two, which reduced each half of the course by two holes and left a round of eighteen. Because St Andrews became the leading authority on the rules of golf, other clubs gradually followed its example, and eighteen became the standard. A popular story claims that the number was chosen because a bottle of whisky contained eighteen shots, but historians regard this as a legend with no evidence behind it.

questions.title: An ancient vending machine
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Click on the paragraph that best relates to the recording. The vending machine may seem like a modern invention, but the earliest known design is nearly two thousand years old. In the first century, the engineer Hero of Alexandria described a device for dispensing holy water in temples. When a worshipper dropped a coin through a slot, it landed on a small pan attached to a lever. The weight of the coin tipped the lever, which opened a valve and released a measured amount of water. When the coin slid off the pan, the lever returned to its original position and the flow stopped. Modern coin-operated machines appeared in the 1880s, when machines selling postcards were installed in London. Today vending machines sell everything from drinks to hot meals, and Japan is famous for having one of the highest numbers of machines per person in the world, partly because of low crime rates, which make it safe to leave them outdoors.

questions.title: Measles and herd immunity

Measles is one of the most dangerous diseases known. When a high proportion of a community is vaccinated, the virus struggles to find new hosts, and even people who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborn babies, are infected. This is called herd immunity. For measles, experts estimate that about ninety-five percent of people need to be immune, one of the lowest thresholds of any disease. The following year, a fourteen-year-old boy became the first patient to receive an injection, and his condition improved slightly. The discovery earned a Nobel Prize in 1923. questions.title: Allbutt's thermometer

Early medical thermometers were about a metre long and could take twenty minutes to give a reading. In 1867, the English doctor Thomas Allbutt designed a much heavier thermometer that took only about five minutes. This made it practical for doctors to measure temperature routinely, helping them track the progress of injuries in their patients. questions.title: Landsteiner's blood types

In 1901, the Austrian scientist Karl Landsteiner showed that human blood falls into different colours, and that mixing incompatible types causes the cells to clump together. His discovery made transfusions far cheaper and led to the development of blood banks. Early blood transfusions were extremely risky, because some patients reacted violently to the donated blood. It was one of the first controlled trials in medicine, although the British navy did not supply citrus juice to all its ships until decades later. In the 1920s, Switzerland and the United States began adding small amounts of iodine to table sugar. Because almost everyone uses salt, the measure reached whole populations at very low cost, and it is often described as one of the most expensive public health measures ever introduced. questions.text: You will hear a recording. Below is a transcription of the recording. Some words in the transcription differ from what the speaker said. Please click on the words that are different. A fever is not simply a sign that something has gone wrong. When the body detects an infection, a region of the brain raises its temperature limit, and we begin to shiver to produce extra heat. Higher temperatures appear to help some immune cells work more slowly, and may make conditions less comfortable for certain patients. Very high fevers, however, still need medical attention. questions.title: Ice-cream headaches

Brain freeze is the sudden headache that can follow eating ice cream too slowly. It happens when something very cold touches the roof of the mouth, causing nearby blood vessels to narrow and then rapidly widen. Nerves in the area send pain signals that the brain interprets as coming from the stomach. Pressing the tongue against the roof of the mouth to warm it can make the pain worse. Motion sickness is thought to result from a agreement between the senses. In a moving car, the balance organs in the inner ear detect motion, but a passenger reading a book sees a page that appears bright. The brain receives mixed signals, which can cause nausea. Looking out at the floor helps because it allows the eyes to confirm the movement the body feels. Motion sickness is thought to result from a conflict between the senses. Many people believe the habit causes arthritis, but studies have found no clear link. One doctor cracked the knuckles of only one hand for sixty years and found no damage between his hands. questions.title: The first emoji
questions.text: You will hear a recording. Below is a transcription of the recording. Some words in the transcription differ from what the speaker said. Please click on the words that are different. questions.title: The Dust Bowl
questions.text: Which TWO causes of the Dust Bowl does the speaker mention? In the 1930s, huge dust storms swept across the southern Great Plains of the United States, a period remembered as the Dust Bowl. In the decades before, farmers had ploughed up millions of hectares of native grassland to grow wheat. The deep roots of the prairie grasses had held the soil in place, even during dry spells. When a long drought arrived in the early 1930s, the exposed topsoil dried out and was carried away by strong winds. Some storms were so large that dust fell on cities on the east coast. Hundreds of thousands of people left the region, many travelling west to California in search of work. The government responded by creating a service to teach soil conservation, encouraging farmers to plough along the contours of the land, rotate crops and plant long rows of trees to break the wind.

questions.title: The Irish famine
questions.text: Which TWO statements about the famine are made by the speaker? Between 1845 and 1852, Ireland suffered one of the worst famines in modern European history. The immediate cause was potato blight, a disease caused by a fungus-like organism that turned potatoes black and rotten in the ground. The disaster was so severe because a large part of the population, especially the rural poor, depended almost entirely on potatoes for food, and most farmers grew the same variety, which had little resistance. Around one million people died, and at least another million emigrated, many to Britain and North America. The famine remains a painful and controversial subject, partly because food, including grain and livestock, continued to be exported from Ireland while people starved, and many historians criticise the government's response as inadequate. Ireland's population has never returned to the level it reached before the famine.

questions.title: Moving the stones of Stonehenge
questions.text: Which THREE statements are supported by the recording? Stonehenge, in southern England, was built in several stages over more than a thousand years, beginning around five thousand years ago. One of its greatest puzzles is how the stones arrived. The smaller bluestones, each weighing a few tonnes, have been traced to hills in west Wales, over two hundred kilometres away. The huge sarsen stones, some weighing more than twenty tonnes, came from a much closer source. In 2020, a chemical analysis of a core drilled from one stone identified a likely origin in an area about twenty-five kilometres to the north. Nobody knows exactly how the stones were moved, since the builders left no written records. Experiments suggest that teams of people could have pulled them on wooden sledges running over timber tracks, and some researchers believe the bluestones may have travelled part of the way by water.

questions.title: Who built the pyramids
questions.text: Which TWO pieces of evidence suggest that the workers were not slaves? For centuries, popular belief held that the pyramids of Egypt were built by huge numbers of slaves, an idea encouraged by ancient Greek writers and, much later, by Hollywood films. Archaeological discoveries near the pyramids at Giza have changed this picture. Since the 1990s, excavations have uncovered a settlement where workers lived, including bakeries and evidence that they ate large amounts of beef. Nearby, archaeologists found the tombs of workers, built close to the pyramids themselves, which would have been an honour unlikely to be given to slaves. Some skeletons show broken bones that had healed properly, suggesting that injured workers received medical care. Many researchers now believe the pyramids were built by a core of skilled, permanent craftsmen, supported by larger groups of labourers who worked in rotation, perhaps as a form of service owed to the state.

questions.title: Viking longships
questions.text: Which TWO features allowed longships to reach places far from the coast or land without a harbour? Viking longships were among the most advanced vessels of their time. They were built using overlapping wooden planks, a technique that made the hulls both strong and flexible, so they could bend with the waves rather than break. Crucially, the ships sat very low in the water, needing only about a metre of depth. This meant they could sail up rivers far inland and be pulled directly onto beaches, allowing raiders to arrive and leave quickly without a harbour. Longships carried a large square sail but also had oars, so crews could row when the wind dropped or when manoeuvring in narrow channels. The bow and stern were almost identical, so a ship could reverse direction without turning around. These vessels carried Norse explorers across the North Atlantic, and archaeological evidence confirms they reached North America around the year one thousand.

questions.title: Apollo 13
questions.text: Which THREE statements about the mission are correct? In April 1970, the Apollo 13 mission was on its way to the Moon when an oxygen tank in the service module exploded. The planned landing was immediately cancelled, and the priority became bringing the three astronauts home alive. The crew moved into the lunar module, the small craft intended for landing, and used it as a lifeboat, although it was designed to support only two people for about two days. A serious problem soon appeared. Carbon dioxide was building up in the cabin, and the square filters from the main spacecraft did not fit the round openings in the lunar module. Engineers on the ground designed a solution using only materials available on board, including plastic bags, cardboard and tape, and talked the crew through building it. After four tense days, the astronauts splashed down safely, and NASA later called the mission a successful failure.

questions.title: After the Tenerife collision
questions.text: Which TWO changes followed the accident? In 1977, two passenger jets collided on a foggy runway on the island of Tenerife, killing five hundred and eighty-three people in the deadliest accident in aviation history. Investigators found that a combination of factors was responsible. Visibility was very poor, radio messages were partly blocked and misunderstood, and one captain began his take-off without clear permission. Other members of his crew appear to have had doubts but did not challenge him forcefully. The disaster led to important changes. Standard radio phrases were tightened, so that the word take-off is now used only when a plane is actually cleared to take off. Airlines also introduced training known as crew resource management, which teaches pilots to work as a team and encourages junior crew members to speak up when they see a problem, however senior the captain. Hospitals and other high-risk workplaces have since adopted similar training.

questions.title: Hubble's blurred vision
questions.text: Which TWO statements about the telescope are correct? When the Hubble Space Telescope was launched in 1990, astronomers expected spectacular images. Instead, the first pictures were disappointingly blurry. Investigators discovered that the telescope's main mirror had been ground to a slightly incorrect shape. The error was tiny, about one fiftieth of the width of a human hair, but for such a precise instrument it was enough to spoil the images. The mistake was traced to a faulty testing device used during manufacture. Because Hubble orbits the Earth, it could be reached by the space shuttle. In 1993, astronauts carried out a complex servicing mission and installed corrective optics that worked rather like glasses. The results were a dramatic success. Hubble went on to produce some of the most famous images in the history of astronomy and was serviced several more times over the following years.

questions.title: The Harvard computers
questions.text: Which TWO achievements does the speaker describe? In the late nineteenth century, the director of the Harvard College Observatory hired a group of women to study thousands of photographic plates of the night sky. They were known as computers, because their job was to calculate and classify, and they were paid far less than male assistants would have been. Yet their work transformed astronomy. Annie Jump Cannon examined hundreds of thousands of stars and developed a system for classifying them by the features of their light, a system still taught today. Henrietta Swan Leavitt studied a type of star whose brightness rises and falls regularly, and found that the length of this cycle was linked to the star's true brightness. This allowed astronomers to calculate distances to faraway stars, and it later helped Edwin Hubble show that the universe extends far beyond our own galaxy.

questions.title: Radar and the Battle of Britain
questions.text: Which TWO advantages of the radar system are mentioned? In the 1930s, the British government asked scientists whether a beam of radio waves could be used as a death ray to destroy enemy aircraft. The physicist Robert Watson-Watt concluded that this was impossible, but he suggested something more useful: radio waves could be used to detect aircraft. By the start of the Second World War, a chain of radar stations along the coast could spot approaching planes long before they arrived. The information was passed to operations rooms, where staff plotted the positions of aircraft on large maps and decided which fighter squadrons to send. This system meant that fighters did not need to patrol the skies constantly, wasting fuel and exhausting pilots. Instead, they could be sent exactly where they were needed. Many historians regard radar as a key factor in the Battle of Britain in 1940.

questions.title: Mosquitoes and malaria
questions.text: Which TWO statements are supported by the recording? The word malaria comes from the Italian for bad air, reflecting an old belief that the disease was caused by foul air rising from swamps. It was a reasonable guess, since malaria was common near marshes, but the real cause was not understood until the late nineteenth century. In 1880, a French army doctor saw tiny parasites in the blood of a patient. The next question was how the parasite passed from one person to another. In 1897 and 1898, Ronald Ross, a British doctor working in India, showed that mosquitoes carried the parasite and transmitted it through their bites, work that earned him a Nobel Prize. The discovery explained the link with swamps, where mosquitoes breed, and it led to practical measures such as draining standing water and sleeping under nets, which remain important today.

questions.title: Bacteria in the gut
questions.text: Which THREE roles of gut bacteria does the speaker mention? The human gut is home to trillions of microorganisms, mostly bacteria, together known as the gut microbiome. For a long time these organisms received little attention, but research over the past two decades has shown that they play important roles in our health. Many of them break down types of dietary fibre that our own digestive system cannot process, producing substances that nourish the cells lining the gut. Some bacteria produce vitamins, such as vitamin K. The microbiome also appears to help train the immune system. The composition of these communities varies greatly between people and is shaped by diet, environment and medicines. A course of antibiotics, for example, can temporarily reduce their diversity. Researchers are also investigating possible links between gut bacteria and mood, but many of these findings are still at an early stage and should be treated with caution.

questions.title: How bacteria resist antibiotics
questions.text: Which THREE statements are made in the recording? When Alexander Fleming accepted the Nobel Prize for the discovery of penicillin in 1945, he warned that misuse of the drug could allow bacteria to become resistant. His warning proved accurate. Bacteria reproduce very quickly, and random changes in their genes occasionally make some of them less vulnerable to a particular antibiotic. When the drug is used, it kills the vulnerable bacteria, but the resistant ones survive and multiply. Bacteria can also pass genes for resistance directly to one another, even across different species, which allows resistance to spread rapidly. Every use of antibiotics creates pressure for resistance, so unnecessary use is particularly harmful. Antibiotics have no effect on viral infections such as colds and flu, yet they have often been prescribed for them. Large quantities have also been used in farming to help animals grow faster, a practice now restricted in many countries.

questions.title: Caffeine and sleepiness
questions.text: Which TWO statements about caffeine are correct according to the speaker? Why does coffee make us feel more alert? During the hours we are awake, a chemical called adenosine gradually builds up in the brain. As it attaches to receptors on nerve cells, it creates a growing sense of sleepiness. Caffeine has a similar shape to adenosine, so it can occupy these receptors without activating them, effectively blocking the signal that tells us we are tired. Caffeine does not provide energy in the way food does; it simply masks fatigue. Its effects also last longer than many people realise. In a typical adult, it takes around five hours for the body to remove half of the caffeine consumed, so an afternoon coffee may still affect sleep at night. People who drink coffee every day also develop tolerance, meaning they need more to feel the same effect, and they may experience headaches if they suddenly stop.

questions.title: Sunlight and vitamin D
questions.text: Which TWO statements about vitamin D are made? Vitamin D is unusual among vitamins because the body can make it for itself. When ultraviolet light from the sun reaches the skin, it triggers a chemical reaction that produces vitamin D. The vitamin helps the body absorb calcium from food, which is essential for strong bones. A severe lack of it in childhood can cause rickets, a condition in which bones become soft and bend. In countries far from the equator, the winter sun is too low in the sky for its ultraviolet rays to be strong enough to produce vitamin D, even on a clear day. People with darker skin, which contains more of the pigment that protects against ultraviolet light, generally need longer in the sun to make the same amount. For these reasons, some health authorities advise people to take supplements during winter, while oily fish and eggs provide smaller amounts through diet.

questions.title: Walking and new ideas
questions.text: Which TWO findings are reported? Many writers and thinkers have claimed that they think best while walking. In 2014, researchers at Stanford University tested this idea. Participants were asked to think of creative uses for everyday objects, such as a button or a tyre, either while sitting or while walking. Most people produced considerably more ideas when walking. Surprisingly, it did not matter whether they walked outdoors or on a treadmill facing a blank wall inside a small room; the act of walking itself seemed to be what mattered. The benefit also continued for a short time after participants sat down again. However, walking did not help with every kind of thinking. On tasks that required finding one correct answer, rather than generating many possibilities, walkers performed no better than those who were sitting. The researchers suggested that a walk might be most useful at the start of a project, when new ideas are needed.

questions.title: Why we sweat
questions.text: Which TWO statements are supported by the recording? Humans are unusually good at sweating. We have millions of sweat glands spread across the skin, far more than most other mammals, and in hot conditions we can lose more than a litre of sweat an hour. Sweat itself does not cool us; the cooling comes when it evaporates, because turning liquid water into vapour takes heat from the skin. This is why humid weather can be dangerous. When the air already contains a lot of moisture, sweat evaporates slowly, and it drips off the body instead of cooling it. Many other animals rely on different methods. Dogs, for example, have few sweat glands and cool down mainly by panting. Some researchers believe our ability to sweat helped early humans hunt by running long distances in the heat, chasing animals until they were exhausted, although this idea is still debated.

questions.title: The eel's life cycle
questions.text: Which TWO statements about European eels are correct? The European eel has one of the strangest life cycles of any fish. For centuries, nobody knew where eels came from, because no one had ever found eel eggs in European rivers. In the early twentieth century, a Danish scientist followed ever smaller eel larvae across the Atlantic and concluded that they hatch in the Sargasso Sea, a region of the western Atlantic. The tiny, leaf-shaped larvae drift on ocean currents for months or even years until they reach the coasts of Europe, where they turn into young eels and swim up rivers. There they may live for decades before making the long journey back across the ocean to breed, after which they die. Remarkably, no one has ever observed eels spawning in the wild. The species is now critically endangered, and scientists are still trying to understand all the reasons for its decline.

questions.title: The coelacanth
questions.text: Which TWO statements about the coelacanth are made? Until 1938, the coelacanth was known only from fossils, and scientists believed it had died out around the same time as the dinosaurs. Then, in December of that year, a fishing boat off the coast of South Africa brought up a strange, large blue fish. A local museum curator, Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer, recognised that it was unusual and contacted a scientist, who identified it as a living coelacanth. The discovery caused a sensation. The fish has thick, fleshy fins that move in a pattern resembling the legs of land animals, which makes it important for understanding how vertebrates moved onto land. A second species was found in Indonesia in 1997. The coelacanth is often called a living fossil, but scientists point out that the term is misleading, because modern coelacanths are not identical to their ancient relatives.

questions.title: Squid of the deep
questions.text: Which TWO statements about the giant squid are correct? For centuries, sailors told stories of enormous sea monsters with long arms, and the giant squid may lie behind some of these legends. Dead specimens occasionally washed ashore, showing that the animals could grow to well over ten metres including their tentacles, but no one had seen one alive in the deep ocean. The first photographs of a living giant squid in its natural habitat were taken by Japanese researchers in 2004. In 2012, a team finally filmed one in the deep sea. Their success depended on being quiet and subtle: instead of bright lights and noisy vehicles, they used a camera with dim red light and a lure that imitated the glow of a jellyfish in distress, which may attract predators. Giant squid also have some of the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, about the size of a dinner plate.

questions.title: The narwhal's tusk
questions.text: Which TWO statements are made about narwhal tusks? The narwhal is a medium-sized whale that lives in the Arctic Ocean, and it is best known for the long spiral tusk that grows from the heads of most males. The tusk is in fact a tooth, which can grow to around three metres in length. In medieval Europe, narwhal tusks were brought back by traders and sold as the horns of unicorns, fetching extraordinary prices because they were believed to have magical powers. The true purpose of the tusk has long been debated. It contains millions of nerve endings, leading some scientists to suggest it can sense changes in the water around it. Others believe it plays a role in competition between males, who may display their tusks to attract females. In 2017, drone footage even showed narwhals using their tusks to tap and stun small fish before eating them.

questions.title: Built for speed
questions.text: Which THREE statements about cheetahs are correct? The cheetah is the fastest land animal, capable of reaching around one hundred kilometres an hour in a few seconds. Its body is built for speed: it has a light frame, long legs and an unusually flexible spine that stretches and bends with each stride, lengthening its step. Unlike most cats, it cannot fully retract its claws, which grip the ground like the spikes on a sprinter's shoes. Its long tail acts as a counterbalance, helping it change direction sharply when chasing prey. However, speed has costs. A chase usually lasts less than a minute, because the cheetah quickly becomes exhausted and overheated. After a successful hunt, it often needs to rest before eating, and during this time larger predators such as lions and hyenas may steal its kill. As a result, cheetahs lose a significant share of the food they catch.

questions.title: How kangaroos hop
questions.text: Which TWO statements about kangaroos are made? Hopping looks like a tiring way to travel, but for large kangaroos it is remarkably efficient. When a kangaroo lands, the long tendons in its hind legs stretch and store elastic energy, rather like springs. This energy is released in the next jump, so the muscles do not have to do all the work. Studies in the 1970s found that, above a certain speed, a hopping kangaroo uses hardly any extra energy as it goes faster. This is very different from animals that run on four legs, which use more and more energy as their speed increases. At slow speeds, however, hopping is less practical. When feeding, kangaroos move in a slower way, using their powerful tail as a kind of fifth leg, supporting their weight while they swing their hind legs forward. Their body shape also makes it very difficult for them to move backwards.

questions.title: Homing pigeons
questions.text: Which TWO methods of navigation does the speaker mention? Homing pigeons can return to their lofts from places hundreds of kilometres away, even if they have never visited them before. How they do this is still not fully understood. Experiments suggest that they use several different cues. On sunny days, pigeons can use the position of the sun as a compass, adjusting for the time of day with an internal clock. When the sky is overcast, they still manage to navigate, and many researchers believe they can sense the Earth's magnetic field. Some Italian studies found that pigeons with an impaired sense of smell struggled to find their way, suggesting that odours carried by the wind may form part of a map. Close to home, familiar landmarks become important. Tracking studies have even shown pigeons following motorways and turning at major junctions, much as a human driver would.

questions.title: Dogs that detect disease
questions.text: Which TWO statements are made in the recording? A dog's sense of smell is far more sensitive than ours, and researchers have been investigating whether dogs can detect diseases by their odour. Many illnesses change the chemical compounds our bodies release, sometimes in tiny amounts. Trained dogs have been used to alert people with diabetes when their blood sugar falls to dangerous levels, and studies have tested dogs' ability to identify certain cancers and infections from samples of breath, urine or clothing.
