Some results have been impressive, but there are practical challenges. Training a detection dog takes time and money, dogs can become tired or distracted, and individual dogs perform differently. For these reasons, many scientists see the dogs not as a replacement for medical tests, but as a guide. By identifying the chemicals the dogs are responding to, researchers hope to design electronic devices that can detect them in the same way.

questions.title: Wildcats and grain stores
questions.text: Which TWO statements about the domestication of cats are correct? Unlike dogs, which people may have actively tamed, cats seem to have largely domesticated themselves. Genetic studies suggest the process began around ten thousand years ago in the Near East, when people started farming and storing grain. The stores attracted mice and rats, and these in turn attracted wildcats. Cats that were less fearful of people could take advantage of this new source of food, and farmers had good reason to tolerate them. Some of the earliest evidence of a close bond comes from a grave on the island of Cyprus, around nine and a half thousand years old, where a person was buried with a cat. Ancient Egypt later played an important role in spreading tame cats and celebrating them in art. Even today, domestic cats remain genetically quite similar to their wild relatives, and many can still survive perfectly well without human help.

questions.title: Vampire bat cooperation
questions.text: Which TWO statements are supported by the recording? Vampire bats feed only on blood, and their lives are finely balanced. A bat that fails to find a meal for two or three nights in a row is at serious risk of starving. On any given night, some bats return to the roost hungry. Researchers have observed that well-fed bats often regurgitate some of their meal to feed these hungry companions. This sharing is not limited to close relatives. Long-term studies have found that bats are more likely to share with individuals that have shared with them in the past, a pattern that looks like a system of mutual help. In experiments, bats that had built up a wider network of sharing partners were better protected when one partner was unavailable. The findings make vampire bats an important example for scientists studying how cooperation develops among animals that are not related.

questions.title: Bees and static charge
questions.text: Which TWO statements are made about bumblebees? As a bumblebee flies, friction with the air gives its body a small positive electric charge. Flowers, meanwhile, tend to carry a slight negative charge. When a bee lands on a flower, some of the charge is transferred, and the electric field around the flower changes for a short time. In 2013, researchers in Britain showed that bumblebees can detect these electric fields and learn to use them. In experiments with artificial flowers, bees learned to tell rewarding flowers from unrewarding ones using electric fields alone. Later work suggested that the bees sense the fields through tiny hairs on their bodies, which move in response. This could help a bee avoid wasting time on a flower whose nectar has just been taken by another insect. It is a reminder that animals may perceive the world through senses we are only beginning to understand.

questions.title: Clownfish and anemones
questions.text: Which THREE statements about clownfish are correct? Clownfish live among the tentacles of sea anemones, which are covered in stinging cells that can paralyse other small fish. Clownfish are protected by a layer of mucus on their skin, which appears to stop the anemone from firing its stinging cells. The relationship benefits both animals. The anemone provides the clownfish with shelter from predators, while the clownfish chases away fish that might eat the anemone, and its waste may provide the anemone with nutrients. Clownfish also have an unusual social structure. Each anemone is usually home to a group led by a single breeding female, the largest fish, and a breeding male. All clownfish are born male. If the female dies, the breeding male changes sex and becomes female, and the next largest fish takes his place. This detail of their biology would change the story of a famous animated film considerably.

questions.title: Figs and their wasps
questions.text: Which TWO statements about figs are made? A fig is not really a fruit in the usual sense. It is a hollow structure lined on the inside with hundreds of tiny flowers, hidden from view. This creates a problem: how can the flowers be pollinated? The answer is a remarkable partnership with tiny insects called fig wasps. A female wasp, carrying pollen, squeezes through a narrow opening into the fig, often losing her wings in the process. Inside, she pollinates the flowers and lays her eggs, and then she dies. Her offspring develop inside the fig, and new females leave carrying pollen to another fig. Many fig species rely on their own particular species of wasp, and neither could reproduce without the other. Because fig trees produce fruit throughout the year, they are an essential source of food for many birds, bats and monkeys in tropical forests.

questions.title: Orchids that deceive
questions.text: Which TWO statements about orchids are correct? Most flowering plants offer pollinators a reward, such as nectar or pollen, in exchange for carrying pollen from one flower to another. A surprising number of orchids, however, offer nothing at all. Estimates suggest that around a third of orchid species attract insects through deception. Some produce bright colours and shapes that resemble nectar-rich flowers, even though they contain no nectar. Others are even more elaborate. Certain orchids produce a scent that closely imitates the chemical signals released by female insects, and their flowers may even look like the female. Male insects are attracted, try to mate with the flower, and pick up pollen, which they then carry to the next orchid that deceives them. The strategy works because the insects are deceived only occasionally, but it does mean that such orchids often depend on a single species of insect for their survival.

questions.title: Sunflowers and the sun
questions.text: Which TWO findings does the speaker report? Young sunflowers really do follow the sun. During the day, the growing plants gradually turn from east to west, and at night they swing back to face east, ready for sunrise. Research published in 2016 showed that this movement is controlled partly by the plant's internal clock, which allows it to anticipate the sun's position rather than simply react to it. The turning is produced by the stem growing faster on one side than on the other. Once the plants mature and their flowers open, they stop moving and most end up facing east. The researchers found that this has an advantage. East-facing flowers warm up more quickly in the morning sun, and warm flowers attract more visits from bees and other pollinators than flowers that face west. So the direction a sunflower faces may have a direct effect on its success in producing seeds.

questions.title: The baobab tree
questions.text: Which TWO statements about baobabs are made? The baobab tree, found across the dry savannahs of Africa, is famous for its enormous, swollen trunk. The trunk stores large quantities of water, which helps the tree survive long dry seasons, and it may lose its leaves for much of the year to reduce water loss. Baobabs can live for well over a thousand years, and some hollow trunks have been used by people as shelters and storage rooms. The trees are also valuable for food: the fruit contains a dry pulp that is rich in vitamin C. In 2018, researchers who had been dating the oldest baobabs reported that several of the largest and most ancient trees had died or lost their oldest parts within the previous decade. They suggested that changes in climate might be involved, but they stressed that more research was needed to be sure.

questions.title: How dandelion seeds fly
questions.text: Which TWO statements are made about the dandelion's parachute? Each dandelion seed hangs beneath a tiny parachute made of around one hundred fine bristles. Surprisingly, this parachute is mostly empty space, yet it keeps the seed airborne so effectively that seeds can travel long distances on the wind. In 2018, researchers in Scotland used wind tunnels to discover how it works. They found that as air flows through the gaps between the bristles, it forms a stable ring of swirling air that sits just above the parachute without being carried away. This ring lowers the pressure above the seed and helps slow its fall. The researchers calculated that the bristle structure is several times more efficient, for its weight, than a solid disc of the same size would be. The discovery has interested engineers who design very small flying devices, which need to stay in the air using as little material and energy as possible.

questions.title: Rolling tumbleweeds
questions.text: Which TWO statements about tumbleweeds are correct? In Western films, tumbleweeds rolling across an empty town have become a symbol of the American frontier. A tumbleweed is the dried upper part of certain plants that, once mature, breaks away from its roots and is blown along by the wind. As it tumbles, it scatters its seeds across a wide area, and a single large plant can release many thousands. Ironically, one of the best-known tumbleweeds in North America, the Russian thistle, is not native there. It is believed to have arrived in the late nineteenth century, mixed in with a shipment of crop seeds brought by farmers from Eastern Europe. It spread rapidly across the plains. Today tumbleweeds can be a real nuisance, piling up against fences and houses, blocking roads, and sometimes presenting a fire risk when they collect in large numbers.

questions.title: Dwarf elephants
questions.text: Which TWO statements are supported by the recording? When animals become isolated on islands, their body size often changes over many generations. Large animals frequently become smaller, a pattern known as island dwarfism. Fossils show that elephants living on several Mediterranean islands, including Sicily and Malta, evolved into dwarf forms, some only about a metre tall. Scientists think that limited food on small islands favoured smaller bodies, which need less energy, and that the absence of large predators removed one of the advantages of being big. The opposite can happen to small animals, which sometimes grow larger than their mainland relatives, a pattern called island gigantism. Examples include giant rats and lizards on certain islands. The discovery of fossils of a small human species on the Indonesian island of Flores has led some researchers to ask whether similar processes may even have affected our own relatives.

questions.title: Tortoises of the Galápagos
questions.text: Which THREE statements are made in the recording? Giant tortoises once lived in huge numbers on the Galápagos Islands. Their ability to survive for many months without food or water proved disastrous for them. From the seventeenth century onwards, sailors and whalers collected thousands of tortoises and stored them alive in the holds of their ships, providing a supply of fresh meat on long voyages. Later, settlers and the animals they introduced added to the damage. Goats, in particular, ate much of the vegetation the tortoises relied on. Several species became extinct. One famous tortoise, known as Lonesome George, was the last known member of his species when he died in 2012. Conservation programmes have since removed goats from several islands and bred tortoises in captivity for release into the wild, and some populations have recovered significantly, although others remain at risk.

questions.title: The kiwi
questions.text: Which THREE statements about the kiwi are correct? The kiwi, New Zealand's national bird, is unusual in many ways. It cannot fly, and its tiny wings are hidden beneath its feathers. It is mostly active at night, and unlike almost all other birds, it has nostrils at the tip of its long beak, which it uses to smell insects and worms in the soil. Perhaps most remarkably, the female lays an enormous egg compared with her body size, around a fifth of her own weight, one of the largest egg-to-body ratios of any bird. Before humans arrived, New Zealand had no land mammals except bats, so the kiwi had few predators on the ground. Today introduced animals, especially stoats, kill most chicks before they are old enough to defend themselves. Conservation programmes collect eggs from the wild, hatch them in safety, and return the young birds once they are large enough to survive.

questions.title: The passenger pigeon
questions.text: Which THREE statements are supported by the recording? In the nineteenth century, the passenger pigeon may have been the most numerous bird in North America, with a population estimated in the billions. Observers described flocks so large that they darkened the sky for hours as they passed. Yet by 1914 the species was extinct; the last known individual, a female named Martha, died in a zoo in Cincinnati. Commercial hunting was a major cause. New technologies played a part: telegraph networks allowed hunters to learn quickly where flocks were nesting, and railways carried vast quantities of meat to city markets. The clearing of forests also removed the birds' habitat. Some scientists believe the species was especially vulnerable because it bred in enormous colonies, and when numbers fell, the remaining small groups may not have been able to breed successfully.

questions.title: Commuting and happiness
questions.text: Which TWO findings does the speaker report? When researchers ask people to describe how they felt during different activities throughout the day, commuting regularly appears among the least enjoyable. Economists have also noticed a puzzle. People who accept a long commute should, in theory, be compensated by something else, such as a higher salary or a larger home. Yet some studies have found that people with long commutes report lower satisfaction with their lives, suggesting that many underestimate the cost of travel when choosing where to live or work. Not all commutes are equal, however. People who walk or cycle to work tend to report higher satisfaction than those who drive or use crowded public transport, perhaps because of the exercise and the predictability of the journey. The growth of working from home has given researchers new opportunities to study how the time saved is actually used.

questions.title: Blind orchestra auditions
questions.text: Which TWO statements are made in the recording? In the 1970s and 1980s, many major orchestras in the United States began holding auditions behind a screen, so that the judges could hear the musician but not see them. Some orchestras even laid carpet on the stage, so that the sound of footsteps would not reveal whether a candidate was wearing high heels. During the same period, the proportion of women in these orchestras increased considerably. A widely cited study published in 2000 concluded that the screens had helped women advance, and the case became a famous example of how removing information can reduce bias. In recent years, some researchers have argued that the statistical evidence in the study was weaker than often claimed. Even so, the idea behind blind auditions has influenced recruitment in other fields, such as removing names from job applications during the first stage of selection.

questions.title: Better job interviews
questions.text: Which TWO statements about interviews are supported? Job interviews are one of the most common ways of choosing employees, yet research suggests that traditional interviews are surprisingly poor at predicting how well someone will perform in a job. In an unstructured interview, the conversation can go in any direction, and interviewers often form a strong impression within the first few minutes, sometimes based on factors such as confidence or shared interests that have little to do with the job. Decades of studies have found that structured interviews work considerably better. In a structured interview, every candidate is asked the same questions, which are based on the skills the job requires, and answers are scored using agreed criteria. Some organisations combine this with work sample tests, in which candidates complete a task similar to the real job. These methods do not remove human judgement, but they help to make it fairer and more consistent.

questions.title: The economics of presents
questions.text: Which TWO points does the speaker make? In 1993, the economist Joel Waldfogel published a paper with a provocative title: The Deadweight Loss of Christmas. He asked students to estimate how much the givers had paid for gifts they had received and how much they would have been willing to pay for them. On average, recipients valued their gifts at noticeably less than the price the giver had paid, and the gap was largest for gifts from more distant relatives. From a purely economic point of view, giving cash would avoid this loss, since people could buy exactly what they wanted. In practice, however, many people feel that giving money is impersonal or even rude. Gift cards offer a compromise, although a proportion of them are never spent. Critics of the study also point out that it ignores sentimental value: a gift can matter because of who chose it, not only because of what it is.

questions.title: Getting used to good fortune
questions.text: Which TWO statements are supported by the recording? A famous study published in 1978 compared people who had won large sums in a lottery with people who had not. Some time after their win, the lottery winners were not significantly happier than the comparison group, and they reported taking less pleasure in ordinary everyday activities. The study is often used to illustrate an idea called hedonic adaptation: people tend to get used to changes in their circumstances, whether positive or negative, and their happiness gradually drifts back towards its usual level. This helps explain why a pay rise or a new car may bring only temporary satisfaction. However, later research has shown that adaptation is not complete for every kind of event. Some experiences, such as long-term unemployment or the loss of a partner, can have lasting effects on well-being.

questions.title: Handedness
questions.text: Which THREE statements are made in the recording? Around one in ten people around the world are left-handed, a proportion that appears to have been fairly stable for thousands of years, judging by evidence from ancient tools and artwork. Handedness is influenced by genes, but no single gene determines it, and environmental factors also play a part. For much of history, left-handed children were often forced to write with their right hand, and the words for left in several languages carry negative meanings. Left-handers are, however, overrepresented at the top level of some sports. In one-on-one contests such as fencing, boxing and tennis, they may have an advantage because most opponents spend their time competing against right-handers and are less familiar with the angles a left-hander creates. Some researchers have suggested that a similar advantage in fighting may help explain why left-handedness has survived throughout human evolution.

questions.title: Childhood amnesia
questions.text: Which TWO explanations for childhood amnesia does the speaker mention? Most adults cannot remember anything from the first three or four years of their lives, even though young children clearly form memories at the time; a two-year-old can remember a visit to the park the week before. This loss of early memories is known as childhood amnesia. Researchers have proposed several explanations. The hippocampus, a brain region important for forming long-term memories of events, is still developing in early childhood, and the rapid growth of new brain cells may disrupt older memories. Language may also play a role: memories formed before children can describe experiences in words may be harder to retrieve later. In addition, many people report early memories that are actually based on family photographs or stories they have heard, rather than on the events themselves. Studies have shown that it is surprisingly easy to create such false memories, especially of early childhood.

questions.title: Bacteria on dropped snacks
questions.text: Which THREE findings are reported? Many people follow the so-called five-second rule, believing that food dropped on the floor is safe to eat if it is picked up quickly. In 2016, researchers in the United States tested this belief. They contaminated different surfaces, including stainless steel, tiles, wood and carpet, with bacteria, and then dropped foods such as watermelon, bread and gummy sweets onto them for different lengths of time. They found that bacteria could move onto food in less than a second, so the rule is not reliable. Longer contact did lead to more contamination, however. Moisture was the most important factor: watermelon picked up the most bacteria, while the gummy sweets picked up the least. Surprisingly, carpet transferred fewer bacteria than steel or tiles, possibly because food touches less of its surface. The researchers concluded that the five-second rule is a significant oversimplification.

questions.title: Recognising a reflection
questions.text: Which TWO statements about the mirror test are made? In 1970, the psychologist Gordon Gallup developed a simple test of whether animals recognise themselves. Chimpanzees were given time to become familiar with a mirror, and then a coloured mark was placed on their faces while they were anaesthetised, in a position they could see only in the mirror. When they woke, several chimpanzees looked in the mirror and touched the mark on their own faces, suggesting they understood that the reflection showed themselves. Since then, great apes, some elephants, dolphins and magpies have been reported to pass versions of the test. Many other animals, including dogs, do not. Critics argue that the test favours species that depend heavily on vision. Dogs rely much more on smell, and researchers have designed experiments suggesting that dogs may recognise their own scent in ways similar to a mirror test.

questions.title: Darwin's earthworms
questions.text: Which TWO statements are made about Darwin's research? Charles Darwin's final book, published in 1881, was not about evolution but about earthworms, and it sold remarkably well. Darwin had studied worms for decades. He measured how quickly objects left on the surface of fields were buried as worms brought soil up from below, and he showed that worms had helped to bury ancient buildings and stones. He argued that worms were enormously important to agriculture, because by constantly swallowing and moving soil they mix it, let air and water in, and make it more fertile. Some of his experiments were charmingly unusual. He tested whether worms could hear by having his son play the bassoon to them, and by playing notes on a piano. The worms showed no reaction to the music, but when their pots were placed on top of the piano, they responded quickly to the vibrations.

questions.title: Pisa's tilt
questions.text: Which THREE statements about the tower are correct? Construction of the famous bell tower in Pisa began in 1173, and it had reached only its third floor when it began to lean. The ground beneath it was soft and uneven, and one side sank more than the other. Work stopped for almost a century because of wars, and this long pause may have saved the tower, allowing the soil to compress and become stronger. When building resumed, the engineers tried to correct the tilt by making the upper floors slightly curved. By the late twentieth century, the lean had become so great that the tower was closed to the public in 1990. Engineers then carefully removed small amounts of soil from beneath the higher side, allowing it to settle and reducing the tilt without straightening it completely. The tower reopened in 2001, and experts believe it should remain stable for centuries.

questions.title: The first kidney transplant
questions.text: Why was the 1954 transplant successful? For centuries, doctors dreamed of replacing failing organs, but early attempts at transplants almost always failed. The main obstacle was the immune system, which recognises tissue from another person as foreign and attacks it, a process called rejection. In 1954, surgeons in Boston carried out the first successful long-term kidney transplant. The patient's donor was his identical twin brother. Because identical twins have almost perfectly matching tissues, the patient's immune system did not reject the new kidney, and he lived for another eight years. Transplants between people who were not identical twins remained very risky until drugs were developed to suppress the immune system. One of the most important of these was introduced in the early 1980s and greatly improved survival. Today, kidney transplants are routine operations in many countries, and the main limit is no longer surgical skill but the shortage of donated organs.

questions.title: Heating wine and milk
questions.text: According to the speaker, where did pasteurisation have its greatest impact? In the 1860s, French winemakers asked the chemist Louis Pasteur why so much of their wine was turning sour. Pasteur examined samples under a microscope and found that spoilage was caused by unwanted microorganisms. He showed that heating wine gently, to a temperature well below boiling, for a short time killed most of these microbes without ruining the taste. The process became known as pasteurisation. Although it was first developed for wine and beer, its greatest impact came later, when it was applied to milk. In the nineteenth century, milk was a common source of dangerous infections, including tuberculosis, especially in growing cities. Laws requiring milk to be pasteurised helped to reduce these diseases dramatically. Today the same principle, using carefully controlled heat to make food safer while keeping its quality, is applied to juices, eggs and many other products.

questions.title: Clarence Birdseye
questions.text: Why did the fish Birdseye saw in Labrador still taste fresh? In the 1910s, the American naturalist Clarence Birdseye spent several winters in Labrador, in northern Canada. There he watched Inuit fishers catch fish in temperatures of around minus forty degrees. The fish froze almost instantly in the icy air, and when they were cooked months later they still tasted fresh. Birdseye realised why. When food freezes slowly, large ice crystals form and damage its cells, so it becomes soft and watery when thawed. Rapid freezing produces much smaller crystals, which cause far less damage. Back in the United States, he developed machines that froze packaged food quickly between cold metal plates. His business was sold in 1929 for a very large sum, and the brand still carries his name. However, frozen food only became common in homes decades later, once household freezers and supermarket freezer cabinets were widespread.

questions.title: The story of ketchup
questions.text: Why did the Heinz company add more vinegar and sugar? The word ketchup probably comes from the name of a fermented fish sauce made in southern China and parts of Southeast Asia. British sailors and traders encountered it in the seventeenth century, and English cooks tried to recreate it at home, using ingredients such as mushrooms, walnuts and oysters. Tomato ketchup appeared in the United States in the early nineteenth century, but early versions often spoiled quickly, and some manufacturers added questionable chemicals to preserve them. In the early twentieth century, the company founded by Henry Heinz developed a recipe with much more vinegar and sugar, which preserved the sauce naturally without such additives. It also sold ketchup in clear glass bottles so that customers could see the product was pure. That sweeter, thicker recipe became the model for the ketchup now eaten around the world, far removed from its salty, fishy origins.

questions.title: The price of saffron
questions.text: According to the speaker, why is saffron so expensive? Saffron is often described as the most expensive spice in the world by weight, and the reason lies in how it is harvested. It comes from a crocus flower, and each flower produces only three thin red threads, called stigmas. These must be picked by hand, usually early in the morning, because the flowers open for only a short time in autumn. Estimates suggest that well over one hundred thousand flowers are needed to produce a single kilogram of dried saffron. Machines have so far been unable to replace skilled workers, because the threads are delicate. Iran produces the great majority of the world's supply, although saffron is also grown in Spain, India and elsewhere. Because of its high price, saffron is also a common target for fraud, with some sellers mixing in dyed plant fibres or other parts of the flower.

questions.title: Decaffeination
questions.text: Which statement about modern decaffeinated coffee is correct? Decaffeinated coffee has a surprising history. In the early twentieth century, the German merchant Ludwig Roselius is said to have received a shipment of coffee beans that had been soaked in seawater during the voyage. The beans had lost much of their caffeine but still tasted of coffee. Roselius developed a commercial process, but it used benzene, a chemical later found to be harmful, and it was eventually abandoned. Today caffeine is removed from green beans before they are roasted. Some methods use solvents that bind to caffeine; others use only water, passing it through filters that capture caffeine molecules; and some use carbon dioxide under very high pressure. None of these methods removes caffeine completely. Decaffeinated coffee usually keeps a small amount, which is why people who must avoid caffeine entirely are advised to check carefully before drinking it.

questions.title: Ripening bananas
questions.text: Why are bananas shipped in cool conditions? Many fruits, including bananas, tomatoes and avocados, continue to ripen after they are picked. The trigger is ethylene, a simple gas that the fruit produces itself. As ethylene levels rise, starches turn into sugars, the fruit softens and its colour changes. This explains the old saying that one bad apple spoils the barrel: a damaged or overripe fruit releases ethylene, which speeds up ripening in the fruit around it. Commercial growers make use of this. Bananas are usually harvested while still hard and green, shipped in cool conditions to slow them down, and then placed in ripening rooms where a controlled amount of ethylene is added. At home, you can speed up ripening by placing an unripe fruit in a paper bag with a ripe banana, which keeps the gas close to it. Other fruits, such as grapes and strawberries, do not ripen further after picking.

questions.title: Sweeteners found by accident
questions.text: What does the speaker imply about these discoveries? Several artificial sweeteners were discovered by accident, often because of poor laboratory hygiene. In 1879, the chemist Constantin Fahlberg was working on coal tar compounds at a university in the United States. That evening at dinner, he noticed that his bread tasted unusually sweet. He realised the sweetness came from a chemical on his hands, which he had not washed properly, and traced it back to his laboratory. The substance was saccharin, which is hundreds of times sweeter than sugar. Decades later, a sweetener called cyclamate was found when a student put his cigarette down on a laboratory bench and then noticed a sweet taste. Another sweetener was discovered in the 1970s when a researcher reportedly misheard an instruction to test a compound as an instruction to taste it. Such practices would be considered dangerous in laboratories today.

questions.title: The MSG scare
questions.text: What did controlled studies of MSG find? In 1968, a doctor wrote a letter to a medical journal describing symptoms such as numbness and weakness after eating at Chinese restaurants. He wondered whether monosodium glutamate, or MSG, a flavour enhancer, might be responsible. The idea spread quickly, and a name for the supposed condition entered popular language. Yet when researchers later carried out controlled studies, in which neither participants nor researchers knew who had received MSG, they did not find consistent reactions at the amounts normally found in food. Glutamate is also present naturally in foods such as tomatoes, mushrooms and aged cheese, which many people eat without concern. Some researchers argue that the rapid spread of fears about MSG reflected cultural bias against foreign food as much as scientific evidence. Food safety agencies generally regard MSG as safe, although a small number of people may be sensitive to very large doses.

questions.title: Use-by and best-before dates
questions.text: What is the main difference between the two kinds of date? Many shoppers throw away food as soon as the date on the packet has passed, but not all dates mean the same thing. In many countries, a use-by date is about safety. It appears on foods that can become dangerous quickly, such as fresh meat and fish, and these foods should not be eaten after that date. A best-before date, by contrast, is about quality. After it, the food may be less crisp or flavourful, but it is usually still safe to eat if it has been stored properly. Surveys suggest that many consumers confuse the two labels, and this confusion contributes to large amounts of household food waste. For this reason, several supermarkets have removed best-before dates from fresh fruit and vegetables altogether, encouraging customers to use their own judgement about whether produce is still good.

questions.title: Eating insects
questions.text: According to the speaker, what is the main barrier to eating insects in many Western countries? Insects are already a normal part of the diet for an estimated two billion people, particularly in parts of Asia, Africa and Latin America. Crickets, beetle larvae and caterpillars can be rich in protein, healthy fats and minerals. Supporters argue that farming insects could be far more efficient than raising cattle. Insects are cold-blooded, so they do not use energy to keep warm, and they convert feed into body weight much more efficiently. They also need less land and water. In many Western countries, however, the main obstacle is not nutrition or cost but disgust. For this reason, companies selling insect products often grind them into flour and add them to familiar foods, such as pasta, biscuits and protein bars, where the insects cannot be seen. Whether this approach will change eating habits on a large scale remains uncertain.

questions.title: How soap cleans
questions.text: Why can water alone not remove grease? Why does soap clean so much better than water alone? Many kinds of dirt, including grease and the oils from our skin, do not mix with water, so rinsing simply slides over them. Soap molecules solve this problem because they have two different ends. One end is attracted to water, while the other avoids water and is attracted to oils and fats. When you wash your hands, the oil-loving ends attach to grease and dirt, and the molecules gather around it in tiny clusters. The water-loving ends face outwards, so the whole cluster can be rinsed away. Soap can also damage certain viruses, which are surrounded by a fatty outer layer that the soap molecules break apart. This is why health authorities recommend washing hands with soap for at least twenty seconds, giving the molecules time to work.

questions.title: Pressure cookers
questions.text: Why does food take longer to cook in boiling water on high mountains? At sea level, water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius. But the boiling point depends on air pressure, and as you climb higher, the pressure falls. On high mountains, water boils at a noticeably lower temperature, so food cooked in boiling water takes much longer to become tender. Climbers near the summit of Everest would find their water boiling at around seventy degrees, which is not hot enough to cook rice or lentils properly. A pressure cooker solves this problem. Its lid seals tightly, so steam cannot escape, and the pressure inside rises. Under this higher pressure, water can reach well over one hundred degrees before boiling, and food cooks much faster. The principle is old: in the seventeenth century, the French scientist Denis Papin demonstrated a steam digester that could soften even bones. Today pressure cookers are especially popular in mountain regions.

questions.title: Shocks from door handles
questions.text: Why are static shocks more common in winter? Most people have felt a small electric shock when touching a door handle after walking across a carpet. This is static electricity. When two materials rub together, electrons can move from one to the other, leaving one surface with a negative charge and the other with a positive charge. The charge builds up on your body until you touch a conductor, such as a metal handle, and it suddenly jumps across, producing a tiny spark. Static shocks are much more common in winter. The reason is not the cold itself but the dry air. When the air is humid, a thin layer of moisture on surfaces allows charge to leak away gradually. In dry conditions, charge builds up instead. Static electricity is usually harmless, but it can be dangerous near flammable vapours, which is why fuel stations and factories take care to prevent sparks.

questions.title: Franklin's rod
questions.text: How does a lightning rod protect a building? In the 1750s, Benjamin Franklin set out to show that lightning was a form of electricity. In his famous kite experiment, he reportedly flew a kite during a storm and collected electric charge in a special jar, although historians still debate exactly how the experiment was carried out. Whatever the details, Franklin used his ideas to design a practical invention: the lightning rod. A pointed metal rod is fixed to the highest part of a building and connected by a thick wire to the ground. If lightning strikes, the current follows this path into the earth instead of passing through the walls and roof, where it could start a fire. Some people at the time objected, believing that lightning was a divine punishment that humans should not interfere with. Nevertheless, lightning rods spread quickly, and they are still used on tall buildings today.

questions.title: The blue LED
questions.text: Why was the blue LED so important? Light-emitting diodes, or LEDs, have existed since the 1960s, but for decades they were used mainly as small red or green indicator lights. To produce bright white light efficiently, engineers needed a blue LED as well, and this proved extraordinarily difficult. Many large companies gave up. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, three researchers working in Japan, Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura, finally succeeded, using a material called gallium nitride that others had considered too hard to work with. Their breakthrough made energy-saving white LED lamps possible, as well as the bright screens in modern phones and televisions. LED lamps use a fraction of the electricity of traditional bulbs and last far longer. In 2014, the three scientists were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics, with the committee noting that the invention would benefit the whole world.

questions.title: Why bicycles stay upright
questions.text: What did the 2011 experiment show? Why does a moving bicycle stay upright, while a stationary one falls over? For many years, the usual explanation was that the spinning wheels act like gyroscopes, resisting any change in their direction. Another popular idea focused on the angle of the front fork. In 2011, however, a team of engineers built an unusual experimental bicycle designed to cancel out both of these effects. Surprisingly, when pushed without a rider, it still balanced itself. The researchers concluded that stability comes from a combination of factors, including how the mass of the bicycle is distributed and how the front wheel is steered. When a bicycle starts to lean, the front wheel tends to turn in the same direction, bringing the wheels back under the frame. A rider does the same thing without thinking, steering slightly into a fall.

questions.title: Swerving free kicks
questions.text: What causes a spinning ball to curve? Footballers who can make the ball swerve in the air are using a principle called the Magnus effect. When a player strikes the ball off-centre, it spins as it travels. The spinning surface drags the surrounding air with it, so air on one side of the ball moves faster than air on the other. This creates a difference in pressure, and the ball is pushed sideways, curving towards the side with lower pressure. One of the most famous examples came in 1997, when the Brazilian defender Roberto Carlos scored a free kick that seemed to be heading well wide before bending sharply into the goal. The same effect explains why tennis players use topspin to make the ball dip, and engineers have even applied it to ships, using tall spinning cylinders on deck to help them move with the wind.

questions.title: Banned swimsuits
questions.text: Why did the governing body change the rules in 2010? At the Beijing Olympics in 2008 and the world championships a year later, swimmers broke world records at an astonishing rate. Much of the credit went to a new generation of full-body swimsuits. Some were made partly or entirely from polyurethane, a material that trapped air, increased buoyancy and squeezed the body into a more streamlined shape, reducing drag in the water. Critics argued that races were becoming contests between suit manufacturers rather than athletes, and that swimmers without the latest suits were at a disadvantage. In response, the sport's governing body introduced new rules from 2010, requiring suits to be made from textile materials and limiting how much of the body they could cover. Many records set in that period stood for years afterwards, and some commentators still describe them as difficult to compare with those set before or since.

questions.title: Super shoes
questions.text: How did the governing body respond to the new shoes? In recent years, running shoes with a stiff carbon-fibre plate inside thick, springy foam have transformed long-distance running. Laboratory studies found that some of these shoes reduced the energy runners needed at a given pace by around four percent on average, a very large improvement at elite level. Marathon times fell sharply, and athletes wearing them set a series of records. The shoes raised a difficult question: at what point does equipment give an unfair advantage? In 2020, the sport's governing body responded not by banning the technology but by setting limits. Shoes used in road races must now have soles no thicker than forty millimetres, and they must be available for the public to buy, so that athletes cannot use secret prototypes. Some experts believe the benefit varies considerably from one runner to another.

questions.title: Training in thin air
questions.text: What is the purpose of the live high, train low approach? Many endurance athletes spend weeks training at high altitude before important competitions. At altitude, each breath contains less oxygen, and over several weeks the body responds by producing more red blood cells, which carry oxygen to the muscles. When the athletes return to lower ground, they may benefit from this extra capacity for a limited time. However, training hard at altitude is difficult, because athletes cannot run as fast in the thin air. This led to an approach known as live high, train low: athletes sleep and rest at altitude but travel down to lower areas for their most intense sessions. The success of runners who grew up in the highlands of Kenya and Ethiopia has also drawn attention to altitude, though researchers stress that many other factors, including culture and opportunity, contribute to their achievements.

questions.title: Goalkeepers and penalties
questions.text: According to the researchers, why do goalkeepers usually dive? A study of penalty kicks in top football leagues found something surprising about goalkeepers. When a penalty is taken, goalkeepers dive to the left or right almost every time, rarely staying in the centre of the goal. Yet the data suggested that staying in the centre gave them a chance of stopping the ball that was at least as good as diving. Why, then, do they dive? The researchers proposed an explanation called action bias. If a goal is conceded while the goalkeeper stays still, it looks as though he did nothing, and he is likely to feel worse and receive more criticism. If he dives and the ball goes the other way, he at least appears to have tried. In other words, the choice may be shaped less by the best chance of saving the ball than by how the outcome will look to others.

questions.title: Riding in the peloton
questions.text: Why are breakaway groups often caught before the finish? In professional cycling races, riders travel in a large, tightly packed group called the peloton. The main reason is air resistance, which accounts for most of the effort a cyclist makes at racing speeds. A rider directly behind another experiences much less drag, and computer simulations have suggested that riders in the middle of a large peloton may face only a small fraction of the air resistance of a cyclist riding alone. This has a strong influence on tactics. Teams place riders around their leader to shelter him from the wind and save his energy for the decisive moments of the race. It also explains why small groups that break away from the peloton are so often caught before the finish: a large group sharing the work at the front can travel faster for longer than a few riders on their own.

questions.title: The smell of swimming pools
questions.text: What does a strong chlorine smell usually indicate? Many people assume that a strong smell of chlorine at a swimming pool means the water is especially clean. In fact, the opposite is often true. Chlorine is added to pools to kill harmful microorganisms, but when it reacts with substances brought in by swimmers, such as sweat, skin oils and urine, it forms compounds called chloramines. It is mainly these chloramines that produce the sharp smell and can irritate the eyes and lungs. A well-managed pool, with good ventilation and the correct balance of chemicals, should have only a faint smell. Pool operators therefore encourage swimmers to shower before entering the water, which reduces the amount of material that reacts with chlorine. So the next time your eyes sting after a swim, it may be a sign that the pool needs more attention, not less.

questions.title: Head injuries in sport
questions.text: Why have some football competitions introduced extra substitutions for concussion? For many years, players who received a blow to the head were often encouraged to carry on, and being knocked out briefly was sometimes treated as part of the game. Attitudes have changed as evidence has grown that repeated head injuries can have serious long-term effects on the brain. Many sports now have formal concussion procedures. In rugby, a player with a suspected head injury may be removed for an assessment by a doctor, and a replacement can come on while this takes place. Several football competitions now allow extra substitutions specifically for concussion, so that teams are not tempted to keep an injured player on the field to avoid being a player short. At amateur level, where doctors are rarely present, the advice is simpler: if in doubt, sit them out.

questions.title: reCAPTCHA
questions.text: What was the main idea behind reCAPTCHA? You have probably been asked to type distorted letters or choose pictures of traffic lights before logging in to a website. These tests, known as CAPTCHAs, are designed to tell humans apart from automated programs. The computer scientist Luis von Ahn, one of their inventors, realised that people around the world were collectively spending an enormous amount of time solving them, and he wondered whether this effort could be put to use. His answer was reCAPTCHA. Instead of random letters, users were shown words from old books and newspapers that computers had failed to read when the pages were scanned. Each time someone typed the word correctly, they were helping to digitise printed texts. Later versions, showing photographs of street scenes, have been used to help train computer systems to recognise objects.

questions.title: Why spam pays
questions.text: According to the study, why does spam remain profitable? Why do spammers keep sending millions of unwanted emails when almost nobody responds? In 2008, a group of computer scientists studied this question by quietly taking control of part of a network used by spammers. They tracked a campaign that sent around three hundred and fifty million emails advertising medicines. Only twenty-eight people went on to make a purchase, a response rate of well under one in ten million. At first glance, this seems like a failure. But sending an email costs the spammer almost nothing, especially when the messages are sent from thousands of infected computers belonging to other people. Even a tiny number of sales can therefore produce a profit. The researchers concluded that spam is sustained by extremely low costs rather than by success in persuading people, and later research suggested targeting the banks that spammers depend on.

questions.title: New password advice
questions.text: What did the revised guidance emphasise? For years, organisations told users to create passwords with a mixture of capital letters, numbers and symbols, and to change them every few months. In 2017, the United States National Institute of Standards and Technology revised its widely followed guidance. It concluded that these rules often made security worse. Complicated requirements led people to choose predictable patterns, such as replacing a letter with a number, and frequent changes encouraged them to make only tiny adjustments or to write passwords down. The new advice emphasised length instead. A long passphrase made of several unrelated words can be both easier to remember and harder to guess. The guidance also recommended checking new passwords against lists of passwords already exposed in data breaches, and forcing a change only if there is evidence that a password has been compromised.

questions.title: Website cookies
questions.text: Why were cookies first introduced? A cookie is a small text file that a website stores on your device. Cookies were introduced in 1994 by a programmer working on an early web browser, who needed a way for an online shop to remember what a customer had put in their basket from one page to the next. Many cookies are still used for such practical purposes, keeping you logged in or remembering your language settings. However, so-called third-party cookies, placed by companies other than the website you are visiting, allow advertisers to follow your activity across many different sites and build a detailed profile of your interests. Concerns about privacy led the European Union to require websites to ask for consent before storing most non-essential cookies, which is why so many sites now show pop-up banners. Several browsers also block third-party cookies by default.

questions.title: Predictive text
questions.text: How do modern predictive keyboards decide which word to suggest? When you type a message on a phone, the keyboard often suggests the next word before you have started it. Early mobile phones used a system called T9, which guessed which word you meant from a sequence of number key presses. Modern predictive keyboards work by calculating probabilities. They are built using enormous collections of text, from which they learn which words are most likely to follow others, and they also adapt to the words you personally use most often. This makes typing faster, but it has side effects. Autocorrect sometimes replaces an unusual but correct word, such as a name, with a more common one, occasionally with embarrassing results. Some linguists also wonder whether constant suggestions might gradually encourage people to use more predictable language, although the long-term effects are not yet clear.

questions.title: Machine translation
questions.text: According to the speaker, why do some languages remain difficult for machine translation? In 1954, researchers in the United States demonstrated a computer that translated about sixty Russian sentences into English, and some predicted that machine translation would be solved within a few years. It took far longer. Early systems relied on rules written by linguists, but human language is full of ambiguity, and rules could not cover every case. A major change came when researchers began using statistics, training systems on huge collections of documents that had already been translated by humans, such as the records of international organisations. Since the mid-2010s, systems based on neural networks have produced far more fluent results. Yet quality still varies enormously between languages. Translation between widely used languages, for which vast amounts of text exist, is often very good, while languages with little available written material remain much harder for machines.

questions.title: Drones carrying blood
questions.text: How are the packages delivered to hospitals? In 2016, Rwanda became the first country to use drones for regular deliveries of blood to hospitals. The service was run by a company called Zipline, working with the national health system. Blood is difficult to manage in rural areas. It must be stored carefully, some types expire quickly, and patients who need it after childbirth or accidents often cannot wait. Previously, a clinic might have waited hours for a delivery by road. Using small fixed-wing drones, the company could deliver within about half an hour. The drones do not land. Instead, they fly low over the hospital and drop the package, which floats down on a small paper parachute, before returning to base. The model has since been extended to vaccines and other medical supplies, and to other countries.

questions.title: Metals in e-waste
questions.text: What example of urban mining does the speaker give? Old mobile phones, laptops and other electronic devices contain small amounts of valuable metals, including gold, silver and copper. In fact, a tonne of discarded phones can contain far more gold than a tonne of ore from a typical gold mine. Recovering these metals from waste is sometimes called urban mining. A striking example came from Japan, which made all the medals for the Tokyo Olympic Games from metals extracted from electronic devices donated by the public over two years. Despite such projects, only a minority of the world's electronic waste is formally collected and recycled. Much of the rest ends up in landfill or is processed informally, sometimes by burning cables and circuit boards in the open air, which exposes workers to toxic fumes. Better design, making devices easier to take apart, could make recycling safer and more profitable.

questions.title: Server farms
questions.text: What happened in the underwater experiment? The data centres that store our emails, photographs and videos contain thousands of computer servers running day and night. These machines produce a great deal of heat, and keeping them cool can use a large share of a data centre's total energy. Companies have tried several solutions. Some have built centres in cold countries, such as Finland and Sweden, where outside air can be used for cooling for much of the year. Others use nearby seawater or lakes. In one experiment, a technology company sealed servers inside a container and placed it on the seabed off Scotland for two years; the servers failed less often than similar ones on land, perhaps because of the stable temperature and the absence of people. Increasingly, data centres are also connected to local heating networks, so that their waste heat can warm homes.

questions.title: Wrist heart-rate sensors
questions.text: Why do some athletes still use chest straps? Many smartwatches and fitness bands can measure your heart rate without any needles or wires. On the underside of the device, small lights, usually green, shine into the skin of your wrist. Blood absorbs green light, so the amount of light reflected back changes slightly as blood pulses through the vessels with each heartbeat. A sensor detects these changes, and software converts them into a heart rate. The method works well when the wearer is resting, but it can become less reliable during vigorous exercise, when arm movements disturb the signal, or if the watch is worn loosely. Some studies have also found that accuracy can vary with skin tone and tattoos. For this reason, many athletes who need precise measurements still use a strap worn around the chest, which detects the heart's electrical activity directly.

questions.title: How Wikipedia works
questions.text: What advice do teachers often give about Wikipedia? When Wikipedia was launched in 2001, many people doubted that an encyclopedia anyone could edit would ever be reliable. Yet it grew rapidly into one of the most visited websites in the world. Its model depends on large numbers of volunteers who write articles, check sources and correct errors. Key rules require information to be supported by published sources and articles to be written from a neutral point of view. Deliberate damage, known as vandalism, is common, but it is often removed within minutes, partly by automated programs. In 2005, the journal Nature compared a selection of science articles with those in another well-known encyclopedia and reported a broadly similar number of serious errors, though the other publisher strongly disputed the study. Teachers often advise students to use Wikipedia as a starting point and to follow its references, rather than citing it directly.

questions.title: The War of the Worlds broadcast
questions.text: According to later researchers, why might newspapers have exaggerated the panic? On the evening of 30 October 1938, an American radio station broadcast a drama based on H. G. Wells's novel The War of the Worlds, presented as a series of realistic news reports about a Martian invasion. The next day, newspapers reported that the programme had caused mass panic, with frightened listeners fleeing their homes. The story became famous as an example of the power of the media. However, later researchers have argued that the panic was greatly exaggerated. Relatively few people were listening to the programme, and there is little evidence of widespread flight. Some historians suggest that newspapers had a reason to exaggerate: radio was a new and growing competitor for advertising, and reports of irresponsible broadcasting helped to portray it as dangerous. Ironically, the myth of the panic may itself show how easily media stories spread.

questions.title: The rise of podcasts
questions.text: What does the speaker identify as the main challenge for podcast producers now? The word podcast was coined in 2004 by a journalist who combined the name of a popular music player with the word broadcast. At first, podcasts were a niche interest, downloaded by relatively small numbers of enthusiasts. Growth accelerated around 2014, when a true-crime series called Serial attracted millions of listeners and showed that audio storytelling could become a mass phenomenon. Since then, the number of podcasts has grown enormously. Part of their appeal is convenience: listeners can choose exactly what they want and listen while commuting, exercising or doing housework. For producers, costs are low compared with radio or television, so it is possible to serve small, specialised audiences, from fans of medieval history to people learning a particular language. The challenge now is not making a podcast but getting anyone to notice it among so many.

questions.title: False stories on Twitter
questions.text: What did the study find about bots? In 2018, researchers published a large study of how true and false news stories spread on Twitter between 2006 and 2017. They examined around one hundred and twenty-six thousand stories that had been checked by independent fact-checking organisations. False stories spread further, faster and more widely than true ones, and this was especially the case for false political news. Many people assume automated accounts, or bots, are mainly responsible, but the researchers found that bots spread true and false news at similar rates. The difference was driven by human users. One possible explanation is novelty: false stories were more often surprising, and people like to share information that seems new. The false stories also tended to provoke stronger emotional reactions, such as surprise and disgust. The findings suggest that fighting misinformation requires changing human behaviour, not just removing automated accounts.

questions.title: Altered photographs
questions.text: What does the speaker say about news agencies today? Many people think that faked photographs are a product of the digital age, but images have been altered almost since photography began. One of the best-known examples comes from the Soviet Union in the 1930s. When officials fell out of favour with Joseph Stalin, they were sometimes removed from official photographs, so that it appeared they had never been present. In one famous case, a senior police official who had been photographed walking beside Stalin simply vanished from later versions of the picture. These changes were made by hand in darkrooms, using techniques such as painting over prints and cutting negatives. Digital software has made alteration much easier, which is why many news agencies now have strict rules forbidding any change to the content of a news photograph beyond basic adjustments such as brightness.

questions.title: Recorded laughter on television
questions.text: Why did laugh tracks remain in use for so long? For decades, television comedies were often accompanied by recorded laughter, known as a laugh track. In the 1950s, a sound engineer named Charles Douglass built a machine containing recordings of different kinds of laughter, from gentle chuckles to loud roars, which he could play at chosen moments. Producers used it to add laughter to shows filmed without an audience, or to boost reactions that seemed too quiet. Many viewers found laugh tracks irritating, yet there was a reason they persisted. Research suggests that laughter is contagious: people tend to laugh more, and rate jokes as funnier, when they hear others laughing. Television producers were, in effect, providing a virtual audience for people watching alone at home. In recent years, many popular comedies have abandoned laugh tracks, trusting viewers to decide for themselves what is funny.

questions.title: Trailers
questions.text: Why were trailers moved to the beginning of the programme? The short advertisements for upcoming films are called trailers, which seems strange, because today they are shown before the main feature. The name comes from the early days of cinema, when these advertisements were shown after the film had finished, trailing behind it. Cinema owners soon noticed that many people left as soon as the main film ended, so the trailers were moved to the beginning of the programme, where the audience was certain to see them. The name, however, remained. Trailers have since become an art form of their own. Editors must attract attention in two or three minutes without revealing too much of the story, and studios often test several versions with audiences before choosing one. With the rise of online video, the release of a trailer for a major film has become a news event in itself.

questions.title: Competitive gaming
questions.text: What does the speaker say about esports careers? Competitive video gaming, known as esports, has grown from small gatherings of enthusiasts into a global industry. Major tournaments now fill large arenas, and millions more watch online. Professional players often train for many hours a day, practising strategies with their teams and studying opponents, much like athletes in traditional sports. Whether esports should count as sport remains a subject of debate. Critics argue that they lack the physical effort that defines sport, while supporters point to the fast reactions, precise hand movements and intense concentration they demand. The question gained new attention when esports were included as official medal events at the Asian Games held in China in 2023. Despite the attention, careers can be very short. Many professional players retire in their mid-twenties, partly because of the pressure of constant competition and the physical strain of long hours of practice.

questions.title: The Jazz Singer
questions.text: According to the speaker, which group lost their jobs because of sound films? In 1927, the film The Jazz Singer included sequences of synchronised speech and song, and audiences were amazed to hear an actor speak on screen. Within a few years, silent films had almost disappeared. The change transformed the industry in ways that went beyond sound itself. Some famous silent stars found their careers in difficulty, because their voices or accents did not suit the roles they were known for, or because they struggled with dialogue. Early sound equipment also created technical problems: noisy cameras had to be placed inside soundproof booths, which made filming less flexible for a time. Another group lost out as well. Many cinemas had employed musicians to play live accompaniment for silent films, and thousands of these jobs vanished as recorded soundtracks took over.

questions.title: Inventing the piano
questions.text: What was the key advantage of Cristofori's instrument? Before the piano, the most common keyboard instrument in European homes and courts was the harpsichord. When a harpsichord key is pressed, a small mechanism plucks the string, and the volume is much the same however hard the key is struck. Around the year 1700, Bartolomeo Cristofori, an instrument maker in Florence, developed a new mechanism in which small hammers struck the strings and then immediately fell back, allowing them to vibrate. Crucially, the harder the player pressed the key, the louder the sound. His instrument was described as a harpsichord with soft and loud, which in Italian included the words piano and forte. The name was eventually shortened to piano. The new instrument took decades to become popular, but composers such as Mozart and Beethoven later wrote music that depended on its range of expression.

questions.title: Tuning an orchestra
questions.text: Why do orchestras tune to the oboe? Before a concert, an orchestra tunes to a single note played by the oboe. There are practical reasons for this. The oboe has a clear, penetrating sound that can be heard across the whole orchestra, and its pitch is relatively stable. The note chosen is usually an A. For much of history, the exact pitch of this A varied considerably from place to place, so an instrument tuned in one city might sound out of tune in another. In the twentieth century, a standard was widely adopted in which the A vibrates four hundred and forty times per second. Even so, the standard is not followed everywhere. Many orchestras tune slightly higher, believing it gives a brighter sound, while groups performing music from earlier centuries often tune lower to recreate the pitch the composers would have known.

questions.title: Ultramarine blue
questions.text: Why did contracts sometimes specify how much ultramarine an artist should use? In Renaissance Europe, the most precious blue pigment was ultramarine. Its name means beyond the sea, because the stone it was made from, lapis lazuli, came from mines in what is now Afghanistan, thousands of kilometres away. Turning the stone into a pure, intense blue was a slow and difficult process: it had to be ground and repeatedly washed to separate the blue particles from impurities. The finished pigment could be more expensive than gold, and contracts for paintings sometimes specified exactly how much ultramarine an artist was to use. Painters often reserved it for the most important figures, such as the robes of the Virgin Mary. In the 1820s, a French society offered a prize for a synthetic version, and a manufacturing method was soon found. Artificial ultramarine was far cheaper, and the colour became available to everyone.

questions.title: The Vermeer forger
questions.text: Why did Van Meegeren admit to forgery? After the Second World War, Dutch authorities discovered that a painting believed to be by Johannes Vermeer had been sold to the senior Nazi Hermann Göring. They traced the sale to a painter named Han van Meegeren and arrested him for selling a national treasure to the enemy, a serious crime. Van Meegeren's defence was astonishing. He claimed that the painting was not a Vermeer at all, but a forgery he had painted himself. To prove it, he painted another work in the style of Vermeer in front of witnesses. He was cleared of the more serious charge but convicted of forgery. Experts were embarrassed, because several of his paintings had been accepted as genuine and displayed in major museums. His case is often cited as a warning that experts can be misled when a discovery confirms what they hope to find.

questions.title: Cinderella around the world
questions.text: What does the speaker say about the glass slipper? The story of Cinderella is often associated with a single famous version, but folklorists have recorded hundreds of related tales from around the world. One of the oldest written versions comes from China, in a collection from the ninth century, in which a young woman named Ye Xian is helped by a magical fish and loses a golden shoe. An even earlier story, recorded by a Greek writer, tells of a woman whose sandal is carried off by an eagle and dropped in front of a king. Many details that people now consider essential, such as the fairy godmother, the pumpkin and the glass slipper, come from a French version published in 1697. By comparing such variations, folklorists try to understand how stories travel between cultures and which elements survive as they are retold.

questions.title: Shakespeare's vocabulary
questions.text: What have digital collections of early books revealed? William Shakespeare is often credited with inventing a remarkable number of English words and expressions. Dictionaries have long listed his plays as the earliest known source for many terms, and phrases such as wild-goose chase are first recorded in his work. However, recent research using large digital collections of early printed books has complicated this picture. Scholars searching these collections have found that many words once credited to Shakespeare were in fact used by other writers before him. Because his works were studied so carefully, they were simply the first place dictionary makers looked. This does not mean his influence was small. He clearly created some words and gave new life to many others, but it suggests that the language of his time was more inventive than a focus on one writer might suggest.

Why do governments tax cigarettes, alcohol and fuel so heavily? Part of the answer lies in a concept economists call price elasticity of demand, which measures how much the quantity people buy changes when the price changes. For some goods, demand is elastic: if the price of one brand of cereal rises, many shoppers simply switch to another. For others, demand is inelastic, because people feel they need the product or have few alternatives. Fuel is a good example in the short term, since most drivers still need to get to work. Taxes on goods with inelastic demand raise large amounts of revenue, because sales fall only slightly. However, this also means such taxes may do less to change behaviour than their supporters hope. Over longer periods, demand often becomes more elastic, as people buy more efficient cars, move closer to work or, in the case of cigarettes, eventually quit. Price elasticity of demand describes how much purchases change when prices change. Goods with inelastic demand, such as fuel in the short term, keep selling when taxed, so taxes on them raise large revenue but may change behaviour less than expected. Over longer periods, demand usually becomes more elastic as people find alternatives, such as efficient cars or quitting smoking.
