Many central banks today are given a clear goal: to keep inflation, the rate at which prices rise, close to a target, often around two percent a year. New Zealand was the first country to adopt such a target, in 1990, and many others followed. The main tool is the interest rate. When inflation is too high, the central bank raises rates, making borrowing more expensive, which tends to reduce spending and cool the economy. When inflation is too low, it cuts rates to encourage borrowing and spending. Why not aim for zero inflation? Economists argue that a small, stable rate gives some room to cut interest rates in a downturn and avoids the danger of falling prices, which can cause people to delay purchases. The approach works best when people trust that the bank will act, because expectations about future prices influence how businesses set prices and workers negotiate wages. Many central banks aim to keep inflation near a target, often about two percent, an approach New Zealand introduced in 1990. They raise interest rates to cool spending when inflation is high and cut them when it is low. A small positive target leaves room to cut rates and avoids falling prices, and success depends on trust shaping public expectations.

questions.title: Who pays for tariffs
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. A tariff is a tax on imported goods. Politicians sometimes describe tariffs as a way of making foreign countries pay, but economists point out that the reality is more complicated. The tax is paid at the border by the company importing the goods, and much of the cost is usually passed on to consumers through higher prices. Foreign producers may absorb part of it by lowering their prices to stay competitive, but studies of recent tariffs have often found that most of the burden fell on buyers in the country that imposed them. Tariffs can protect particular domestic industries from competition, preserving some jobs. However, they can also raise costs for other domestic businesses that rely on imported materials, and they may provoke other countries to respond with tariffs of their own, harming exporters. For these reasons, economists generally regard tariffs as a costly way of supporting industry. Tariffs are taxes on imports paid by importing companies, and much of the cost is usually passed on to domestic consumers rather than foreign producers. They can protect certain industries and jobs, but they raise costs for businesses using imported materials and may lead to retaliation that harms exporters, so economists generally see them as a costly form of support.

questions.title: Public goods
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Economists use the term public good for something that has two special features. First, it is difficult to prevent anyone from benefiting from it. Second, one person's use does not reduce the amount available to others. Street lighting is a common example. Once a street is lit, everyone who walks along it benefits, and one extra person does not make the light dimmer. This creates a problem known as free riding. If a private company tried to sell street lighting, many residents would refuse to pay, knowing they would benefit anyway, so the service would probably not be provided at all, even though most people want it. This is why public goods such as street lighting, national defence and flood defences are usually funded through taxes. Economists debate which goods truly fit this definition, but the idea helps explain why some services are provided by governments rather than markets. A public good is one that nobody can easily be excluded from and whose use by one person does not reduce it for others, such as street lighting. Because people can benefit without paying, free riding means private firms would rarely supply it, so such goods, including defence and flood protection, are usually funded through taxes.

questions.title: Moral hazard
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Moral hazard is a term from the insurance industry. It describes the risk that people become less careful when they are protected from the consequences of their actions. Someone with full insurance on a bicycle, for example, might be less careful about locking it. Insurers respond in several ways. They often require customers to pay the first part of any claim themselves, known as an excess, so that the customer still has an incentive to avoid losses. They may also offer lower prices to people who take precautions, such as fitting alarms. The idea became widely discussed after the financial crisis of 2008, when governments rescued large banks. Critics argued that if banks expect to be saved when things go wrong, they may take bigger risks in the future. Regulators have since introduced rules requiring banks to hold more of their own capital, so that they carry more of the cost of their mistakes. Moral hazard is the tendency for people to take less care when protected from the consequences of their actions. In insurance, companies reduce it with an excess and discounts for precautions. After the 2008 crisis, bank rescues raised fears that banks would take bigger risks, so regulators now require banks to hold more capital and bear more of their losses.

questions.title: The market for lemons
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. In 1970, the economist George Akerlof published a paper about the market for used cars, which helped him win a Nobel Prize. His key point was that sellers usually know much more about the quality of a car than buyers do. A buyer cannot easily tell a reliable car from a poor one, known in American slang as a lemon, so they are only willing to pay an average price. But at that price, owners of good cars may decide not to sell, because they would receive less than the car is worth. As good cars leave the market, the average quality falls, buyers lower the price they will pay, and the problem gets worse. This process is called adverse selection. Many features of modern markets exist partly to reduce it, including warranties, inspection reports, online reviews and brand reputations, all of which give buyers more reliable information. George Akerlof showed that in the market for used cars sellers know more about quality than buyers, so buyers pay only an average price. Owners of good cars then withdraw, lowering average quality and prices further, a process called adverse selection. Warranties, inspections, reviews and brand reputations help by giving buyers more reliable information about what they are buying.

questions.title: Pigouvian taxes
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. When a factory pollutes a river, the people living downstream bear part of the cost, yet the factory does not pay for it. Economists call such a cost an externality. Because the factory does not pay the full cost of its activities, it may produce more pollution than society would choose. In the early twentieth century, the British economist Arthur Pigou suggested a solution: tax the activity causing the harm, at a level matching the damage it does. The polluter then has a financial reason to reduce pollution, and it is free to decide how, whether by installing new equipment, changing its processes or producing less. Many economists favour such taxes because they reduce harm at the lowest overall cost. Setting the right level can be difficult, however, because the damage is not always easy to measure, and taxes can be politically unpopular, especially when they raise prices for consumers. An externality is a cost, such as pollution, that falls on others rather than on the business causing it, leading to too much harm. Arthur Pigou proposed a tax on such activities in line with the damage, giving polluters a reason to cut pollution in the cheapest way. However, damage is hard to measure and such taxes can be unpopular.

questions.title: Automatic pension enrolment
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Many people know they should save for retirement, yet they put it off. Behavioural economists have found that the default option has a powerful effect on what people do. In traditional pension schemes, employees had to actively sign up, and many never did. When employers instead enrol workers automatically, while allowing them to leave the scheme if they wish, participation rises dramatically. The United Kingdom introduced automatic enrolment in workplace pensions from 2012, and the proportion of eligible employees saving into a pension increased substantially over the following years, particularly among young and lower-paid workers. Nobody is forced to save, because anyone can opt out, but inertia now works in favour of saving rather than against it. Critics point out that automatic enrolment does not guarantee that people save enough, and the default contribution rates may still leave many with modest retirement incomes. Because people often delay saving, the default option strongly affects pension participation. When the United Kingdom introduced automatic enrolment from 2012, allowing workers to opt out, the share of employees saving rose substantially, especially among young and lower-paid workers. However, critics note that default contribution rates may still leave many people with modest retirement incomes.

questions.title: Limits on rents
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Rent control, which limits how much landlords can charge or how quickly rents can rise, is popular with many tenants, who value the protection it offers against sudden increases. Most economists, however, have been sceptical of strict rent controls. They argue that when rents are held below market levels, landlords have less incentive to maintain their properties or to build new rental housing. Some owners may convert apartments into homes for sale, reducing the supply of rental housing. A well-known study of San Francisco found that tenants who benefited from rent control were more likely to stay in their homes, but landlords reduced the number of rental units available, which may have pushed rents up elsewhere in the city. Supporters of rent regulation respond that milder forms, such as limiting annual increases, can provide stability for tenants without the worst side effects, especially if combined with building more homes. Rent control protects tenants from sudden increases and is popular, but many economists argue that holding rents below market levels discourages maintenance and new building. A San Francisco study found tenants stayed longer but landlords reduced rental supply, possibly raising rents elsewhere. Supporters say milder limits, combined with building more homes, can give stability with fewer drawbacks.

questions.title: M-Pesa
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. In 2007, a mobile phone company in Kenya launched a service called M-Pesa, which allowed people to send and receive money using simple text messages. Customers could deposit and withdraw cash at small shops acting as agents. At the time, most Kenyans did not have a bank account, and sending money to relatives in rural areas often meant trusting a bus driver with an envelope of cash. M-Pesa spread rapidly, and within a few years it was used by a majority of adults in the country. Research suggested that access to the service helped households cope with unexpected problems, such as illness or a poor harvest, because relatives could quickly send support. One study estimated that it helped lift a significant number of households out of poverty. The service has since expanded to other countries, and it is often cited as an example of technology developed in Africa shaping financial services elsewhere. M-Pesa, launched in Kenya in 2007, let people send money by text message and use local shops to deposit and withdraw cash, serving many without a bank account. It spread rapidly, helping households cope with shocks such as illness or poor harvests through fast support from relatives, and research suggests it reduced poverty. It has since expanded to other countries.

questions.title: The first public collections
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. For centuries, collections of rare objects belonged to kings, nobles and wealthy scholars, and were usually seen only by invited guests. The idea of a museum open to the public developed gradually. One of the earliest examples is the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, which opened in 1683 to house a collection donated to the university, and which admitted visitors who paid a fee. In the following century, the British Museum opened in London in 1759, allowing free entry, although visitors initially had to apply for tickets in advance. After the French Revolution, the Louvre in Paris opened in 1793, displaying former royal collections as the property of the nation. These institutions reflected new ideas that knowledge and culture should be shared more widely. Today museums continue to look for ways to reach people who rarely visit, through free entry, online collections and events. Collections of rare objects were once private, but public museums developed gradually. Early examples include the Ashmolean in Oxford in 1683, the British Museum in 1759 and the Louvre in 1793, which displayed royal collections as national property. They reflected the idea that culture should be shared, and museums still seek ways to reach people who rarely visit.

questions.title: The founding of the Red Cross
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. In 1859, a Swiss businessman named Henri Dunant witnessed the aftermath of the Battle of Solferino in northern Italy, where tens of thousands of soldiers lay wounded with little medical help. He organised local people to care for the injured, regardless of which side they had fought on. Afterwards he wrote a book describing what he had seen and proposing two ideas: that every country should have volunteer relief societies trained to help the wounded in war, and that there should be an international agreement protecting them. Both ideas became reality. The International Committee of the Red Cross was founded in Geneva in 1863, and in 1864 the first Geneva Convention was signed, protecting wounded soldiers and the medical staff caring for them. Dunant later shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901, although by then he had lost his fortune and lived in poverty. After seeing thousands of wounded soldiers at Solferino in 1859, Henri Dunant organised care for both sides and proposed national volunteer relief societies and an international agreement protecting them. The Red Cross was founded in 1863 and the first Geneva Convention signed in 1864. Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901, despite living in poverty.

questions.title: The first Paralympics
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. The Paralympic Games grew out of work at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England, where the neurologist Ludwig Guttmann treated soldiers and civilians with spinal injuries after the Second World War. At the time, such injuries were often seen as the end of an active life, but Guttmann believed that sport could aid physical rehabilitation and restore confidence. In 1948, on the same day the London Olympics opened, he organised an archery competition for patients in wheelchairs. The event grew each year and soon included international teams. In 1960, a competition held in Rome, just after the Olympic Games there, is now recognised as the first Paralympic Games, with around four hundred athletes. Over time, the Games expanded to include athletes with a wider range of impairments. Since 1988, the Paralympics have been held in the same city as the Olympics, and they now attract thousands of athletes and large global audiences. The Paralympics began with Ludwig Guttmann's work at Stoke Mandeville Hospital, where he used sport to rehabilitate people with spinal injuries after the Second World War. His 1948 wheelchair archery competition grew into international events, and the 1960 Rome games are recognised as the first Paralympics. The Games later included more impairments and, since 1988, share the Olympic host city.

questions.title: Where surnames come from
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. For much of history, most people had only one name. As populations grew, this caused confusion, especially for officials collecting taxes or recording property. Surnames developed gradually to solve this problem, and in many European languages they fall into a few main types. Some describe a person's job, such as Smith, Baker or Miller. Others refer to where someone lived, such as Hill or Brook. Many come from a father's name, such as Johnson, meaning son of John, or its equivalents in other languages. A fourth group began as nicknames describing appearance or character. Not all cultures followed the same path. In Iceland, most people still use a name based on their father's or mother's first name rather than a fixed family surname. Japan made family names compulsory for all citizens only in 1875, when the government required everyone to register one. As populations grew, single names caused confusion for officials, so surnames developed gradually. In many European languages they come from jobs, places, a father's name or nicknames. Other cultures differ: people in Iceland still mostly use names based on a parent's first name, and Japan required all citizens to register a family name only in 1875.

questions.title: A short history of the passport
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Travel documents have existed for centuries, but for most of history people could cross many borders without them. In the nineteenth century, the spread of railways made international travel much easier, and many European countries relaxed or abandoned passport requirements. The First World War changed this. Governments, worried about spies and keen to control the movement of people, introduced strict passport rules, and they remained in place after the war. In 1920, an international conference organised by the League of Nations agreed a standard format, a small booklet with a photograph and a description of the holder, which was the basis for the modern passport. Many travellers at the time objected to having their photographs taken for official purposes, seeing it as treating them like criminals. Since then, passports have added machine-readable pages and electronic chips storing the holder's details. A passport was often unnecessary in the nineteenth century, when railways made travel easier and rules were relaxed. The First World War brought strict controls that remained afterwards, and in 1920 a League of Nations conference agreed a standard booklet with a photograph, the basis of today's passport. Some travellers objected, and modern passports add electronic chips.

questions.title: The oldest universities
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Which is the oldest university in the world? The answer depends on how a university is defined. The University of al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, founded in 859 by a woman named Fatima al-Fihri, is often described as the oldest continuously operating institution of higher learning, although it began as a mosque with a school attached. In Europe, the University of Bologna, dating from 1088, is usually considered the first university in the modern sense: a self-governing community of students and teachers that awarded degrees. Interestingly, at Bologna it was the students who initially held much of the power, hiring teachers and even fining them if they started late or skipped difficult topics. Oxford and Paris followed soon after, with teachers playing a larger role in their organisation. These medieval institutions established features that still exist today, including degrees, faculties and academic dress. The answer depends on definition. Al-Qarawiyyin in Morocco, founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, is often called the oldest continuously operating institution of higher learning, while Bologna, from 1088, is usually seen as the first university in the modern sense. At Bologna, students initially held power over teachers, and medieval universities established degrees, faculties and academic dress.

questions.title: A slow welcome for the fork
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Forks now seem an essential part of eating in many countries, but they were slow to be accepted in Europe. Large forks were used in kitchens for centuries, but small forks for eating were more common in the Byzantine Empire. According to a famous story, when a Byzantine princess married into a Venetian noble family in the eleventh century and ate with a golden fork, some church leaders condemned her behaviour as excessively refined. Forks gradually spread through Italy, where they were useful for eating pasta, but many other Europeans continued to eat with knives, spoons and their fingers. In the early seventeenth century, an English traveller described Italian forks as a curious custom. It was not until the eighteenth century that forks became common in much of Europe. In many parts of the world, of course, people continued to eat with chopsticks or their hands, which remain the most common methods globally. Eating forks were used in the Byzantine Empire but spread slowly in Europe. A Byzantine princess using a golden fork in Venice was reportedly criticised, and forks became popular in Italy partly for pasta, while elsewhere people used knives, spoons and fingers until the eighteenth century. Worldwide, chopsticks and hands remain the most common ways of eating.

questions.title: The history of the toothbrush
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. People have cleaned their teeth for thousands of years, using chewed twigs from certain trees, some of which are still used today in parts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. The bristle toothbrush appears to have been developed in China, where records describe brushes made with hairs from pigs attached to handles of bone or bamboo. In England, a man named William Addis is credited with starting the first mass production of toothbrushes in the late eighteenth century. According to the company's history, he had the idea while in prison, when he made a brush from a small bone and some bristles. Brushing did not become a daily habit for most people until the twentieth century. Soldiers in the Second World War were required to brush their teeth and brought the habit home. The introduction of nylon bristles in the 1930s also made toothbrushes cheaper and more hygienic. People cleaned their teeth with chewed twigs for thousands of years, and bristle toothbrushes were developed in China using pig hair. William Addis began mass production in England in the eighteenth century, reportedly after making a brush in prison. Daily brushing became common only in the twentieth century, helped by wartime habits and cheaper, more hygienic nylon bristles.

questions.title: Loneliness and health
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Loneliness is usually thought of as an emotional problem, but researchers increasingly treat it as a public health issue. Large studies following people over many years have found that social isolation and loneliness are associated with a higher risk of early death, as well as heart disease, stroke and depression. One widely discussed analysis suggested that the effect on mortality was comparable to well-known risk factors such as obesity. Scientists are still investigating why. Loneliness may cause chronic stress, disrupt sleep and make people less likely to exercise or seek medical help. Importantly, being alone and feeling lonely are not the same; some people live alone happily, while others feel lonely in a crowd. In 2018, the United Kingdom appointed a government minister with responsibility for loneliness, and some doctors now refer patients to community groups and activities, an approach known as social prescribing. Researchers increasingly treat loneliness as a public health issue, since studies link isolation and loneliness to early death, heart disease, stroke and depression, possibly through stress, poor sleep and less healthy behaviour. Being alone differs from feeling lonely. The United Kingdom appointed a minister for loneliness in 2018, and doctors may use social prescribing to connect patients with community activities.

questions.title: Exercise and low mood
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Physical activity is well known to benefit the heart and muscles, but there is also strong evidence that it helps mental health. Reviews combining many studies have found that regular exercise can reduce symptoms of depression, and in some trials its effect was comparable to that of talking therapies or medication for mild to moderate cases. Several explanations have been proposed. Exercise may affect chemicals in the brain linked to mood, improve sleep, reduce inflammation and provide a sense of achievement. Group activities can also offer social contact. Importantly, benefits have been found for many types of exercise, including walking, and not only for intense training. However, experts stress that exercise is not a replacement for professional treatment in severe depression, and that one of the difficulties is that depression itself reduces energy and motivation, so people may need support to get started. Research shows that regular exercise can reduce symptoms of depression, sometimes as much as therapy or medication in mild to moderate cases, possibly by affecting brain chemicals, sleep, inflammation and confidence. Many activities, including walking, help. However, exercise does not replace treatment for severe depression, and because depression reduces motivation, people may need support to start.

questions.title: Short sight and outdoor play
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Short-sightedness, or myopia, has become far more common in recent decades. In some cities in East Asia, a large majority of young people finishing school are now short-sighted, compared with a much smaller share a few generations ago. The change has happened too quickly to be explained by genes alone. For many years, reading and close work were blamed, but research increasingly points to another factor: time spent outdoors. Children who spend more time outside tend to be less likely to become short-sighted, and one explanation is that bright daylight affects how the eye grows. In a trial in China, schools that added an extra outdoor class each day saw fewer new cases of myopia. As a result, some countries now encourage schools to give children more time outside. Severe myopia matters because it increases the risk of serious eye diseases later in life. Myopia has risen sharply, especially in East Asian cities, too quickly for genes alone to explain. Research suggests a lack of time outdoors is important, possibly because bright daylight affects eye growth, and a Chinese trial found an extra daily outdoor class reduced new cases. Some countries now encourage outdoor time, since severe myopia raises the risk of eye disease.

questions.title: How painkillers work
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Common painkillers work in different ways. Drugs such as ibuprofen and aspirin belong to a group called non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. They block enzymes that produce substances called prostaglandins, which contribute to pain, fever and swelling. Because they reduce inflammation, they are often recommended for injuries such as sprains. However, they can irritate the stomach and are not suitable for everyone. Paracetamol, known as acetaminophen in some countries, also reduces pain and fever, but it has little effect on inflammation, and scientists are still not entirely sure how it works. It is gentle on the stomach, but taking more than the recommended dose can seriously damage the liver, which is why pack sizes are limited in some countries. Doctors often point out that combining different painkillers safely can be more effective than increasing the dose of one, but people should always follow medical advice. Anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and aspirin block prostaglandins, reducing pain, fever and swelling, but they can irritate the stomach. Paracetamol reduces pain and fever with little effect on inflammation, and how it works is not fully understood; it is gentle on the stomach, but overdoses can damage the liver. Combining painkillers safely may help, following medical advice.

questions.title: Lactase persistence
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. All human babies can digest lactose, the sugar in milk, using an enzyme called lactase. In most mammals, including most humans historically, production of this enzyme falls after weaning, so adults who drink large amounts of milk may suffer from stomach discomfort. However, in some populations, many adults continue producing lactase throughout life. This trait, called lactase persistence, is common in northern Europe and among some herding groups in East Africa and the Middle East. Genetic studies show that it evolved separately in different regions, through different mutations, within the last several thousand years, after people began keeping dairy animals. This is one of the clearest examples of recent human evolution, and of culture shaping biology: where milk was an important food, people who could digest it may have had an advantage. Worldwide, however, most adults still have a reduced ability to digest lactose. Babies digest lactose, but in most people lactase production falls after weaning. In some populations, including northern Europeans and certain East African and Middle Eastern herders, lactase persistence evolved separately within the last few thousand years after dairy farming began. It is a clear example of recent evolution shaped by culture, though most adults worldwide still digest milk poorly.

questions.title: Why fingers wrinkle
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. After a long bath, our fingers and toes become wrinkled. For a long time, this was thought to be a simple result of skin absorbing water and swelling. But in the 1930s, doctors noticed that fingers did not wrinkle if the nerves to them had been damaged, showing that wrinkling is an active process controlled by the nervous system. When skin is soaked, blood vessels beneath it narrow, and the skin surface folds. Why would the body do this? In 2013, researchers reported that people with wrinkled fingers were quicker at moving wet objects from one container to another, suggesting that wrinkles might improve grip in wet conditions, like the tread on a tyre. Other studies, however, have not found the same advantage, so the question remains open. Doctors have occasionally used the wrinkling test to check whether nerves in the hand are working properly. Fingers wrinkle in water not through simple swelling but through an active process controlled by nerves, since damaged nerves prevent it; blood vessels narrow and the skin folds. A 2013 study suggested wrinkles improve grip on wet objects, but other studies disagree, so the purpose remains uncertain. Doctors have used the test to check nerves in the hand.

questions.title: Learning styles
questions.text: You will hear a short lecture. Write a summary for a fellow student who was not present at the lecture. You should write 50-70 words. You have 10 minutes to finish this task. Your response will be judged on the quality of your writing and on how well your response presents the key points presented in the lecture. Many people believe that each of us has a preferred learning style, such as visual, auditory or hands-on, and that students learn best when teaching matches that style. Surveys have found that large numbers of teachers around the world accept this idea. Yet when researchers have tested it properly, the evidence has been weak. To support the theory, a study would need to show that visual learners do better with visual teaching while auditory learners do better with spoken teaching. Reviews of the research have found very few studies meeting this standard, and those that exist generally do not support the idea. People certainly have preferences, but preferring a method does not mean learning more from it. In the 1960s, the psychologists Robert Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson told teachers at an American school that certain pupils had been identified by a test as likely to make rapid intellectual progress. In reality, these pupils had been chosen at random. At the end of the year, some of the selected children, particularly younger ones, showed greater gains in test scores than their classmates. The researchers concluded that teachers' expectations had influenced the pupils' progress, perhaps because teachers gave them more attention, encouragement and challenging work. The study became famous as the Pygmalion effect. It has also been criticised. Later researchers questioned its methods, and attempts to repeat it found smaller or inconsistent effects. Most psychologists now agree that teacher expectations can influence pupils, but that the effect is usually modest rather than dramatic. Even so, the idea encourages teachers to hold high expectations for all students. questions.title: Testing yourself to remember

Many students revise by rereading their notes and textbooks, often several times. It feels productive, because the material becomes familiar. However, research on memory suggests that a different method is much more effective: testing yourself. In many experiments, students who practised recalling information, for example by answering questions or writing down everything they could remember, performed better on later tests than students who spent the same time rereading. This is known as the testing effect, or retrieval practice. The effort of retrieving information from memory seems to strengthen it and make it easier to recall in the future. Tests also reveal what a student does not know, allowing them to focus on weak areas. Researchers note that the practice tests do not need to be marked or to count towards grades. Simple techniques, such as flashcards or covering notes and explaining a topic aloud, can provide the same benefit. Do students learn more by taking notes by hand or on a laptop? A widely reported study in 2014 found that students who typed tended to copy lectures word for word, while those who wrote by hand, being slower, had to summarise in their own words. On questions testing understanding, the handwriting group performed better. The study was influential, and some lecturers banned laptops from their classrooms. However, later attempts to repeat the experiment produced mixed results, and a larger replication found that the difference was small and not reliable. What seems more consistent is that the way students process information matters more than the tool. Summarising, reorganising ideas and reviewing notes later all help learning, whichever method is used. Laptops also bring a separate problem: distraction. Studies have found that students who browse the internet during lectures learn less, and may even distract classmates sitting nearby. Reading aloud to young children is often recommended by teachers and health professionals, and research supports the advice. Picture books contain a wider range of vocabulary than most everyday conversation, so children who are read to regularly hear many words they would rarely encounter otherwise. One study estimated that children whose parents read to them daily would hear over a million more words by the time they started school than children who were never read to. Shared reading also helps children understand how stories are structured, connect spoken and written language, and develop concentration. Benefits appear to be greatest when adults make it interactive, asking questions, pointing to pictures and encouraging children to predict what will happen next, rather than simply reading the words. One of the most influential studies, known as Project STAR, took place in the American state of Tennessee in the late 1980s. Thousands of young pupils and their teachers were randomly assigned to small classes of around fifteen pupils or to regular classes of around twenty-two to twenty-five. Because the assignment was random, differences in results could be linked to class size itself. Pupils in small classes performed better in the early years, and the benefits were larger for children from disadvantaged backgrounds. Some follow-up studies found lasting advantages, such as higher rates of college entry. However, smaller classes are expensive, because they require more teachers and classrooms. When California reduced class sizes rapidly in the 1990s, it had to hire many inexperienced teachers, and the gains were smaller than expected. Policymakers therefore weigh class size against other uses of the same money. The term digital divide describes the gap between people who have access to the internet and digital technology and those who do not. Globally, a large share of the population still does not use the internet, and most of these people live in low-income countries and rural areas. But the divide is not only about access. Researchers also point to differences in the quality of connection, the devices people use and the skills needed to benefit from them. These differences became especially visible when schools closed during the pandemic and lessons moved online. In the early days of the web, search engines ranked pages mainly by counting how often the search words appeared on them. This was easy to manipulate: a page could simply repeat popular words many times. In the late 1990s, two graduate students at Stanford University, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, developed a different approach called PageRank. It treated a link from one page to another as a kind of vote. A page linked to by many other pages was likely to be important, and a link from an important page counted for more than a link from an obscure one. This idea helped their search engine, Google, produce much more useful results, and it grew rapidly. Modern search engines use hundreds of signals, and link-based ranking led to new forms of manipulation, such as creating networks of fake links, which search companies continue to fight. In 1965, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded the chip maker Intel, observed that the number of components that could be placed on a computer chip was doubling roughly every year. He later revised the rate to about every two years. His observation, known as Moore's law, was not a law of nature but a prediction, and for decades the industry treated it almost as a target. As transistors became smaller, chips became faster, cheaper and more energy-efficient, which explains why a modern smartphone is far more powerful than the computers that guided the first Moon landings. In recent years, however, progress has slowed. Transistors are now so small that they approach the size of atoms, making further shrinking extremely difficult and expensive. Engineers are responding in other ways, such as stacking components in three dimensions and designing specialised chips for particular tasks, such as artificial intelligence. In the late 1990s, governments and businesses around the world became concerned about a problem known as the millennium bug, or Y2K. Many older computer systems stored years using only their last two digits, to save expensive memory. The year 1999 was recorded as ninety-nine, so when the date changed to 2000, some systems might read it as 1900, causing errors in calculations involving dates, from bank interest to scheduling. Organisations spent enormous sums checking and correcting their software. When the new year arrived, very few serious problems occurred. Some people concluded that the danger had been exaggerated and the money wasted. Many engineers who worked on the problem argue the opposite: that failures were rare precisely because so much work had been done in advance. The episode is sometimes used to illustrate a difficulty with prevention. When a problem is successfully avoided, it can look as though it never existed. When you send a photo over the internet, it does not travel as a single piece. Instead, it is broken into many small packets of data, each labelled with its destination and its place in the sequence. The packets may travel by different routes through the network, and at the other end they are put back together in the right order. If a packet is lost or damaged, it can simply be sent again. This method, called packet switching, was developed in the 1960s by researchers in the United States and Britain. It differed from the telephone network, which created a dedicated connection for the whole length of a call. Packet switching makes much more efficient use of the network, because many users can share the same connections, and it is resilient, since data can be routed around damaged or congested parts of the network. When people consider buying an electric car, one of their most common concerns is range anxiety: the fear that the battery will run out before they reach a charging point. Surveys suggest this worry often exceeds the reality. Most daily journeys are far shorter than the range of modern electric cars, and many owners charge at home overnight, so they start each day with a full battery. Long journeys still require planning, and the availability and reliability of public chargers vary greatly between regions. Cold weather can also reduce range noticeably, because batteries work less efficiently and energy is needed to heat the car. The mantis shrimp is a small, brightly coloured marine animal with one of the most powerful strikes in the animal kingdom. Some species have club-like limbs that they fire forward at extraordinary speed to smash the shells of crabs and snails. The strike is so fast that it causes bubbles to form and collapse in the water, producing an additional shock wave, a process called cavitation. In aquariums, mantis shrimp have been known to crack glass. Scientists have studied how the animal's clubs survive repeated impacts without breaking. They are built in layers arranged in a spiral pattern, which stops cracks from spreading. This structure has inspired engineers developing lightweight, impact-resistant materials for helmets, body armour and aircraft. The common cuckoo does not build a nest or raise its own young. Instead, the female lays her eggs in the nests of other bird species, a strategy known as brood parasitism. Her egg often closely resembles those of the host species in colour and pattern, reducing the chance that it will be rejected. After hatching, the cuckoo chick usually pushes the host's eggs or chicks out of the nest, so that it receives all the food. The host parents then raise the cuckoo, even when it grows much larger than they are. This relationship has been described as an evolutionary arms race. Host species that learn to recognise and reject strange eggs survive better, so cuckoos that lay more convincing eggs are favoured, and so on. Some host populations have become very good at detecting cuckoo eggs, while cuckoos in turn have evolved to lay their eggs very quickly, sometimes in only a few seconds. Dragonflies are among the most successful hunters in the animal world. Studies have found that some species catch their prey in the vast majority of attempts, a success rate far higher than that of lions or sharks. Their secret lies partly in their flight. Each of their four wings can be controlled independently, allowing them to hover, change direction instantly and even fly backwards. But researchers believe their brains matter just as much. Rather than simply chasing their prey, dragonflies predict where it will go and fly on a course to intercept it, much as a fielder runs to where a ball will land. Specialised nerve cells help them track a single target while ignoring others in a swarm. Many dog owners are convinced that their dogs look guilty when they have done something wrong, such as eating food from the table. In 2009, the researcher Alexandra Horowitz tested this belief. Owners were asked to leave the room after telling their dog not to eat a treat. In some cases the dog ate it; in others, the researcher removed it. When the owners returned, they were sometimes told, falsely, that the dog had eaten the treat. The dogs showed the so-called guilty look, lowering their heads and avoiding eye contact, most strongly when owners scolded them, whether or not they had actually eaten the treat. The study suggests that the guilty look is a response to the owner's behaviour rather than evidence that the dog feels guilt about its actions. This does not mean dogs lack emotions, but it warns against assuming that animals interpret situations exactly as humans do. Polar bears look white, but their fur is not actually white. Each hair is transparent and hollow, and it appears white because it scatters visible light, in the same way that snow and ice do. Glass frogs, found in the forests of Central and South America, have skin on their undersides so transparent that their hearts and other organs can be seen. When they rest on leaves during the day, their bodies look pale green and their outline is hard to see, which helps them avoid predators. There was a puzzle, however. Blood is red and should make the frogs easy to spot. In 2022, researchers used special imaging to study sleeping glass frogs and discovered that the animals remove most of the red blood cells from circulation and store them in their liver, which is covered by a reflective layer. This made the frogs two to three times more transparent while resting. When the frogs woke and became active, the red blood cells returned to circulation. Many hoverflies have yellow and black stripes that make them look like wasps or bees, yet they cannot sting. A harmless species benefits by resembling a dangerous or unpleasant one, because predators that have learned to avoid the dangerous species will also avoid the mimic. The strategy works best when mimics are less common than the species they copy. If mimics become too common, predators may eat many of them without being stung, learn that the pattern is not always dangerous, and begin attacking both. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched in December 2021, observes the universe mainly in infrared light, which is emitted by warm objects. This allows it to see very distant galaxies, whose light has been stretched into the infrared, and to look through clouds of dust where stars are forming. The solution is a sunshield about the size of a tennis court, made of five thin layers, which blocks heat from the Sun, Earth and Moon. The cold side of the telescope stays at around minus two hundred and thirty degrees Celsius. Look at the Moon through binoculars and you will see countless craters, the scars of impacts by asteroids and comets over billions of years. The Earth has been struck just as often, and in fact more, because it is larger and its gravity is stronger. So why does the Earth have so few visible craters? The answer is that our planet constantly renews its surface. Wind, water and ice erode craters over time, plants cover them, and sediments bury them. Over longer periods, the movement of tectonic plates recycles large parts of the Earth's crust. The Earth's atmosphere also burns up many smaller objects before they reach the ground. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, no weather and no moving plates, so its craters can survive almost unchanged for billions of years. This makes the Moon a valuable record of the history of impacts in our part of the solar system. In the silent era, films were shot at a range of speeds, often by cranking the camera by hand. When sound arrived in the late 1920s, the soundtrack was recorded on the same strip of film as the images, so the speed had to be fixed and consistent. Twenty-four frames per second was adopted as a compromise. It was fast enough to produce smooth motion and acceptable sound quality, but slow enough to keep the cost of film, which was expensive, under control. The standard has lasted for nearly a century, even though digital cameras could easily record faster. Some directors have experimented with higher frame rates, which make motion sharper, but many viewers found the result looked too much like television or video, and the slight blur of twenty-four frames has become part of what audiences think a film should look like. Timbuktu, in present-day Mali, was a major centre of trade and Islamic scholarship between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries. Caravans crossing the Sahara brought gold, salt and books, and wealthy families built up private libraries of handwritten manuscripts on subjects including astronomy, medicine, law and mathematics. Many of these manuscripts survived for centuries, kept in family collections, often in difficult conditions. In 2012, armed groups occupied the city, and there were fears that the manuscripts would be destroyed. Librarians and families secretly packed hundreds of thousands of documents into metal trunks and smuggled them south to the capital, Bamako, by road and by river. Some manuscripts were burned, but the great majority were saved. The bicycles can be viewed before you buy by arrangement.", "label": "B"}, {"text": "Evening classes at Millbrook College. Millbrook College is running ten-week evening courses in Spanish, Italian and Mandarin, starting in the week of 14 April. Classes last two hours and are held once a week. Beginners are welcome in all three languages, and an intermediate group will also run in Spanish if at least eight people enrol. The fee is £95 per course, with a reduced rate of £60 for people over sixty-five and for full-time students. Course books are not included in the fee. Places can be booked online or in person at the college office, which is open until 7 p.m. from Monday to Thursday. Each class has a maximum of fifteen students, so that everyone has a chance to speak.", "label": "C"}, {"text": "Found at Millbrook station. Items left on trains or at Millbrook station are kept at the lost property office next to the ticket hall for one month. After that, anything unclaimed is given to local charities, except for passports and bank cards, which are handed to the police. To collect an item, you will need to describe it and show some form of identification. There is no charge for collecting lost property in person, but items that have to be sent by post will be charged at cost. The office is open from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday to Friday; it is closed at weekends and on public holidays. Umbrellas, which make up the largest group of items handed in, are kept for only two weeks.", "label": "D"}, {"text": "The farmers' market is moving. Millbrook's monthly farmers' market, which has been held in the car park behind the town hall for the past twelve years, is moving to a new home. From May, the market will take place in Victoria Park, beside the bandstand, on the first Sunday of every month from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. The move will make room for twenty more stalls, including several selling hot food. Parking will be available at the park's north entrance, but visitors are encouraged to walk or cycle if they can. Stallholders who wish to apply for a place should contact the market office by the end of March. Dogs on leads are welcome, and a shuttle bus will run from the railway station on market days.", "label": "E"}, {"text": "Volunteer drivers wanted. Millbrook Community Transport is looking for volunteer drivers to take older residents to hospital appointments. Volunteers use their own cars and are paid a mileage allowance to cover fuel costs. You will need to have held a full driving licence for at least three years, and you must be willing to give at least one morning or afternoon a fortnight. No previous experience of care work is needed, as all new drivers attend a half-day training session. For an application form, visit the Community Transport office on Station Road or telephone 01632 960 418. Journeys usually take place on weekdays between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m.", "label": "F"}]

reading_passages.title: Westfield Adult Education: Autumn Short Courses
reading_passages.text: [{"text": "First Aid for Parents. This one-day course covers the most common emergencies involving babies and young children, including choking, burns and high temperatures. It runs on Saturday 11 October from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. and costs £40, which includes a light lunch. Everyone who completes the day receives a certificate, although this is not a professional qualification and cannot be used for work in childcare. Parents may not bring children to the session. Grandparents and other carers are also welcome to attend. The course is taught by a paramedic with many years of experience. Places are limited to twenty and usually fill quickly, so we recommend booking early.", "label": "A"}, {"text": "Introduction to Bookkeeping. Aimed at people who run a small business or are planning to start one, this eight-week course explains how to keep simple accounts, record expenses and prepare for a tax return. Sessions take place on Tuesday evenings from 6.30 to 8.30 p.m. Participants should bring their own laptop, as the college computer room is not available in the evenings. No previous knowledge of accounting is needed. The fee is £120, and payment can be made in two instalments if you prefer. By the end of the course, you should be able to set up a simple spreadsheet to track the money coming into and going out of your business.", "label": "B"}, {"text": "Photography with Your Phone. Learn to take better photographs using nothing more than the phone in your pocket. Over four Thursday afternoons, you will practise composition, lighting and simple editing. Two of the sessions are held outdoors in the town centre; if the weather is poor, these will be moved indoors and a different topic will be covered instead. The course is free for people who are currently unemployed, and costs £45 for everyone else. Please make sure your phone is fully charged before each session. You do not need an expensive phone, as the techniques work on most models from the last five years. At the end of the course, a selection of participants' photographs will be displayed in the college library.", "label": "C"}, {"text": "Cooking on a Budget. In six weekly sessions at the Riverside Community Centre kitchen, you will learn to plan meals, reduce food waste and cook healthy dishes for less than £2 a portion. All ingredients are provided and are included in the course fee of £75, and you will take home what you cook each week. Numbers are limited to ten people in each group because of the size of the kitchen, so early booking is advised. Please tell us about any food allergies when you enrol. Sessions are led by a professional chef who has worked in several local restaurants, and aprons are provided.", "label": "D"}, {"text": "Job Interview Skills. Run in partnership with several local employers, this two-evening course helps you prepare for job interviews. On the first evening, managers from local firms explain what they look for in candidates. On the second, each participant takes part in a practice interview, which is filmed so that you can watch it back and receive feedback. The course is free, but places must be reserved in advance. It is particularly suitable for people who are returning to work after a long break. You will also receive advice on writing a covering letter and on answering difficult questions, such as why you left your last job. Please bring a copy of your current CV to the first session, even if it is not yet complete, as it will be used during the practice interview.", "label": "E"}, {"text": "Beginners' Yoga. This ten-week class introduces the basic positions and breathing techniques of yoga. It is suitable for all ages and fitness levels, and mats are provided, although you are welcome to bring your own. Wear loose, comfortable clothing and avoid eating a large meal in the two hours before a class. If you are pregnant or have a back injury, please bring a note from your doctor confirming that you can take part. The fee is £85 for the full course, and a free trial class is held in the first week. Classes are held on Monday evenings in the main hall, which has changing facilities and showers. The tutor has taught yoga at the college for over ten years and will suggest simple exercises that you can practise at home between classes.", "label": "F"}]

reading_passages.title: Harlow Logistics Staff Handbook: Annual Leave and Absence
reading_passages.text: [{"text": "Annual leave entitlement. Full-time employees are entitled to 25 days of paid annual leave each year, in addition to public holidays. Part-time staff receive the same entitlement calculated in proportion to the hours they work; for example, someone who works three days a week receives 15 days. The leave year runs from 1 April to 31 March. Staff who join or leave the company part-way through the year receive a share of the full entitlement, which the payroll team will calculate. After five years of continuous service, employees receive two additional days of leave each year, and after ten years a further three days. Your remaining entitlement is shown on the online staff portal and is updated at the start of every month.", "label": "A"}, {"text": "Booking leave. All leave must be requested through the online staff portal and approved by your line manager before you make any travel arrangements. Requests for periods of more than five working days should be submitted at least four weeks in advance, while shorter periods require one week's notice. Managers aim to respond to requests within three working days. Because the warehouse is especially busy in the weeks before major public holidays, leave requested for December is allocated in the order in which requests are received, and no more than a quarter of any team may be absent at the same time. If a request is refused, your manager will explain the reason and suggest alternative dates where possible. Leave that has been approved will only be cancelled by the company in an emergency, and you will be compensated for any costs you cannot recover.", "label": "B"}, {"text": "Carrying leave over. We encourage staff to take their full entitlement within the leave year, as regular breaks are important for health and concentration. However, up to five unused days may be carried over into the following year, provided they are taken before the end of June. Any days carried over that have not been used by that date will be lost. In exceptional circumstances, such as long-term illness, a manager may agree to extend this deadline, but such requests must be made in writing to the Human Resources department. Staff who are close to the carry-over limit will receive a reminder from the payroll team in January.", "label": "C"}, {"text": "Reporting sickness. If you are unable to come to work because of illness, you must telephone your line manager, rather than send a text message or an email, before the start of your shift, or no later than one hour after it begins if you are too unwell to call earlier. You should explain the nature of the illness and say when you expect to return. If your manager is not available, you should call the duty supervisor instead. Failure to report absence correctly may result in the day being treated as unauthorised leave, which is unpaid. If you become ill while you are at work, tell your supervisor before leaving the site so that your absence can be recorded correctly.", "label": "D"}, {"text": "Evidence and returning to work. For absences of up to seven calendar days, you will be asked to complete a self-certification form on your first day back. For longer absences, you must provide a fit note from a doctor or another qualified health professional. When you return after any absence of more than two weeks, you will have a short meeting with your manager to discuss whether temporary changes to your duties or hours would help you settle back in. These meetings are intended to be supportive and are not part of any disciplinary process. Self-certification forms are available from the staff portal or from reception. If you are absent frequently, your manager may suggest a referral to the company's occupational health adviser.", "label": "E"}, {"text": "Other types of leave. Employees may take up to two days of paid compassionate leave following the death of a close family member, and further unpaid leave may be granted at the manager's discretion. Staff who serve as volunteers with the emergency services are entitled to up to ten days of paid leave a year for training and call-outs. Requests for time off to attend medical appointments should, where possible, be made for the beginning or end of a shift, so that disruption to the team is kept to a minimum. Parents may also request unpaid parental leave, which should be discussed with the Human Resources department at least four weeks in advance.", "label": "F"}]

reading_passages.title: Riverside Hotel Group: A Guide for New Front-of-House Staff
reading_passages.text: [{"text": "Welcome. This guide explains the main arrangements for new front-of-house staff, including receptionists, porters and restaurant hosts. It should be read together with your contract of employment, which sets out your hours and pay. During your first two weeks, you will be paired with an experienced colleague, known as your 'buddy', who can answer everyday questions about the hotel and its routines. More formal matters, such as holiday requests or changes to your contract, should always be discussed with your department manager rather than with your buddy. Your buddy will also show you around the building on your first day, including the fire exits and assembly points. At the end of your third month, you will have a review meeting with your department manager.", "label": "A"}, {"text": "Uniform. The hotel provides three sets of uniform, which remain the property of the company and must be returned when you leave. Uniforms are cleaned free of charge by the hotel laundry: simply leave them in the marked bags in the staff changing room before the end of your shift, and they will be ready within two days. Name badges must be worn at all times in public areas of the hotel. Staff are asked to wear plain black shoes, which are not supplied by the hotel, and to keep jewellery to a minimum. Hair should be neat and tidy, and long hair must be tied back when working in the restaurant. Replacement uniform items can be ordered from the housekeeping department if yours become damaged, although the cost of any items lost through carelessness may be taken from your pay.", "label": "B"}, {"text": "Shift patterns. Front-of-house departments operate 24 hours a day, and most staff work a rota of early, late and occasional night shifts. Rotas for the following fortnight are published every Friday. If you wish to swap a shift with a colleague, both of you must agree, and the swap must also be approved by the duty manager at least 48 hours in advance. Staff working a night shift receive an additional payment for each hour worked between midnight and 6 a.m., and a free hot meal is provided during the break. Rotas are planned so that no one works more than two night shifts in a row, and anyone who has difficulty with a particular shift pattern should speak to their department manager.", "label": "C"}, {"text": "Training. All new staff complete a two-day induction, covering fire safety, customer service standards and the hotel's booking system. In addition, the company offers a range of optional courses, including languages and first aid. These courses are free of charge and take place during working hours, but places are limited and are allocated by department managers. Staff who complete a recognised qualification in hospitality may be eligible for a one-off bonus, and details can be obtained from the Human Resources office. The induction also includes a tour of each department, so that you understand how your role fits with the work of others. Language courses are offered in French, Spanish and Mandarin, reflecting the countries our guests most often come from.", "label": "D"}, {"text": "Staff facilities. A staff canteen on the lower ground floor serves breakfast, lunch and dinner at subsidised prices. Lockers are available in the changing rooms, and keys can be collected from the security office on your first day. A small deposit is taken, which is returned when the key is handed back. Staff are not permitted to use the guest gym or swimming pool, but they can join a local fitness centre at a discounted rate through the company's partnership scheme. The canteen is open from 6 a.m. until 11 p.m., and a vending machine is available at other times. A quiet room is also provided for staff who need to rest during their breaks.", "label": "E"}, {"text": "Guest feedback. Comments from guests are reviewed every week, and members of staff who are mentioned positively are recognised in the monthly staff newsletter. Complaints are handled by the duty manager, and staff should never try to resolve a serious complaint on their own. If a guest becomes aggressive, staff should remain calm, avoid arguing, and call security using the emergency number printed on the back of their name badge. Staff are encouraged to pass on suggestions for improving the guest experience, and the best idea each quarter receives a small prize. Any comments that mention health or safety concerns are passed immediately to the duty manager, who will decide what action needs to be taken.", "label": "F"}]

reading_passages.title: A Library of Things
reading_passages.text: [{"text": "When the fictional town of Bellford opened a lending room for household equipment, its organisers resisted calling it a shop. Residents would borrow objects rather than buy them, returning each one for somebody else to use. The project began in a room beside the public library in 2018. Its initial stock came entirely from donations, although the team rejected items without instructions or with missing parts. Many donors imagined that their rarely used possessions would immediately become popular. The organisers were less certain: an object that was useful to its owner might be too specialised for a shared collection. They therefore recorded requests before deciding which additional equipment to acquire. The room was modest, with open shelves for small objects and lockable cupboards for powered equipment. Visitors could examine a catalogue at the entrance without becoming members. This mattered because many people initially assumed that borrowing required a complicated application. Staff wanted the first conversation to concern the job a resident hoped to complete, rather than the name of a particular machine. Sometimes a simpler object already on the shelves was sufficient.", "label": "A"}, {"text": "The first year challenged the assumption that larger objects would attract the most interest. Carpet cleaners accounted for more loans than any other category, while a collection of heavy garden machines was borrowed infrequently. Interviews suggested that transporting those machines was a greater obstacle than operating them. The team also discovered that a long waiting list could be misleading. Several residents had registered for the same weekend and would not accept alternative dates. Rather than simply purchasing duplicates of everything on the list, staff began recording when requests were made and whether a later loan would still be useful. This distinguished a persistent shortage from a brief seasonal peak.", "label": "B"}, {"text": "The lending procedure changed in 2020. Initially, every borrower had paid the same refundable deposit. Organisers replaced this with a deposit waiver for residents referred by local support organisations, while keeping the ordinary deposit for other borrowers. Both groups remained responsible for reporting damage. Staff also introduced a short demonstration before anyone could borrow a powered tool for the first time. This was not a formal qualification: borrowers watched a safe-use demonstration and practised the basic controls under supervision. A printed checklist travelled with each tool. The annual membership fee, by contrast, remained unchanged throughout the first three years, even though the collection grew.", "label": "C"}, {"text": "Behind the counter, maintenance required more work than the founders had expected. Volunteers inspected every returned object and entered faults in a shared log. A red label meant that an item could not be lent until it had been repaired and checked again. Replacement parts were purchased from the maintenance budget, not from a separate charge imposed on the next borrower. The log eventually revealed that three models of the same appliance required different filters. Standardising future purchases would make repairs simpler, but immediately discarding the existing models would waste working equipment. Staff chose to standardise gradually, replacing machines only when repair was no longer practical.", "label": "D"}, {"text": "Evaluating the environmental benefits proved difficult. Counting loans was straightforward; establishing what would have happened without the service was not. Some borrowers said they would otherwise have bought a new object, but others would have borrowed from a neighbour or abandoned the job. The evaluation report therefore refused to treat every loan as a purchase prevented. It also recorded journeys to collect equipment, because an extra car trip could offset part of the environmental saving. The writer considers this caution a strength rather than a failure. Claims about reduced consumption are more credible when they acknowledge uncertainty, and a busy lending desk alone is not proof of an environmental success.", "label": "E"}, {"text": "Bellford's experience suggests that shared ownership is as much a service-design problem as a storage problem. In the writer's view, expanding the collection should come after making the existing stock easier to borrow. Convenient opening hours and reliable maintenance deserve priority over an impressive catalogue. The writer also argues that paid coordination is necessary for a dependable long-term service; goodwill is valuable, but should not be treated as an unlimited supply of labour. A proposed delivery service might help residents who cannot carry equipment, yet its costs and environmental effects still need investigation. The sensible next step is a small trial, not an immediate promise to deliver every object to every address.", "label": "F"}]

reading_passages.title: Building with Grass
reading_passages.text: [{"text": "Bamboo is often described as a tree, but it is in fact a grass, and one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth. Some species can grow several tens of centimetres in a single day during their growing season, and a stem can reach its full height within a few months. A bamboo plantation can be harvested after three to five years, whereas timber from most trees takes decades to mature, and because the plant regrows from its underground root system, it does not need to be replanted after each harvest. People in Asia, Africa and Latin America have built with bamboo for thousands of years. In Colombia, for example, a large native species known locally as guadua has long been used for houses and bridges, and it has become the basis of a distinctive modern architecture.", "label": "A"}, {"text": "The qualities that make bamboo useful to builders are closely connected with its structure. The stem, known as a culm, is a hollow tube divided at intervals by solid nodes, which stiffen it and prevent it from buckling. Its fibres run along its length, giving it great strength in tension; relative to its weight, this strength is often compared favourably with that of steel. Bamboo is also light and flexible. When the ground shakes, a bamboo frame tends to bend rather than break, and because the structure is light, it generates smaller forces during an earthquake than heavy masonry does. Bamboo houses have survived earthquakes that destroyed brick and concrete buildings nearby. These properties, combined with its low cost and wide availability, explain why so many architects and engineers have become interested in the material.", "label": "B"}, {"text": "Bamboo does, however, have serious weaknesses. Its stems contain starch, which attracts beetles and other insects, and in damp conditions it is readily attacked by fungi. Untreated bamboo used outdoors may last only a few years before it begins to rot. Durability can be greatly improved by treatment. The most common method involves soaking the culms in a solution of borax and boric acid, which makes them unattractive to insects and fungi and is relatively safe to handle. Design matters too. Builders who work with bamboo often say that a building needs 'good boots and a good hat': the bamboo must be raised above the ground on a foundation of stone or concrete, so that it does not absorb moisture from the soil, and protected by a roof with wide overhangs, so that rain does not reach the walls.", "label": "C"}, {"text": "Engineering with bamboo presents its own difficulties.
