Because granular interactions are governed by frictional contact and dissipative collisions rather than microscopic thermal fluctuations, they operate under distinct physical laws that continue to challenge condensed matter physicists.", "label": "A"}, {"text": "The secret to how granular materials bear structural loads lies in the internal architecture of force chains. In a continuous homogeneous solid, such as steel or concrete, mechanical stress distributes smoothly and predictably throughout the material. In a granular pack, by contrast, stress is distributed in an intensely inhomogeneous, hierarchical pattern. Weight and external forces are channeled along delicate, branching networks of touching grains called force chains, which carry the vast majority of the mechanical load while adjacent, unstressed particles remain essentially inert. Because these force-bearing chains are fragile and anisotropic, a minor change in the direction or magnitude of an applied load can trigger sudden localized buckling. When force chains collapse, a solid heap can instantaneously liquefy into a catastrophic moving avalanche—a sudden phase change known in physics as a jamming-to-unjamming transition.", "label": "B"}, {"text": "When loose grains are poured steadily onto a flat surface, the resulting conical pile exhibits another hallmark of granular physics: the angle of repose. Grains accumulate until the slope of the pile reaches a characteristic maximum incline, typically between thirty and thirty-five degrees for dry quartz sand, governed by inter-particle friction and particle shape. In 1987, physicists Per Bak, Chao Tang, and Kurt Wiesenfeld utilized this sandpile geometry to introduce the revolutionary theory of self-organized criticality. They demonstrated that a sandpile built to its angle of repose naturally organizes itself into a critical state. Once this threshold is reached, dropping a single additional grain onto the apex can trigger anything from an imperceptible local shift of three grains to a massive, system-wide catastrophic landslide. The distribution of avalanche magnitudes follows a scale-invariant power law, demonstrating that complex systems can generate catastrophic events without any external trigger.", "label": "C"}, {"text": "When heterogeneous mixtures containing particles of different sizes or densities are shaken or sheared, granular media exhibit counter-intuitive sorting behaviors. In ordinary fluid suspensions, gravity causes heavier and larger particles to settle toward the bottom. In granular physics, however, vertical vibration frequently causes large, dense objects to rise to the top while smaller grains migrate to the bottom—a phenomenon popularly known as the 'Brazil nut effect'. Physicists have identified two primary mechanisms driving this size segregation: void percolation and granular convection. During the upward acceleration of a vibration cycle, transient voids open beneath larger particles; smaller grains easily trickle down through these microscopic gaps, preventing the larger object from sinking back down. Simultaneously, vertical vibration sets up convective circulatory rolls inside the container, carrying large particles upward along the center, where they become stranded on the surface because they are too large to re-enter narrow downward currents descending along container walls.", "label": "D"}, {"text": "Controlling granular behavior is a multi-billion-dollar imperative across modern civil, chemical, and agricultural engineering. In industrial storage hoppers and agricultural grain silos, dry particulates frequently refuse to discharge smoothly under gravity. As particles funnel toward a narrow exit orifice, they spontaneously interlock into rigid parabolic arches, known as stress bridges or jams, that completely arrest the flow of material. Conversely, when internal arches collapse unpredictably, the sudden downward rush of tons of grain can produce violent acoustic vibrations, structural resonance, and asymmetrical pressure differentials that rupture massive steel and concrete silos. To prevent costly bridging, engineers design specialized mass-flow hoppers with steep wall angles, polish interior surfaces with low-friction coatings, and install ultrasonic vibrators and internal distribution inserts that systematically break force chains.", "label": "E"}, {"text": "On a planetary scale, the physics of granular flow dictates some of the most destructive natural geomorphic hazards, including snow avalanches, volcanic pyroclastic density currents, and catastrophic debris flows. In mountainous regions, rising global temperatures and retreating permafrost are destabilizing rock slopes, unleashing millions of tonnes of rocky debris into river valleys. When dry debris mixes with torrential seasonal rainfall, it transforms into a saturated, non-Newtonian slurry that travels down valleys at highway speeds, carrying colossal boulders in suspension. Because interstitial pore-water pressure counteracts gravitational friction between individual grains, saturated debris flows can travel across exceptionally gentle gradients without losing kinetic momentum. Deciphering the microscopic physics of grain-scale friction, pore pressure dissipation, and granular rheology remains indispensable for engineering early-warning radar systems, designing retention barriers, and safeguarding mountain populations against catastrophic landslides.", "label": "F"}]

reorder_items.title: Papyrus Manufacture in the Nile Delta
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In ancient Egypt, the marshlands of the Nile Delta provided abundant thickets of Cyperus papyrus reeds.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Craftsmen harvested these aquatic stems and stripped away the fibrous green outer rinds to expose the white pith.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "This spongy pith was sliced into thin longitudinal strips, which were arranged in two overlapping perpendicular layers on wooden boards.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Workers then pounded the wet sheets with heavy wooden mallets, forcing the cellular sap to weld the fibers together.", "label": "p4"}, {"text": "After thorough sun drying and smoothing with polished stones, the resulting scrolls formed durable writing surfaces that endured for millennia.", "label": "p5"}]

reorder_items.title: Roman Hypocaust Heating Systems
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Imperial Roman architects designed monumental public thermae that accommodated thousands of bathers daily.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Heating these cavernous vaulted chambers required an ingenious underfloor warming infrastructure known as a hypocaust.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Slave-tended outdoor furnaces generated intense hot flue gases that were channeled beneath raised tile floors supported by brick pillars.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "From these underfloor voids, the hot air ascended through hollow terracotta wall pipes, warming both floors and masonry walls evenly.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Ancient Roman Mosaic Tesserae Crafting
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In ancient Roman architecture, decorative floor mosaics were an essential feature of public villas and bathhouses.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Artisans created these intricate decorative surfaces by cutting colored stones, marble, and colored glass into tiny cubical pieces called tesserae.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "On top of a leveled rubble foundation, workers spread a fresh bedding layer of wet lime and pozzolan mortar.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Craftsmen pressed individual tesserae firmly into this damp mortar bed according to painted geometric patterns.", "label": "p4"}, {"text": "Finally, liquid grout was rubbed across the joints and the surface was polished with abrasive sand to create a seamless, durable pavement.", "label": "p5"}]

reorder_items.title: Watergate Pound Locks in Inland Waterways
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In early medieval canal networks, transport barges moving between rivers of differing elevations had to be hauled over steep, dangerous earth ramps.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "To overcome this hazard, hydraulic engineers developed the pound lock, featuring a closed rectangular chamber enclosed by two separate water gates.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "When a vessel entered the lock, operators closed the entry gates and opened underwater sluice valves to adjust water levels inside the chamber.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Once water levels equalized with the adjoining canal reach, the opposite gates opened to allow the barge to float smoothly onward.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Rag Parchment Sizing in Samarkand
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In the eighth century, the Silk Road oasis city of Samarkand emerged as a renowned hub for high-grade manuscript production.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Local artisans refined Chinese techniques by substituting raw mulberry bark with discarded linen rags and hemp fibers.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "These softened rags were macerated in water-driven stamp mills, producing an exceptionally fine and homogeneous cellulose slurry.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "After lifting the sheets on wire sieves, workers coated the dry paper with starch size made from fermented wheat flour.", "label": "p4"}, {"text": "This starch sizing sealed the porous surface, preventing liquid calligraphy ink from bleeding and giving Samarkand paper its legendary longevity.", "label": "p5"}]

reorder_items.title: Alpaca Fiber Grading in the Andes
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Indigenous pastoralist communities throughout the high Andean altiplano have raised domesticated alpacas for thousands of years.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "The primary economic value of these camelids lies in their remarkably soft, hollow-core fleece, which provides superior thermal insulation.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Following seasonal shearing, experienced sorters painstakingly grade the raw wool by hand into distinct fineness categories based on fiber diameter.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "The finest category, baby alpaca, is reserved for luxury lightweight textiles, while coarser fibers are spun into rugged blankets and ropes.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Polynesian Double-Hulled Catamarans
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Ancient Polynesian navigators colonized thousands of isolated islands across millions of square kilometres of open Pacific Ocean.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "This unprecedented maritime expansion was made possible by the development of ocean-going, double-hulled sailing canoes.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Shipwrights connected two parallel wooden hulls with flexible lashed crossbeams, supporting a raised central deck and woven pandanus sails.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "This dual-hull architecture provided immense stability in heavy ocean swells without capsizing, allowing voyagers to transport families, livestock, and crops over thousands of nautical miles.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Evolution of Baleen Whales
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Early fossil ancestors of modern baleen whales were modest-sized marine predators equipped with sharp teeth.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Approximately thirty million years ago, a dramatic change in oceanic circulation triggered widespread upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "In response to massive blooms of krill and zooplankton, ancestral mysticetes gradually lost their teeth in favor of fibrous keratinous baleen plates.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "These comb-like filters enabled bulk filter feeding, allowing baleen whales to grow into the largest animals to have ever lived on Earth.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Acoustics of Stradivari Violins
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Violins crafted in seventeenth-century Cremona by Antonio Stradivari are renowned for their extraordinary tonal depth and projection.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "For centuries, luthiers and physicists debated whether this legendary acoustic quality stemmed from secret varnishes or instrument geometry.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Recent dendrochronological analysis revealed that Stradivari used Norway spruce harvested during the Little Ice Age, when unusually cold summers produced exceptionally narrow, uniform growth rings.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "This uniform wood density, combined with chemical mineral soaks containing alum and borax, created an ultralight acoustic soundboard that vibrates with peerless clarity.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Traditional Windcatchers in Desert Architecture
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Settlements built across the arid deserts of the Middle East faced extreme daytime temperatures without modern electrical cooling.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "To maintain comfortable indoor conditions, vernacular architects incorporated tall vertical ventilation towers known as windcatchers.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "These architectural towers rose high above rooftop levels to catch faster, cooler breezes blowing across the upper atmosphere.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Internal vertical baffles funneled this fresh air downward through basement water pools, cooling and humidifying the air before releasing it into living rooms.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Archaeology of Mohenjo-Daro Drains
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "The Bronze Age cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation, dating to roughly 2500 BCE, exhibited unmatched municipal town planning.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "A defining feature of sites like Mohenjo-Daro was a sophisticated city-wide network of covered sanitary drains.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Individual domestic bathrooms channeled wastewater into baked-brick conduits running along the centers of major streets.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "These public drains were covered with removable flat limestone slabs, allowing municipal maintenance workers to clear accumulated silt and avoid urban contamination.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Parchment Preparation from Untanned Hides
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Before paper manufacturing spread across Europe, medieval scribes transcribed manuscripts onto parchment prepared from untanned animal hides.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Tanners first soaked raw pelts in vats of slaked lime solution for several days to dissolve natural fats and loosen hair follicles.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Workers then scraped the dehaired skins clean and stretched them taut across circular wooden frames called herse.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "While stretched under tension, artisans shaved the skin with a crescent-shaped lunellum knife to produce a smooth, velvet writing surface.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Physics of Curling Stones
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In the winter sport of curling, players slide polished granite stones across a prepared sheet of ice toward a target circular house.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Unlike ordinary objects sliding on friction, a rotating curling stone curls in the same direction as its rotational spin.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "To manipulate this curved trajectory, teammates vigorously sweep the pebbled ice directly in front of the moving stone with broom heads.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "This friction temporarily melts a microscopic thin film of liquid water, reducing drag and extending the stone's distance and steering line.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Viking Sunstone Polarisation Navigation
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Early medieval Norse seafarers crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean between Scandinavia, Iceland, and Greenland.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Navigating across these high-latitude seas was fraught with peril due to frequent overcast skies, dense fog, and prolonged polar twilights.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Historical sagas recount that Norse navigators relied on optical crystals known as solarsteinn (sunstones) to find their bearings when the sun was hidden.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Modern optical experiments confirmed that transparent crystals of Iceland spar (calcite) polarize diffuse daylight, allowing navigators to pinpoint the sun's exact celestial position behind heavy clouds.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Ancient Olive Pressing Beam Presses
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Olive oil was an indispensable agricultural staple across the ancient Mediterranean, used for cooking, lighting, and religious rituals.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Harvested olives were initially crushed in large circular stone basins (the trapetum) to break the fruit pulp without shattering the bitter inner pits.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "The resulting mash was scooped into woven hemp baskets and stacked beneath colossal wooden lever beams weighted with stone counterweights.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "As the lever pressed downward, virgin oil and dark bitter water filtered through the weave into settling vats, where pure oil was skimmed from the surface.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Mechanics of Woodpecker Skulls
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Woodpeckers repeatedly hammer their beaks into solid tree trunks with deceleration forces exceeding one thousand times the force of gravity.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Biomechanical engineers investigated how these birds routinely survive such violent impacts without suffering concussions or brain trauma.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Micro-CT imaging revealed that the bird's brain is tightly encased within dense, spongy cranial bone that disperses mechanical shockwaves.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Furthermore, an elongated hyoid bone wraps completely around the skull like a natural safety harness, damping vibrations before they can reach delicate brain tissues.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Crucible Smelting of Ancient Wootz Blades
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "During the first millennium BCE, metallurgists in southern India developed Wootz, an ultra-high-carbon crucible steel of legendary strength.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Smiths sealed porous iron ore, dry wood chips, and plant leaves inside airtight refractory clay crucibles before placing them in high-heat charcoal furnaces.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "The burning vegetation emitted carbon monoxide that rapidly infused into the molten iron, raising its carbon content to roughly 1.5 percent.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "When slowly cooled over days, the steel precipitated micro-bands of hard iron carbides that produced the wavy watered patterns characteristic of historical Damascus swords.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Venetian Glass Blowing Guilds
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "During the Middle Ages, the Republic of Venice dominated the European trade in luxury glassware and mirror manufacture.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "In 1291, Venetian authorities enacted a strict decree ordering all glassmaking furnaces to be relocated to the isolated island of Murano.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "While officially framed as a fire-prevention measure for the wooden city, the relocation primarily served to safeguard secret chemical recipes from rival European nations.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Glassblowers on Murano were forbidden from leaving the republic under penalty of death, preserving a Venetian commercial monopoly that endured for centuries.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Architecture of Stepwell Wells
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In the semi-arid states of western India, monsoonal rainfall is intensely seasonal, followed by months of acute scorching drought.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "To secure dependable water supplies throughout the dry season, medieval kingdoms engineered monumental subterranean stepwells known as baolis.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "These structures incorporated descending flights of stone stairs flanked by multi-tiered carved pavilions that reached deep subterranean water tables.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "As the water table fluctuated between seasons, residents could descend to whatever depth the water stood, while the shaded masonry provided a cool communal sanctuary from the desert heat.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Cold Storage Icehouses in Historic Estates
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Before the advent of mechanical refrigeration, maintaining fresh dairy, meat, and vegetables during hot summer months was a major domestic challenge.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Estate owners resolved this difficulty by constructing deep subterranean icehouses sheltered beneath wooded hillsides.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "During freezing winter months, estate laborers harvested thick ice blocks from frozen ornamental ponds and packed them into the underground chambers.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Insulated with thick layers of dry straw and heavy timber doors, these subterranean storage vaults kept ice frozen throughout the following summer.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Enzymatic Digestion in Carnivorous Flora
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In nutrient-deficient habitats like waterlogged bogs, standard plants struggle to absorb essential nitrogen and phosphorus from the soil.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Carnivorous pitcher plants overcame this environmental barrier by evolving modified cup-shaped leaves that trap unwary insects.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Insects slipping into the pitcher drown in an acidic pool of digestive fluid secreted by specialized glandular cells lining the interior walls.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Potent proteolytic enzymes then dissolve the prey's soft tissues, allowing the plant to absorb vital nitrogen compounds directly through its foliage.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Ancient Roman Milestones and Surveying
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "The administrative cohesion of the Roman Empire was anchored by an expansive highway network extending over eighty thousand kilometres.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "To map and regulate transit along these arteries, surveyors (agrimensores) erected cylindrical stone milestones at intervals of precisely one Roman mile.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Each carved pillar indicated the distance to Rome or the nearest provincial capital, alongside the name of the emperor who funded the road's construction.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "These markers enabled imperial couriers and military legions to calculate journey times and coordinate logistical movements across vast continental distances.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Aerodynamics of Maple Seed Whirlybirds
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In autumn, mature maple trees shed winged aerodynamic seed pods known to botanists as samaras.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Instead of falling straight to the forest floor, the asymmetrical seed auto-rotates rapidly around its center of gravity like a miniature helicopter.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "This continuous spinning creates a stable leading-edge vortex above the winglet, dramatically increasing aerodynamic lift.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "By drastically slowing its descent velocity, the spinning samara allows passing wind currents to carry the seedling far away from the shade of the parent tree.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Bronze Age Tin Mining in Cornwall
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "During the Bronze Age, metallurgical production required alloying soft copper with approximately ten percent tin to forge durable weapons and tools.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Because geological tin deposits are exceptionally rare in the Mediterranean, ancient smiths relied on long-distance maritime trade routes to southwestern Britain.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "In Cornwall, miners extracted heavy black cassiterite pebbles from alluvial stream gravels using panning and trenching techniques.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "The smelted tin ingots were then shipped across the English Channel and transported across Europe, sustaining the continent's Bronze Age economy.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Optics of Camera Obscura
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "The foundational optical principle behind modern photography was observed in antiquity: the camera obscura.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "When sunlight passes through a tiny pinhole into a completely darkened chamber, light rays traveling in straight paths cross at the aperture.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "This geometric intersection projects an inverted and reversed color image of the illuminated exterior scene onto the opposing wall.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "By the Renaissance, artists like Leonardo da Vinci and Johannes Vermeer utilized portable camera obscura boxes fitted with glass lenses to trace perspectives with lifelike accuracy.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Tungsten Filament Incandescent Bulbs
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Early electric incandescent light bulbs relied on carbonized bamboo or cellulose filaments that burned out after a few hundred hours.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "In 1904, Hungarian and American chemists sought a more resilient alternative with a higher melting point to prevent filament evaporation.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "They turned to metallic tungsten, an element capable of operating at white-hot temperatures exceeding 2,500 degrees Celsius without melting.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "When encased within glass bulbs filled with inert argon gas rather than a vacuum, coiled tungsten filaments delivered thousands of hours of reliable illumination.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Physiology of Deep Diving Seals
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Weddell seals in Antarctica routinely dive to depths exceeding six hundred metres in search of fish, remaining submerged for over an hour.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "To achieve these extraordinary dives on a single breath, the seals rely on extreme physiological adaptations that minimize oxygen consumption.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Upon descending, an involuntary mammalian dive reflex abruptly slows their heart rate from eighty beats per minute to fewer than fifteen.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Simultaneously, peripheral blood vessels constrict, shutting off blood flow to muscles and skin to prioritize oxygen delivery exclusively to the brain and heart.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Navigation of Dung Beetles by Starlight
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "After fashioning a fresh ball of herbivore dung, African dung beetles must roll it away from crowded communal mounds in a straight line.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Rolling in an erratic circle risks returning to the mound, where aggressive rivals will steal the hard-earned food ball.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Behavioral experiments conducted in South African planetariums demonstrated that nocturnal beetles climb atop their ball and perform an orientation dance.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "By referencing the diffuse polarization of the Milky Way across the night sky, the beetles maintain flawless straight courses even on moonless nights.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Submerged Bog Oak Wood Mineralization
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Thousands of years ago, vast primeval oak forests grew across the lowland basins of the British Isles and northern Europe.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "As regional climates became wetter, rising water tables submerged the trees, which fell and became buried in anaerobic peat bogs.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Over millennia, acidic, oxygen-starved bog water dissolved iron salts, which reacted chemically with natural tannins in the oak wood.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "This geochemical reaction transformed the timber into bog oak, a lustrous jet-black semi-fossilized hardwood prized by cabinetmakers for fine furniture.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Waxed Linen Cartography in Mediterranean Navigation
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "During the late Middle Ages, maritime merchants expanding Mediterranean trade routes required precise navigational maps that could withstand damp sea air.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Italian and Catalan cartographers developed portolan charts drawn on durable animal vellum and treated linen cloth.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Draughtsmen coated the woven linen backing with bees wax and natural resins to make the maps impervious to saltwater spray.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Using magnetic compass directions, they inked radiating network lines across the water-resistant charts, enabling navigators to plot reliable open-sea bearings.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Domestication of Maize in Oaxaca
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "The wild ancestor of modern domesticated maize is teosinte, a wild grass native to the Balsas River valley of southwestern Mexico.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Teosinte bore only tiny spikes containing five to ten hard, triangular kernels encased in impenetrable stony fruit cases.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Approximately nine thousand years ago, indigenous foragers in Oaxaca began selectively cultivating plants that displayed rare genetic mutations that prevented kernel casing formation.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Centuries of systematic selective breeding gradually transformed this modest wild grass into modern corn with hundreds of soft, exposed grains on a central cob.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Engineering of Medieval Catapults
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In medieval siege warfare, attacking forces required heavy artillery capable of breaching thick stone castle curtain walls.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "By the twelfth century, military engineers developed the counterweight trebuchet, an immense gravity-powered throwing machine.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "The machine operated on the principle of a seesaw lever: a massive box filled with dozens of tonnes of stones was raised on the short arm.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "When released, the heavy counterweight fell rapidly, swinging the long throwing arm and slinging stone boulders weighing over one hundred kilograms across hundreds of metres.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Ancient Mayan Cenote Sinkholes
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "The limestone plateau of the Yucatan Peninsula in southern Mexico possesses virtually no surface rivers, streams, or freshwater lakes.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "To support large urban populations, ancient Maya city-states relied entirely on cenotes—colossal natural sinkholes formed by collapsed cave ceilings.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "These circular vertical shafts punctured the porous limestone bedrock, exposing deep, subterranean groundwater aquifers filled with crystalline rainwater.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Major urban centers like Chichen Itza were built directly around these life-sustaining sinkholes, which served both as municipal water reservoirs and as sacred portals for religious offerings.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Traditional Terracotta Roof Tile Manufacturing
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Throughout the Mediterranean basin, building durable roofs that could withstand intense sun and winter rain required ceramic roofing materials.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Artisans began the manufacturing process by excavating local alluvial clays and kneading the raw earth with water in foot-treading pits.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "The prepared clay was pressed into curved wooden molds to form distinctive semi-cylindrical pan and cover tiles.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "After drying slowly on shaded wooden racks to prevent shrinkage cracks, the tiles were fired in wood kilns until the minerals fused into waterproof terracotta.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Aerodynamics of Hummingbird Hovering
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Hummingbirds are the only avian species capable of sustained, stationary hovering and sustained backwards flight.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Unlike other birds, which produce aerodynamic lift almost exclusively during the downward wingbeat, hummingbirds generate lift on both strokes.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Their ball-and-socket shoulder joints allow them to swivel their rigid wings upside down at the stroke reversal point in a continuous horizontal figure-eight motion.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "This symmetrical bilateral flapping pattern generates steady upward aerodynamic support that keeps the tiny bird perfectly motionless while sipping floral nectar.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Seismology of Deep Moonquakes
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Between 1969 and 1972, Apollo astronauts deployed a network of passive seismometers across the lunar surface to record vibrations.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "These instruments detected thousands of deep moonquakes originating between eight hundred and one thousand kilometres beneath the lunar crust.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Analysis of the recorded wave signatures revealed that these tremors occur on a regular monthly cycle matching the Moon's eccentric orbit around Earth.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Gravitational tidal forces exerted by Earth cyclically squeeze and deform the lunar mantle, proving that celestial tides can trigger internal fracturing on extraterrestrial bodies.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Traditional Felt Production from Sheep Wool
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Felt is widely recognized by anthropologists as humanity's earliest fabricated textile, predating spinning wheels and woven cloth.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Pastoral nomadic artisans produced dense felt sheets by shearing raw wool fleece and carding the tangled fibers into broad, layered mats.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "These layered wool mats were thoroughly saturated with hot water and alkaline soap to relax the microscopic scales along each fiber shaft.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Artisans then rolled the wet mats around wooden poles and rhythmically pressed them for hours, causing the scales to interlock permanently into warm, windproof fabric.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Ancient Qanat Subterranean Irrigation Channels
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In the arid plateaus of ancient Persia, communities developed qanats to transport mountain groundwater across vast desert distances.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Miners first sank a vertical mother well deep into an alluvial fan at the foothills until tapping the subterranean water table.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "From this source, diggers excavated a gently sloping underground tunnel extending miles toward lowland agricultural fields.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Vertical shafts were spaced along the tunnel route to provide ventilation and allow workers to haul out excavated soil and debris.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Evolution of Geckos Climbing Pads
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Geckos possess an astounding ability to scurry up vertical glass panes and run effortlessly across polished ceilings upside down.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "For decades, zoologists assumed their adhesion relied on chemical glues, suction cups, or microscopic mechanical claws.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Electron microscopy revealed that gecko toe pads are covered with millions of microscopic keratinous hairs called setae, which branch into billions of spatulae.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "When these nanoscale spatulae come into intimate contact with a surface, weak intermolecular van der Waals forces produce immense collective adhesion without leaving sticky residues.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Structural Mechanics of Gothic Vaults
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Romanesque churches of the early Middle Ages were characterized by thick, monolithic stone walls with few windows to support massive barrel vaults.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "In the twelfth century, French master masons pioneered ribbed groin vaulting combined with pointed arches to overcome this structural confinement.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Pointed arches channeled the vertical dead weight of the stone ceiling directly downward into slender clustered columns rather than outward against exterior walls.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "By adding exterior flying buttresses to absorb residual lateral thrust, architects could replace heavy masonry walls with soaring expanses of stained glass.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Stratified Soil Trenching in Historical Archaeology
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Uncovering the chronological sequence of human occupation at an ancient settlement requires meticulous stratigraphical excavation.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Archaeologists begin by laying out a precision metric grid across the site and digging vertical exploratory trenches.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "As excavators peel back successive layers of earth, distinct soil strata representing different cultural eras become visible in the trench walls.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "By recording the precise three-dimensional coordinate of every discovered pottery sherd and stone tool within these layers, researchers reconstruct the timeline of human activity.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Ecology of Epiphytic Bromeliads
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In the dense canopies of tropical rainforests, ground-level sunlight is severely limited, prompting plants to seek alternative habitats high on tree branches.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Epiphytic bromeliads evolved a specialized aerial architecture: tightly overlapping leaf bases that form an impermeable central water cistern.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "These aerial phytotelmata capture rainfall, falling leaf detritus, and insect droppings, creating suspended aquatic micro-ecosystems high in the canopy.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Specialized tree frogs, aquatic insects, and crabs spend their entire life cycles inside these treetop pools, while the bromeliad absorbs nutrients directly through foliar trichomes.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Physics of Boomerang Returning Flight
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Aboriginal Australians invented the returning boomerang thousands of years ago, crafting it from curved hardwood branches for hunting and ceremonial use.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "The weapon's ability to fly in an enormous circular arc and return to the thrower depends on two intersecting aerodynamic principles.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Each wing of the boomerang is sculpted into an asymmetric aerofoil; as it spins horizontally through the air, the forward-sweeping wing generates more lift than the retreating wing.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "This lift imbalance exerts an uneven aerodynamic torque that induces gyroscopic precession, causing the spinning trajectory to curve continuously until it returns to its origin point.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Ancient Egyptian Faience Glazing
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In ancient Egypt, craftspeople produced faience—a non-clay ceramic material with a bright, glassy turquoise sheen prized as a synthetic alternative to turquoise stone.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "The raw body paste was prepared by mixing crushed quartz sand, alkaline natron salts, copper oxide colorant, and lime with water into shaped figurines.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "As the shaped objects dried in the hot Egyptian sun, soluble copper and natron salts effloresced to the exterior surface, forming a powdery white crust.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "When fired in wood kilns, this mineral crust melted into a self-glazing, brilliant blue vitreous coating that permanently sealed the porous quartz core.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Navigation of Sea Turtles by Geomagnetism
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Newly hatched loggerhead sea turtles emerge from coastal beach nests and embark on multi-year transoceanic migrations across open seas.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Despite crossing thousands of miles of featureless ocean without visual landmarks, juvenile turtles maintain precise navigational headings.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Biologists placed young turtles inside controlled magnetic coils, altering the local magnetic inclination and field intensity.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "The turtles systematically reoriented their swimming direction in response to the artificial fields, proving they possess an innate internal magnetic map that guides their trans-oceanic navigation.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Metallurgy of Ancient Platinum in Ecuador
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In pre-Columbian South America, indigenous metallurgists of the La Tolita culture crafted ceremonial jewelry from platinum centuries before European scientists knew the metal existed.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Working with platinum presented an immense technological hurdle: its melting point of 1,768 degrees Celsius far exceeded the heat capability of charcoal blowpipe furnaces.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "La Tolita smiths devised a powder metallurgy technique known as sintering: mixing fine platinum grains with low-melting gold dust on a charcoal hearth.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "The molten gold flowed around the platinum granules, binding them into an alloy that could be repeatedly heated, hammered, and polished into gleaming masks and ornaments.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Evolution of Penguin Feathers
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "Unlike flighted birds whose feathers are arranged along distinct linear tracts with bare skin beneath, penguins possess a completely uniform, continuous feather coat.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "This specialized plumage is an evolutionary adaptation for enduring continuous submersion in freezing sub-Antarctic waters.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Each feather is short, stiff, and densely packed, featuring an oily waterproof outer barb and a downy, insulating underlayer.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "This dense arrangement traps a permanent layer of warm air next to the skin, preventing cold seawater from breaching the thermal barrier during deep fishing dives.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Chemistry of Ancient Birch Pitch Glue
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "In the Middle Paleolithic era, Neanderthals produced birch bark pitch, widely recognized as humanity's earliest manufactured synthetic adhesive.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "Extracting pitch from white birch bark required an exacting pyrotechnic process called anoxic dry distillation.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Neanderthals rolled sheets of bark inside sealed earthen pits beneath charcoal fires, heating the material to roughly four hundred degrees Celsius in the complete absence of oxygen.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "The heating vaporized complex betulin resins, which condensed into a dark, pliable tar that Neanderthals used to haft stone spear points securely onto wooden shafts.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: Clepsydra Outflow Clocks in Ancient Greece
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "To regulate speaking times in Athenian law courts, ancient Greeks relied on the clepsydra, a calibrated outflow clock.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "The device consisted of a cylindrical stone vessel fitted with a pierced bronze outflow nozzle near its base.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Before an orator began their legal address, court attendants filled the container with a measured volume of water and unstopped the nozzle.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "As liquid drained steadily through the orifice, the descending surface line marked equal increments of elapsed time on internal scale rings.", "label": "p4"}]

reorder_items.title: The Braiding of Incan Suspension Cables
reorder_items.text: [{"text": "The rugged topography of the Andes Mountains presented immense geographic barriers to transit within the Inca Empire.", "label": "p1"}, {"text": "To span yawning river chasms where wooden timber or stone arches were impossible, Incan engineers developed suspension spans woven entirely from wild ichu grass.", "label": "p2"}, {"text": "Local communities harvested tough mountain grass, braided it into small cords, and twisted these cords into massive cables as thick as a human torso.", "label": "p3"}, {"text": "Anchored into solid stone abutments on opposite canyon rims, these woven grass cables supported foot bridges that carried imperial couriers and llama caravans safely across alpine gorges.", "label": "p4"}]

listening_parts.title: You will hear a man phoning a holiday activity centre to book a course for his daughter.
listening_parts.text: Receptionist: Good morning, Riverside Holiday Activity Centre. How can I help you? Caller: Hello. I'd like to book a place on one of your summer courses for my daughter, please. Receptionist: Of course. I'll fill in a booking form for you. Could I have your daughter's name? Caller: Yes, it's Emily Hartley. That's H, A, R, T, L, E, Y. Receptionist: Thank you. And how old is Emily? Caller: She's ten at the moment, but she'll be eleven by the time the course starts, so I suppose you should put eleven. Receptionist: Yes, we go by the age on the first day. Now, which course is she interested in? At the moment we still have places on sailing, climbing and mountain biking. Caller: She did sailing last year and enjoyed it, but this time she's really keen on climbing. Receptionist: Climbing, then. There are two climbing courses in August. The first one runs from the seventh to the eleventh, but I'm afraid that one's full. The second runs from the fourteenth to the eighteenth. Caller: The second one's fine. We're away at the beginning of the month anyway. Receptionist: Good. Most of our courses start at nine o'clock, but because the climbing group travels to the quarry first, that one starts at half past nine each day. Caller: Half past nine. That's easier for us, actually. What does she need to bring? Receptionist: She'll need a packed lunch every day, and she should wear trainers rather than sandals. We provide the helmets and the harnesses, so she doesn't need those. But please make sure she brings a hat, because the group is outdoors for most of the day. Caller: A hat. Right. Is there anything else you need to know? Receptionist: Yes. Does Emily have any allergies or medical conditions? Caller: She's not allergic to anything we know of, except peanuts. She has to be careful with those. Receptionist: Peanuts. I'll make a note of that, and we'll tell the instructors. Now, about payment. The course costs one hundred and twenty pounds, but if you've booked with us before, you get a discount. Caller: We came last year, yes. Receptionist: In that case there's a discount of ten per cent. It used to be fifteen, but that changed in January. Caller: Ten per cent is still very welcome. Receptionist: One more question for our records. How did you first hear about the centre? Was it the radio advertisement? Caller: I think my wife heard something on the radio, but actually we found you through the local newspaper. There was an article about your summer courses. Receptionist: The newspaper, lovely. And finally, who will be collecting Emily at the end of each day? Caller: I'll bring her in the mornings, but I work in the afternoons, so her grandmother will collect her. Receptionist: Her grandmother. She'll need to show some identification on the first day. Caller: No problem, I'll let her know. Receptionist: That's everything. We'll email you a confirmation this afternoon. Caller: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

listening_parts.title: You will hear a ranger talking to a group of visitors at Oakfield Nature Reserve.
listening_parts.text: Ranger: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Oakfield Nature Reserve. My name's Sam and I'm one of the rangers here. Before you set off, I'd like to tell you a little about the reserve and show you where things are on the map. The land here has an interesting history. Many visitors assume it was once farmland, because of the farms that surround it, but in fact, for most of the last century, this was a quarry. Sand and gravel were dug out here until the nineteen eighties, and the lake you'll see is simply the old quarry pit, which filled with water when the digging stopped. We've made quite a few changes recently. Last year we opened the visitor centre, and a lot of people ask whether the café is new, but it has been here for years. What's really new this year is the boardwalk across the wet meadow, which means you can now get close to the reed beds without getting your feet wet. If you'd like to join a guided walk, they leave from the visitor centre. In the summer they used to start at ten, but we found that most families arrive a bit later, so now there's one walk a day, at eleven o'clock. There's also a bat walk on Friday evenings, but that has to be booked in advance. We ask all visitors to follow a few simple rules. Dogs are welcome as long as they're kept on a lead, and feeding the ducks is fine as long as you use the special food we sell in the shop. What we do not allow anywhere on the reserve is the use of drones, because they disturb nesting birds. You might be wondering how a place like this is paid for. We do receive a small grant from the local council, and we've had lottery money for particular projects such as the boardwalk, but the reserve depends mainly on the membership fees paid by our supporters, so please do think about joining. Now, if you look at your map, you'll see the main entrance at the bottom. As you come through the main entrance, the café is immediately on your left. Don't confuse it with the ticket office, which is on the right-hand side of the entrance. If you follow the main path north, you'll come to a bridge over the stream. Straight after the bridge, on your left, you'll find the picnic area, with tables and a small play area for children. From the bridge, take the path to the right, which runs along the southern shore of the lake. Some people expect the bird hide to be at the north end of the lake, where the old boathouse was, but that building is now used for storage. The new bird hide is where the lakeside path ends, on the far eastern side of the lake. Back on the main path, carry on north. Where the woodland begins on your left, you'll see the wildflower meadow, which runs along the southern edge of the trees. It's at its best in June. And at the very top of the reserve, where the main path ends, there are toilets next to the viewing point. Right, has anyone got any questions before we start?

listening_parts.title: You will hear two students, Maya and Tom, discussing their project on food waste with their tutor.
listening_parts.text: Tutor: So, Maya and Tom, how's the food waste project going? Maya: Quite well, I think. As you know, we decided to focus on the main canteen. Tutor: Remind me why you chose the canteen rather than the halls of residence. Tom: Well, at first we assumed the halls would produce more waste, but we couldn't get access to them. Then the canteen manager contacted the department. She'd read about our course and asked if any students could help her reduce the amount of food being thrown away, so that decided it. Tutor: That's a useful contact to have. And how did the first survey go? Maya: Not as well as we'd hoped. We had plenty of responses, over two hundred, and it only took about five minutes to fill in. The trouble was that some of the questions were confusing. For example, we asked how often people wasted food, and people understood that in very different ways. Tom: So we rewrote those questions for the second round, and gave examples. Tutor: Good. What about the waste data itself? Was there anything you didn't expect? Tom: We expected most of the waste to come from lunch, because that's the busiest meal. And it did, in total. But what surprised us was that breakfast produced more waste per person than any other meal. People take cereal and toast and then rush off to lectures. Tutor: Interesting. Have you thought about how you'll present all this? Maya: We were going to write it up as a standard report. Tutor: That's fine, but I think the canteen staff would find it easier to use if you also produced a short summary with charts, as well as the full report. Managers rarely have time to read forty pages. Maya: That makes sense. We could do a two-page version. Tutor: And what's your next step? Tom: We'd thought about interviewing the kitchen staff, but they're very busy at the moment, so we've agreed to spend a week weighing the waste from each meal ourselves, to check the figures the canteen gave us. Tutor: Sensible. Now, you've come up with a number of ideas for reducing waste. Which ones are you recommending? Maya: The first is to use smaller plates. The evidence from other universities is really strong, and the manager has already ordered them, so there's no reason to wait. We'll recommend introducing them straight away. Tom: Then there's the idea of a daily menu vote, where students choose the next day's dishes online. We like it, but we don't know whether enough people would take part, so we'd want to run it for a month in one canteen before deciding. Maya: Discounted leftovers after seven in the evening was another suggestion. Unfortunately the manager told us that food safety rules don't allow cooked food to be kept and sold later, so that one's out. Tom: Posters showing how much food is wasted each week were popular in our survey, and they're cheap, so we'll recommend putting those up immediately. Maya: And finally, a composting scheme. It sounds good, but we're not sure how much of the waste is actually suitable for composting, so we'd like to try it with the kitchen waste only, for a trial period, and see what happens. Tutor: That all sounds very sensible.

listening_parts.title: You will hear part of a lecture about soundscape ecology.
listening_parts.text: Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about a relatively young field of research called soundscape ecology. Most ecologists study what they can see: they count plants or track animals. Soundscape ecologists study what they can hear. Their aim is to record and understand all of the sounds in a habitat, and to use those sounds as a way of measuring how healthy that habitat is. Soundscape ecologists usually divide the sounds they record into three groups. The first group, known as biophony, is made up of the sounds produced by living organisms: birds singing, insects calling, frogs croaking, even the clicking of shrimps. The second group, geophony, is the sound of the non-living environment, such as wind in the trees, running water and, on the coast, the waves. The third group is called anthrophony, and it covers the sounds that humans make. Road traffic is the obvious example, but in many quiet places the most common human sound is actually aircraft passing overhead. So how is this research done? Rather than sending people into the field to listen, researchers use small, weatherproof recorders which can be left in place for several months at a time. That produces an enormous amount of sound, far more than any person could listen to, so the recordings are analysed by software which picks out patterns, for example how busy the soundscape is at different times of day. Some of the most striking results have come from studies of coral reefs. A healthy reef is a noisy place, full of the crackle of shrimps and the calls of fish. A damaged reef, on the other hand, is much quieter. Researchers found that healthy reefs were consistently louder than damaged ones, and this difference matters, because young fish rely on sound to locate a reef when they are ready to settle. In one experiment, loudspeakers playing the sounds of a healthy reef were placed on damaged sections of reef, and the number of young fish arriving there almost doubled. Of course, the method has its limits. A recording can tell us that a species is present, and roughly how active it is, but it cannot tell us about the health of individual animals. For that, traditional observation is still needed. Nonetheless, sound gives us a cheap and continuous way of watching over habitats which are difficult or dangerous to visit, and I expect it to become a standard tool.

listening_parts.title: You will hear a woman phoning a trampoline park to book a birthday party.
listening_parts.text: Assistant: Jump Zone, Kelly speaking. Mother: Hi, I'd like to book a birthday party for my daughter. Assistant: Lovely. How old will she be? Mother: Seven. Assistant: And what date? Mother: Saturday the ninth of November. Assistant: Let me check. The morning is booked, but we have a slot at two o'clock. Mother: Two is fine. Assistant: How many children? Mother: About fifteen. Assistant: Our standard package covers up to twenty children and costs a hundred and eighty pounds. That includes an hour of jumping and forty-five minutes in the party room. Mother: What about food? Assistant: We provide pizza and drinks. If you want a cake, you'll need to bring your own. Mother: That's fine. Do the children need anything? Assistant: They must wear our special grip socks, which cost two pounds a pair, and every child needs a form signed by a parent. Mother: Can parents send the forms in advance? Assistant: Yes, they can complete them on our website. Mother: Great. Assistant: Could I have your name? Mother: Alison Greaves. G, R, E, A, V, E, S. Assistant: We'll need a deposit of fifty pounds to confirm.

listening_parts.title: You will hear a radio interview about a new city cycle hire scheme.
listening_parts.text: Presenter: Now, with me is Laura Kent, who manages the city's new cycle hire scheme, CityRide. Laura: Thanks. The scheme launches next Monday, with five hundred bikes at sixty docking stations across the city. Half of the bikes are electric, which should help people with the hills in the north of the city. Using the scheme is simple. You download our app, and you can unlock a bike by scanning a code on the handlebars. The first thirty minutes of every ride are free for members, and after that it costs one pound for each additional half hour. Annual membership is ninety pounds, but students pay half price. When you finish, you must return the bike to a docking station; if you leave it anywhere else, you'll be charged a fine of twenty pounds. Presenter: What about safety? Laura: Every bike has lights that come on automatically, and we strongly recommend wearing a helmet, although it isn't compulsory. We'll also be running free cycling lessons for adults at weekends. Presenter: Where will the stations be? Laura: The largest station is outside the central railway station, with fifty bikes. There are also stations at all three universities and at the main hospital. We did consider putting one at the airport, but it's too far out, so we decided against it. Presenter: And how will you know if the scheme is working? Laura: We'll judge it mainly by how many car journeys it replaces, which we'll measure through a user survey.

listening_parts.title: You will hear two engineering students, Lucy and Omar, discussing a design competition.
listening_parts.text: Lucy: Omar, the competition deadline is getting close. How's the water filter design coming along? Omar: The prototype works, but it's slower than we hoped. It takes about two hours to filter a litre. Lucy: The judges said the most important thing was cost, not speed, didn't they? Omar: That's right. They want something families can afford, so our target is under five dollars per filter. Lucy: And are we within that? Omar: Just. The most expensive part is the ceramic container. Lucy: I wonder if we could use a plastic bottle instead. Omar: I thought of that, but plastic can release chemicals in hot weather. Lucy: OK, we'll keep the ceramic. What did the tests show about the water quality? Omar: It removed almost all the bacteria, which is the main thing. Lucy: Brilliant. How are we presenting it to the judges? Omar: We have ten minutes, and they want a live demonstration, so we'll need to bring dirty water with us. Lucy: Let's go through the problems we had and what we did about each. The first was the sand clogging up. Omar: We solved that by adding a layer of gravel on top. Lucy: Then the bad taste. Omar: We added charcoal, which fixed it. Lucy: The container cracking? Omar: We switched to a thicker clay. Lucy: And the leaking lid? Omar: We fitted a rubber seal. Lucy: And finally, the instructions being confusing. Omar: We replaced the text with pictures, so they work in any language.

listening_parts.title: You will hear part of a lecture about the first balloon flights.
listening_parts.text: Lecturer: Today I'd like to talk about the first human flights, which were made not in aeroplanes but in balloons. The story begins in France in 1783 with two brothers, Joseph and Etienne Montgolfier, who ran a paper-making business. They noticed that heated air could lift light objects, and began experimenting with bags made of paper and cloth. The principle is simple. Hot air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so a large bag of hot air rises, rather as a cork rises in water. The Montgolfiers believed at first that the smoke itself was responsible, and they burned straw and wool to produce as much smoke as possible. Their first public demonstration took place in June 1783. In September, at the royal palace of Versailles, they sent up a balloon carrying three animals: a sheep, a duck and a rooster. The animals landed safely after about eight minutes, which reassured people that it was possible to survive high above the ground. The first free flight with people on board followed in November 1783, when two men flew over Paris for about twenty-five minutes. Only ten days later, a rival balloon filled with hydrogen, a gas much lighter than hot air, made its own flight. Hydrogen balloons could stay in the air far longer, but hydrogen is highly flammable, which made them dangerous. For most of the following century, balloons were used mainly for science and entertainment. Scientists used them to study the upper atmosphere, and during the siege of Paris in 1870 balloons carried letters and passengers out of the surrounded city. Modern hot-air ballooning became popular only in the 1960s, when new materials such as nylon and burners fuelled by propane made balloons cheaper and safer. Today most balloon flights are for tourism, especially in places with calm and predictable winds.

listening_parts.title: You will hear a woman phoning a cycle tour company to book a tour for her colleagues.
listening_parts.text: Agent: Good afternoon, Greenway Cycle Tours, Paul speaking. How can I help? Woman: Hello. I'm interested in one of your guided tours for a group from my office. Agent: Lovely. How many people would it be? Woman: There are twelve of us. Well, it was going to be twelve, but two people have dropped out, so ten. Agent: Ten, fine. And which tour were you thinking of? We have the river tour, the castle tour and the vineyard tour. Woman: The castle one sounds interesting, but some of my colleagues aren't very fit, and I've heard it's quite hilly. Agent: It is. The river tour is completely flat. Woman: Then the river tour, please. Agent: When would you like to go? Woman: We were thinking of a Friday in June. Agent: Let me check. The sixth is full, but the thirteenth is free. Woman: The thirteenth is perfect. Agent: The tour starts at ten, and it's about thirty kilometres in total, with a stop for lunch at a pub by the water. Woman: And what does it cost? Agent: It's forty-five pounds per person, which includes the bike and a helmet. Lunch is extra. Woman: OK. Do people need to bring anything? Agent: Just comfortable shoes and a waterproof jacket. We supply water bottles. Woman: Where do we meet? Agent: At our shop, which is on Mill Lane, opposite the station. Woman: Great. And could I have a contact number for the guide on the day? Agent: The guide will be Karen, and I'll text you her number the day before. Can I take your name? Woman: It's Susan Ashworth. A, S, H, W, O, R, T, H. Agent: Thank you, Ms Ashworth. I'll send you a confirmation email.

listening_parts.title: You will hear the manager of a new leisure centre talking to local residents.
listening_parts.text: Manager: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to hear about the new Westfield Leisure Centre, which opens next month. I know many of you have been waiting a long time for this. The project was delayed by almost a year. People often assume that was because of money, but in fact the funding was agreed early on. The delay happened because the builders discovered old mine tunnels under the site, and the foundations had to be redesigned. The centre has been designed with families in mind. The main pool is twenty-five metres long, and there's a separate learner pool. What we're most proud of, though, is the climbing wall, which is the tallest in the region. Opening hours will be from six in the morning until ten at night on weekdays. At weekends we'll open at eight, and close at the same time as on weekdays. Membership is available in several forms. We expected most people to choose monthly membership, but in fact the most popular option so far is the family pass, which covers two adults and up to three children. Parking has been a concern for some residents. There are only eighty spaces, so we're encouraging people to cycle, and we've installed covered racks for two hundred bicycles. Buses also stop right outside. Now let me tell you about some of the activities for different groups. For older residents, we'll run gentle exercise classes every weekday morning, and these will be free of charge for the first three months. For teenagers, the sports hall will be open on Friday nights with basketball and music, run by youth workers. Parents with babies can join our aqua classes, but these need to be booked online because spaces are limited. For people recovering from injuries, we'll offer sessions with a physiotherapist, which require a letter from your doctor. And finally, for local schools, we'll provide swimming lessons during the school day, and schools will receive a discount of thirty per cent.

listening_parts.title: You will hear two students, Leo and Priya, discussing their presentation on urban farming with their tutor.
listening_parts.text: Tutor: Come in, Leo and Priya. So, you're presenting on urban farming next week. How are you getting on? Leo: Pretty well. We chose the topic because Priya visited a rooftop farm in the city centre last summer. Priya: Yes, I'd read about vertical farms, but actually seeing the rooftop farm made me want to find out more. Tutor: Good. What do you see as the main benefit of urban farming? Leo: Well, people often say it reduces transport costs, and it does, a little. But the research we read suggests the main benefit is educational: it reconnects city people with where their food comes from. Tutor: Interesting. What was the hardest part of the research? Priya: Finding reliable figures. Lots of websites give numbers for how much food city farms produce, but they often don't say where the figures come from. We ended up relying on two academic studies. Tutor: Sensible. And how are you going to structure the presentation? Leo: We thought we'd start with a short video of the rooftop farm, but the file is too large for the classroom computer. So we'll begin with a photograph and a question for the audience instead. Tutor: That could work well. How long is it? Priya: We have fifteen minutes. We'd planned twenty, but we cut the section on history. Tutor: Now, you've looked at several types of urban farm. What did you conclude about each? Leo: Rooftop farms were the most successful in the studies we read, because they get plenty of sunlight, but they're expensive to set up, as buildings often need strengthening. Priya: Community gardens were different. They produce relatively little food, but they're excellent for bringing neighbours together. Leo: Vertical farms, the indoor ones with stacked shelves and artificial light, use very little water, but their energy costs are enormous. Priya: Then there are school gardens. Their main value is teaching children, and they cost almost nothing to run. Leo: And finally, farms on unused land, like old car parks. The problem there is that the land often isn't guaranteed; the owners can take it back for building at any time. Tutor: That's a nice range. I look forward to it.

listening_parts.title: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of preserving food in sealed containers.
listening_parts.text: Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about a technology that most of us use every day without thinking about it: the preservation of food in sealed containers. At the end of the eighteenth century, armies and navies faced a serious problem. Fresh food spoiled quickly, and soldiers on long campaigns often suffered from poor diets. In 1795 the French government offered a prize of twelve thousand francs to anyone who could find a reliable way of preserving food. The prize was eventually won by Nicolas Appert, a confectioner from Paris. Appert's method was to seal food inside glass bottles, close them with cork, and then heat the bottles in boiling water. He did not know why the method worked. That explanation came decades later, when Louis Pasteur showed that heat kills the microorganisms that cause food to decay. Glass had one obvious weakness: it broke easily. In 1810 an Englishman, Peter Durand, was granted a patent for preserving food in containers made of tin-coated iron, and within a few years a factory in London was supplying canned food to the Royal Navy. Early cans were heavy and extremely difficult to open. The instructions on some of them advised using a hammer and chisel. Remarkably, a practical can opener was not invented until almost fifty years after the first cans appeared. Canned food changed the way people ate. It allowed explorers to travel for years at a time, and by the end of the nineteenth century it had made fruit, vegetables and fish available all year round in cities far from where they were produced. There were problems, however. Some early cans were sealed with lead solder, which could contaminate the food, and it took many years before safer methods were adopted. Today most cans are made of steel or aluminium, and they are among the most widely recycled packaging materials in the world.

listening_parts.title: You will hear a man phoning a festival office to volunteer.
listening_parts.text: Coordinator: Hello, Brookfield Summer Festival volunteers' office. Man: Hi, I saw your advert for volunteers and I'd like to sign up. Coordinator: Great. Let me take some details. What's your full name? Man: Daniel Okafor. That's O, K, A, F, O, R. Coordinator: Thanks. And how old are you, Daniel? We need volunteers to be over eighteen. Man: I'm twenty-three. Coordinator: Lovely. What's your address? Man: Flat 4, 27 Seaton Road. Coordinator: And which area would you like to work in? We need people for car parking, the information tent and litter collection. Man: I'd prefer the information tent. I'm good with people. Coordinator: Perfect. The festival runs from Thursday to Sunday. Which days can you do? Man: I work on Thursdays, so Friday to Sunday. Coordinator: That's fine. Shifts are six hours long. Have you volunteered before? Man: Yes, I helped at a marathon last year. Coordinator: Excellent. All volunteers get a free T-shirt. What size are you? Man: Large, please. Coordinator: And do you have any dietary requirements? We provide meals for volunteers. Man: I'm vegetarian. Coordinator: Noted. Finally, you'll need to attend a training session. There's one on the twelfth of July and another on the nineteenth. Man: The twelfth is better for me. Coordinator: Great. It's at the town hall at seven in the evening.

listening_parts.title: You will hear an instructor welcoming a group to an activity centre.
listening_parts.text: Instructor: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Ashcombe Activity Centre. I'm Jo, and I'll be looking after you this week. Before we start, a few things about the centre. It was originally built as a farm school in the nineteen sixties. Most people think it was a hospital, because of the long corridors, but it was always used for education. The centre is run by a charity, and most of our instructors are volunteers, although I'm one of the few paid staff. During your stay, the most important rule is about the lake. You may be keen to swim, but nobody may go in the water without an instructor, even strong swimmers. Meals are served at set times. Breakfast is at half past seven, and please don't be late, because the kitchen closes at half past eight. If you have a problem during the night, don't go to the office; call the number on your door, and the duty instructor will come to you. Now, look at the plan of the main building. You come in through the main entrance at the bottom, and reception is on your left. You can leave your valuables in the lockers, in the first room on your right as you come in. Carry on along the main corridor. The climbing wall is in the room on your left just after the cross corridor, opposite the café. At the end of the building, the equipment store is the last room on your right, at the far end, and that's where you'll collect helmets and life jackets. The changing rooms are in the room on your left just before the cross corridor, next to reception. And if it rains in the evening, the games room is the last room on your left, at the far end, with table tennis and board games.

listening_parts.title: You will hear two students, Hannah and Marcus, discussing a report on their museum work placement.
listening_parts.text: Hannah: Hi Marcus. Have you got a minute to talk about our museum placement report? Marcus: Sure. How did you find the placement overall? Hannah: I really enjoyed it. I thought I'd spend most of my time in the archives, but actually I was mainly working with visitors, which I preferred. Marcus: Same for me. The thing that surprised me most was how few staff there are. The museum relies on just six full-time employees. Hannah: I know. And the director told me their biggest challenge isn't money, it's attracting teenagers, who hardly ever visit. Marcus: That's what our report should focus on, then. What did you think of the new digital guide? Hannah: The technology was impressive, but visitors found the headphones uncomfortable, so a lot of them gave up after ten minutes. Marcus: That's a good point to include. Now, our tutor wants the report by the end of the month. Should we aim for five thousand words? Hannah: She said four thousand is the minimum, so let's aim for about four and a half thousand. Marcus: OK. Let's divide up the work. Who's going to write the introduction? Hannah: I'll do that, since I've already drafted some notes. Marcus: Fine. I'll collect the visitor statistics; I've got the contact at the museum. Hannah: What about the interviews with staff? There are quite a lot. Marcus: Let's share those; you take the curators and I'll take the education team. Hannah: Good. And the recommendations? Marcus: You're better at that kind of thing. You write them and I'll check them. Hannah: OK. Then the photographs. Marcus: I took most of them, so I'll choose which ones to use.

listening_parts.title: You will hear part of a lecture about the axolotl.
listening_parts.text: Lecturer: This morning I'd like to introduce you to one of the most studied animals in biology: the axolotl, a salamander that comes from a single lake system near Mexico City. Axolotls are unusual in several ways. Most salamanders begin life in water, breathing through gills, and later change into land-living adults with lungs. Axolotls, however, usually never complete this change. They keep their feathery external gills and remain in the water throughout their lives, a condition known as neoteny. They can nevertheless reproduce, just like the adults of other species. What has made axolotls famous in laboratories is their power of regeneration. If an axolotl loses a leg, it can grow a complete new one, including bones, muscles and nerves, usually within a few weeks, and without leaving a scar. Even more remarkably, they can repair damage to the spinal cord, and even to parts of the heart and brain. How do they do it? After an injury, cells at the wound form a structure called a blastema, a mass of cells that can develop into the different tissues needed to rebuild the missing part. Researchers hope that understanding this process may one day help doctors to improve healing in humans, although that goal is still a long way off. Axolotls also have a very large genome, around ten times the size of the human genome, which made it difficult for scientists to decode. It was fully sequenced only in 2018. Sadly, while axolotls are common in laboratories and as pets, they are critically endangered in the wild. Their only natural habitat, the canals of Xochimilco, has been damaged by pollution and the growth of the city, and introduced fish such as carp and tilapia eat their eggs and young. Conservation projects now work with local farmers to create refuges where the water is filtered and protected.

listening_parts.title: You will hear a woman phoning a pet care service to arrange for someone to look after her cat.
listening_parts.text: Assistant: Happy Paws Pet Care, this is Tom. Woman: Hello, I'm going away next month and I need someone to look after my cat. Assistant: Of course. Can I start with your name? Woman: Yes, it's Rachel Lindqvist. That's L, I, N, D, Q, V, I, S, T. Assistant: Thank you. And your address? Woman: 15 Orchard Close, in Fenwick. Assistant: Great, that's within our area. What's your cat's name? Woman: She's called Pepper. Assistant: How old is she? Woman: She's nine. Actually, no, she had her birthday in May, so she's ten now. Assistant: Ten. And the dates you need? Woman: From the third to the seventeenth of August. Assistant: Two weeks. We usually visit twice a day. Would that suit you? Woman: She's quite independent, so once a day would be enough. Assistant: Once a day, then, in the morning or the evening? Woman: The evening, please. That's when she eats. Assistant: Does she need any medicine? Woman: Yes, she takes a tablet for her heart, crushed into her food. Assistant: I'll make a note. Any other instructions? Woman: Please could you water my plants as well? Assistant: Certainly, there's no extra charge for that. How would you like to leave the key? Woman: I'll leave it with my neighbour at number 17. Assistant: Perfect. Our rate is twelve pounds per visit. Woman: That's fine.

listening_parts.title: You will hear a radio interview with the organiser of a food festival.
listening_parts.text: Presenter: And now for our guest, Maria Costa, who's organising this year's Harbourside Food Festival. Maria: Thanks for having me. This is the festival's tenth year. It started as a small market with just a dozen stalls, and this year we'll have over a hundred and twenty. Presenter: That's a big change. What's new this year? Maria: Well, we've always had cookery demonstrations, and the children's area has been running for years. The new thing is a zero-waste zone, where all the food is served without any plastic. Presenter: Is the festival free? Maria: Entry is free on Friday, but on Saturday and Sunday there's a small charge of five pounds, which goes to the lifeboat charity. Presenter: And what's the best way to get there? Maria: Please don't drive; there'll be no parking near the harbour. We're running a free boat service from the marina, which is the most relaxing way to arrive. Presenter: What about the weather?
